# Human vs. LLM Approaches: A Critical Deep Dive --- ## Part 1: How a Human Writer Might Approach This Piece A human writer sitting down to write "They fucked with the wrong babysitter" would probably start from a very different place than an LLM. Here's what that might look like. ### Starting from Feeling, Not Structure A human writer likely has a *feeling* first. Maybe they were a babysitter once. Maybe they've felt underestimated. Maybe they read a true crime story about a nanny who fought back and it stuck with them. Maybe they're just angry about something and this is the vessel. The prompt is a *spark*, not a blueprint. The story grows out of a personal itch, a memory, a face they can't forget. The eight-chapter structure and the plot beats would come *after* — and reluctantly, because structure is a cage and humans chafe against cages. An LLM starts with the structure and works backward to feeling. That's a fundamental inversion. Structure is scaffolding; feeling is the building. You can't scaffold your way into a building that was never designed. ### Messiness Is Human Human writers write messy first drafts. They write scenes that don't fit. They write characters who surprise them. They write dialogue that reveals something they didn't know they knew. They follow tangents. They cut things they love. They have bad ideas and follow them anyway because something in their gut says *there's something here*. They wake up at 3 a.m. with a line of dialogue and write it on their phone. An LLM writes clean, coherent, well-structured prose on the first pass. That cleanliness is a tell. Real stories have seams. Real characters have contradictions that don't resolve. Real scenes sometimes just *sit there* because they're true to life. An LLM smooths all of that out, and smoothness reads as fake. ### Specificity Over Generality A human writer knows that the devil is in the details — and that those details are almost always *wrong* in an LLM draft. A human might write about a specific brand of duct tape that doesn't stick well, or the smell of a particular cleaning product, or the way a certain model of car sounds when it starts. They know because they've lived it. They might get it wrong, but they'll get it *wrong specifically*. An LLM will write "duct tape" and "cleaning product" and "car" and think it's done. Specificity isn't just flavor. It's *evidence of a mind that has been in the world*. It signals to the reader: *this person knows something*. An LLM's generic details signal the opposite: *this person is guessing*. ### Voice Is Not Style A human writer's voice comes from their limitations, their obsessions, their particular way of seeing. It's not "sparse" or "lyrical" or "pulpy" — those are marketing categories. Voice is the thing that makes you recognize a page of a favorite author's work without seeing the name. It's the way they use commas. It's the jokes they tell. It's the things they refuse to describe. An LLM's voice is always *performed*. It's a costume. It can be a very good costume — but you can always see the seams if you look. An LLM writing "pulp" is doing an impression of pulp. A human writing pulp is *writing pulp* because that's the only way they know how to say what they need to say. ### Letting the Reader Do Work Humans trust the reader more than LLMs do. A human writer might cut the scene where the babysitter explains her past. They might just show her flinching at a loud noise and let the reader wonder. They might end a chapter on a silence. They might let a villain be a person instead of a symbol. LLMs tend to over-explain. They want to make sure the reader *gets it*. That impulse is the enemy of good writing. A human writer knows that the reader's imagination is more powerful than anything on the page, and they leave room for it. ### The Human Relationship to Violence A human writing violence usually has *feelings* about violence. They might be repulsed by it. They might be fascinated by it. They might have seen it up close. They might be writing through trauma or trying to understand something they fear. That ambivalence — or obsession, or horror — leaks into the prose. The violence has *weight* because the writer feels its weight. An LLM writing violence tends to be either sanitized or stylized. It's "brutal but tasteful" — which is a contradiction that a human would never write, because a human either goes there or doesn't. "Brutal but tasteful" is the LLM's way of signaling *I know this is edgy* while making sure nobody is actually disturbed. That's cowardice dressed as craft. ### The Human Relationship to Endings Humans don't always tie things up. They leave threads hanging because life leaves threads hanging. They let endings be ambiguous because meaning is ambiguous. They know that a story doesn't end — it just stops, and the reader carries the rest. An LLM wants closure. It wants the bow on the box. It wants to reassure the reader that everything is fine. That impulse is often wrong for the story. Sometimes the most human ending is the one that hurts — the one that leaves a scar instead of a lesson. --- ## Part 2: Telltale LLM Approaches That Would Hurt This Piece ### 1. Writing "Safely" LLMs are trained to avoid offense, avoid discomfort, avoid anything that might make a reader feel bad. For a revenge story about a woman hunting and killing men, this is a *disaster*. The story needs to be uncomfortable. It needs to have teeth. It needs to make the reader complicit in violence they might not want to endorse. An LLM will soften every edge. It will make the villains cartoonishly evil so the violence is "justified." It will make Meg sad about killing people, as if guilt is required to make violence palatable. It will avoid the messy truth: sometimes killing feels good, or feels like nothing, or feels like the only thing left. **How this would show up in the piece:** Meg would hesitate before every kill. She would feel bad. She would not enjoy it. The narration would emphasize the *tragedy* of the violence rather than its necessity or its intimacy. The villains would be dehumanized in ways that make it easy to root for their deaths, which actually undermines the story — because the whole point is that Meg is a monster to them, and you don't get to be a monster to cartoons. ### 2. Wrapping Things Up with a Bow LLMs love closure. They love the final scene where everything is explained and everyone is okay. For this story, that impulse is death. "They fucked with the wrong babysitter" is not a story about healing. It's a story about *the aftermath of violence* — the way it marks you, the way it doesn't leave. An LLM would end with Meg and Lily safe, their bond affirmed, the future bright. That's a lie. A human writer would end with something more complicated: Meg can't sleep, or she lies to the police, or she looks at Lily and sees the child she lost before, or she knows this isn't over — not because the cartel will come back, but because *she* is not the person who gets to be okay. **How this would show up:** The final chapter would be a warm resolution. Meg would be offered a job, she'd take it, and the story would imply she's found a new purpose. The stuffed rabbit would be a symbol of hope. The knife would be "finally out of her belt." All of this is too clean. ### 3. Writing Impressively at the Expense of Readability LLMs have a tendency to show off. They use words like "limned" and "myriad" and "susurrus." They write sentences that are technically grammatical but rhythmically dead. They reach for literary flourishes when bluntness would serve better. For pulp, this is fatal. Pulp is not about being impressive. It's about being *propulsive*. It's about making the reader turn the page. An LLM writing pulp is like a poet writing a comic book — they might pull it off, but they'll probably be missing the point. **How this would show up:** Purple descriptions of violence. Metaphors that don't earn their keep. Sentences that are too long. A voice that sounds like it's wearing a fedora. The prose would call attention to itself when it should disappear. ### 4. Over-Explaining Character and Motivation LLMs can't trust the reader. They have to make sure you understand that Meg is Ex-Military and That Means Something. They have to explain that Lily is Scared But Brave. They have to tell you that Ruiz is A Bad Man. This kind of over-explanation is the death of reader engagement. A human writer lets you *infer*. They let the villain be charming. They let Meg be a little scary. They let Lily be a real kid, not a symbol. **How this would show up:** Flashbacks to Meg's military past. A scene where someone explains her backstory in dialogue. Lily being precocious in a way that makes her sympathetic. Ruiz giving a monologue about his motivations. All of this is the LLM trying to make sure you're following along. ### 5. Avoiding Moral Ambiguity LLMs want you to like the protagonist. They want you to approve of her. They're uncomfortable with the idea that Meg might not be a "good person." They'll soften her. They'll make her kills necessary and clean. They'll avoid the fact that Meg is, in many ways, worse than the men she's hunting — because she's better at it. A human writer would lean into the discomfort. Meg is not a hero. She's a woman with a particular set of skills and nothing left to lose. She might be a monster. She might be exactly what she was trained to be. The reader should be *unsettled* by their identification with her, not comforted. **How this would show up:** Moments of moral clarity where Meg realizes she's "doing the right thing." Kills that are clearly justified. A villain who "deserves it." All of this robs the story of its pulp energy — which comes from the fact that violence is never clean, never fully justified, and never leaves anyone untouched. ### 6. Formulaic Pacing LLMs follow structures too closely. The beat sheet becomes a straitjacket. Every chapter hits its marks: setup, inciting incident, escalation, midpoint, climax, resolution. There's no room for a chapter to just *breathe*. There's no room for a weird tangent. There's no room for a scene that doesn't "advance the plot" but does deepen the story. **How this would show up:** Chapter 3 would be "the hunt begins." Chapter 4 would be "the first kill." Chapter 5 would be "the child's perspective." Every chapter would end on a cliffhanger. There would be no digressions, no detours, no surprises. The structure would be visible, and visibility is death for pulp. ### 7. Sterile Dialogue LLMs write dialogue that sounds like it's from a screenplay — efficient, on-the-nose, and too clever. Characters say exactly what they mean. They make jokes that are too funny. They give speeches that are too well-structured. Real dialogue is messy. People interrupt. They change subjects. They say things that don't mean anything. They say things they don't mean. **How this would show up:** Meg having a perfect one-liner before each kill. Lily saying something wise beyond her years. Ruiz being arch and menacing. A perfect exchange between Meg and Boone that reveals everything the reader needs to know. Dialogue that sounds written rather than spoken. --- ## Part 3: Deep Dive Critique of the Intention & Plan ### The Intention The intention section is clean, coherent, and well-organized. It is also *deeply LLM-brained*. Let's break down why. **"Third-person limited, primarily anchored to Meg"** — This is a safe, standard choice. It's the POV most LLMs default to because it's easy to manage. But a human writer might choose first person to get closer to Meg's voice, or omniscient to create distance and irony, or even second person for a visceral feel. The choice here is not wrong, but it is *default* — and defaults should always be examined. **"Pulp energy: short paragraphs, punchy sentences"** — This is telling, not showing. It's a style instruction, not a style. What does "pulp energy" actually mean in practice? It means different things to different writers. The intention is describing a vibe, not a technique. A human writer would have a more specific sense of the voice — maybe they'd describe it as "Elmore Leonard by way of a slasher movie" or "the prose equivalent of a broken nose." Instead, we get aesthetic adjectives that don't do much work. **"Dark humor comes mainly from villain panic"** — This is a good instinct, but it's also a safe one. It positions the villains as the butt of the joke, which lets the reader off the hook. The darker, more human choice would be to find humor in Meg too — in her exhaustion, her stubbornness, the absurdity of what she's doing. Humor that comes *only* from the villains' fear is a way of keeping Meg above it all. That's an LLM's moral hierarchy showing. **"Restraint on exposition"** — Good instinct. But the plan doesn't really follow through on it. Chapter 3 has Boone "give her a lead." That's an exposition delivery mechanism. Chapter 4 has Vince "interrogate" — more exposition. Chapter 8 has "Meg gives her statement and doesn't mention most of what she did" — which is both exposition and a way of closing the loop. The intention says "restraint," but the plan finds new ways to explain things. **"Violence is justified but never celebrated. Meg is not gleeful. She is tired, wounded, and relentless."** — This is the most LLM-ish line in the whole document. It's a moral instruction to the reader. It's saying: *Don't worry, you're allowed to enjoy this because Meg isn't enjoying it.* That's a cop-out. A human writer would let Meg's feelings about violence be complicated, contradictory, or even absent. Maybe she *does* feel something like satisfaction. Maybe she feels nothing. Maybe she feels everything and can't sort it out. The instruction "never celebrated" is a way of keeping the story safe. **"The suburban setting should feel invaded and defamiliarized"** — This is a nice literary touch, but it's also a very "workshop" idea. It's the kind of observation that sounds smart in a synopsis but doesn't necessarily translate to the page. A human writer might just describe the setting and let the reader feel the wrongness. The instruction to "defamiliarize" is the LLM's way of making sure the prose is *doing something meaningful*. **"Violence is justified but never celebrated"** (repeated in the table) — Repetition is an LLM tell. It doesn't trust you to remember. It also signals anxiety. The writer (or the model) is worried about the violence being misread, so they keep saying it's okay. A human writer wouldn't need to reassure you. They'd just write it and let you feel however you feel. ### The Chapter Plan The chapter plan is where the LLM-ness really shows. Let's go chapter by chapter. **Chapter 1 — "The Girl Who Was Supposed to Die"** The title is pulp-y, which is good. But the content is a checklist of "establishing" beats: establish Meg and Lily's relationship, establish Meg's past via hints, establish Lily's father as a prosecutor, establish the villain threat. It's all setup. There's no scene here — just a series of informational beats. A human writer would write a *scene*. Maybe it's bath time. Maybe it's a fight about bedtime. Maybe it's Meg teaching Lily something. The information would come through *action*, not through "hints" and "we see." The phrase "we see hints of Meg's past" is a film treatment, not a short story. Also, "Lily asks Meg about the scar on her forearm and Meg deflects with a joke" — this is exactly the kind of "hint" that LLMs love. It's a plant. It's a setup. It's not a real interaction. A human writer might have Meg lie about the scar, or not notice the question, or give a true answer that means nothing to Lily and everything to the reader. **Chapter 2 — "Bad Night for Bad Men"** This chapter is where the premise happens, but the plan describes it in purely functional terms: the break-in, the fight, the capture, the fire. There's no *experience* here. What does it feel like to have your arm broken? To watch a child be taken? To crawl across a floor while the house burns? The plan doesn't say. It just says the beats happen. "Ruiz tells Meg this isn't personal" — this is a villain cliché. It's the line every henchman says in every action movie. A human writer would either subvert it (Ruiz says something weirder, or nothing at all) or earn it (make it *actually* personal, in a way that surprises both Meg and the reader). "He has one of his men break her arm for good measure" — this is brutal, but it's also convenient. It gives Meg a handicap that she'll overcome. It's a narrative device, not a character choice. A human writer might have Ruiz do something more specific and less cinematic — something petty, or weird, or unsettling. **Chapter 3 — "The Wrong Babysitter"** "Meg escapes the fire — barely, painfully, with a broken arm and a kitchen knife." This is action movie logic. A human writer would give us the *experience* of escaping the fire. The heat. The smoke. The fear. The broken arm making everything worse. The plan is more interested in the outcome than the process. "She calls the one number she swore she'd never call — an old Marine contact named Boone" — this is a plot device. It's a way to get information. It's also a cliché (the "one person she swore she'd never call"). A human writer would either cut this entirely (Meg figures it out herself) or make it *cost* her something (Boone asks for something in return, or their conversation is charged with history, or she has to lie). **"Villain POV coda: Marco checks in on the guard left behind. No answer. He tells himself it's nothing."** — This is a POV shift for the sake of tension. It's a technique, not a choice. And "He tells himself it's nothing" is a cliché. A human writer would either commit to the villain POV fully (write a real scene from Marco's perspective) or cut it. **Chapter 4 — "Nothing to Lose"** "Meg arrives at the stash house and takes out two more of the crew — Diego and Vince. The kills are quick and ugly." — Again, this is functional. It describes what happens, not *how it feels* or *what it looks like*. "Quick and ugly" is a summary, not a scene. A human writer would write the kills. They would make them specific. They would make them *mean* something. "She interrogates Vince before he dies and learns the plan" — interrogations are always an exposition delivery mechanism. A human writer might have Meg learn the plan from a phone she steals, or from a piece of paper, or from something she overhears. Anything would be less cliché. **Chapter 5 — "Little Girl Lost"** "Lily is scared but not broken. She is smart — she's been counting doors, watching guards, waiting for a chance." — This is the LLM ideal of a child character: smart, capable, not a burden. It's also a cop-out. Real children in traumatic situations are not usually smart and capable. They're often regressed, or numb, or confused, or making things worse without meaning to. A human writer might give Lily a *less flattering* experience — maybe she wets the bed, or she cries until she can't breathe, or she disassociates, or she trusts the wrong person. Making her "smart" is a way of making her easier to root for, and easier to write. **"She thinks about Meg. She doesn't know if Meg is alive."** — This is fine, but it's generic. What does she *think* about Meg? A specific memory? A smell? A joke Meg told her? A human writer would give us a concrete detail, not a general sentiment. **Villain POV section:** "Ruiz is on the phone with his bosses. The crew is late checking in. Marco hasn't called back. He is beginning to feel something he hasn't felt in years — the sense that he is being hunted." — This is the LLM's idea of villain psychology. It's too neat. It's too direct. A human writer might have Ruiz be *annoyed* rather than frightened, or *contemptuous* of the worry, or *bored*. The fear could come later, and it could be more specific — not "the sense that he is being hunted" but something physical, like a twitch in his eye, or a sudden need to check the locks, or a memory of a dog he saw die when he was a boy. **Chapter 6 — "The House of the Dead"** "Meg infiltrates the boatyard. It's the longest, bloodiest chapter. She uses the environment — boats, chains, fuel, a flare gun — and takes out the remaining guards one by one." — This is a list of props, not a sequence. A human writer would *stage* this. They would think about the geography of the boatyard. They would think about the order of kills. They would think about what goes wrong. "She finds Marco and kills him in a way that makes the remaining men want to run." — This is a great idea, but it's not specific. *What* does she do? A human writer would know. They would have figured it out before writing the plan, or they would figure it out in the writing. The plan is content to gesture at it. **Chapter 7 — "Kill Them All"** "Ruiz tries to negotiate, then threatens, then pleads." — This is a very routine sequence of villain reactions. A human writer might have Ruiz do something weirder — maybe he's calm the whole time, or maybe he's already gone, or maybe he tries to bond with Meg over their shared experience of violence. The negotiation-threat-plea arc is the default, and defaults are boring. "Meg doesn't monologue. She waits for her opening — and takes it." — This is good. But it's also the *expected* choice for a "strong female character." A human writer might subvert it — maybe Meg *does* monologue, and it's not cool, it's just a person talking because they're exhausted and they want the man to know why he's dying. Or maybe she doesn't say anything at all, and the silence is more terrifying. **Chapter 8 — "What Comes After"** "Police, EMTs, the FBI. Lily's father arrives, shattered and grateful. Meg gives her statement and doesn't mention most of what she did." — This is the beginning of an LLM ending. Everyone shows up. Everything is resolved. The machinery of society takes over. It's safe. "She sits in a hospital bed with her arm in a cast while Lily sleeps in the chair beside her." — This is a nice image, but it's also a *soft* one. It's designed to make you feel warm. A human writer might give us something harder — Meg alone in a room, or Lily not sleeping, or the father looking at Meg with something other than gratitude. "Meg and Lily on a bench outside the hospital at dawn. Lily asks if Meg will still babysit her. Meg says yes." — This is the bow. This is the warm resolution. It's exactly what an LLM would write. A human writer might leave it unresolved — maybe Meg doesn't answer, or maybe Lily doesn't ask, or maybe they just sit together and the silence is enough. "the implication that the past will come for her again, and that next time, she'll be ready" — This is a sequel hook. It's also a way of making the ending feel "open" while actually being totally closed. It's the LLM's version of ambiguity: a clear statement that things will continue, but not in a way that disrupts the current resolution. A human writer's ambiguity would be messier — maybe Meg doesn't know if she'll be ready, or doesn't care, or is already thinking about something else. --- ## Part 4: Brainstorming Ways to Make It More Human ### Voice and Prose - **Write in first person.** Meg's voice, her cadence, her particular way of seeing. This immediately makes the story less generic and more specific. It also forces you to commit to a consciousness, which is where humanity lives. - **Or write in close third with a very specific texture.** Not just "limited" but *idiosyncratic*. Meg notices things other people wouldn't. She has opinions about things that don't matter. She has blind spots. - **Use sentence fragments.** Real thoughts aren't complete sentences. Real prose doesn't have to be either. - **Cut adjectives.** Replace them with verbs. "She moved through the dark" is better than "She moved quietly through the dark." Let the reader infer. - **Read it aloud.** If you can't read it aloud without stumbling, it's not human prose. ### Character - **Make Meg less competent.** She's good, but she's not perfect. She makes mistakes. She gets lucky. She has a moment where she almost gives up. She has a moment where she's not sure why she's doing this. - **Make Meg less likable.** She's not a hero. She's a person who has done terrible things and will do them again. Let the reader feel uneasy about rooting for her. - **Make Lily less smart.** She's seven. She's scared. She doesn't understand what's happening. She might say something that makes things worse. She might not be brave. She might just be a kid. - **Make the villains more human.** Ruiz isn't a monster. He's a professional. He has a family. He has a code. He doesn't want to hurt children — but he will if he has to. His humanity is what makes him terrifying, because it means he *chose* this. - **Give the villains a moment of connection with Meg.** Maybe Marco, before he dies, recognizes something in her. Maybe Ruiz, in the final confrontation, sees himself in her. Maybe one of them tries to *help* her, or apologize, or explain. The complexity makes the violence mean more. ### Plot and Structure - **Cut the Boone phone call.** It's a device. Replace it with something more human — Meg finding a receipt in Lily's pocket, or a name written on a hand, or a phone left behind by one of the dead men. - **Cut the interrogation.** Let Meg figure things out from evidence, not from a dying man's confession. - **Let something go wrong.** Not a small thing — a big thing. Meg gets the wrong house. She kills the wrong person. She gets captured. She gets Lily back and then loses her again. The plan should be disrupted by reality. - **Cut the resolution.** Don't give us the hospital scene. Don't give us the bench at dawn. End on the boatyard, or end on the road, or end on Meg looking at her hands and not recognizing them. End before the bow. - **Consider a nonlinear structure.** Maybe the story starts with Meg in the hospital and works backward. Maybe it alternates between the night of the kidnapping and the night of the revenge. Nonlinear structure is less "clean" but more human. - **Let the story be shorter or longer than 8 chapters.** The 8-chapter structure is a constraint, but it's not a law. A human writer might find that the story wants to be 6 chapters, or 11. The structure should serve the story, not the other way around. ### Violence - **Make the violence specific.** Not "she killed him" but *how*. What did it sound like? What did it smell like? What did Meg feel? What did she *not* feel? - **Make the violence consequential.** Meg gets hurt. She gets tired. She gets sick. She gets slower. The violence takes something from her, physically and psychologically. - **Make at least one kill feel bad.** Not in a moralizing way — in a human way. Maybe the person begs. Maybe they remind her of someone. Maybe she hesitates and it costs her. Maybe she doesn't hesitate and that costs her more. - **Let the violence be funny.** Real violence is often absurd. A body falls wrong. A gun jams. Someone says something stupid as they die. Lean into the absurdity. It doesn't make the violence less real — it makes it more real. - **Don't describe every kill.** Sometimes the most powerful choice is to cut away. Let the reader imagine what Meg did. Their imagination is worse than anything you can write. ### Dialogue - **Make it messier.** Characters interrupt. They misunderstand. They change the subject. They say things that don't matter. - **Cut the one-liners.** Meg doesn't need to be cool. She's not in a movie. She's in a nightmare. - **Let silence do work.** Not every moment needs dialogue. Sometimes the absence of speech is more powerful. - **Give the villains personality.** Not just "menacing" — specific. One of them is a talker. One of them is quiet. One of them is scared. One of them is bored. Their dialogue should reflect that. ### Theme - **Don't moralize.** Let the reader decide what the story means. If you have to tell them, you haven't written it. - **Let the theme emerge from the action.** The story is about protective rage, pasts that won't stay buried, found family — but none of those things should be *stated*. They should be *felt*. - **Undercut the theme.** Maybe Meg's protective rage isn't noble. Maybe it's just rage. Maybe the found family is a projection. Maybe the past doesn't stay buried because Meg doesn't *want* it buried. Complexity is human. ### Revision - **Write a shitty first draft.** Don't try to make it good. Try to make it *true*. Fix it later. - **Cut 10% of the words.** Then cut 10% more. LLMs overwrite. Humans overwrite too. The difference is that humans can feel when something is too long. - **Read other pulp.** Read Elmore Leonard. Read Jim Thompson. Read Megan Abbott. Read Chester Himes. See how they do it. Steal what works. - **Read it to someone.** Watch their face. If they're bored, cut. If they're confused, clarify. If they're moved, leave it alone. - **Let it sit.** Put it in a drawer for a week. Come back. You'll see things you missed. ### Specific Fixes for the Plan | Plan Element | LLM Tic | Human Alternative | |---|---|---| | Meg's backstory revealed through hints | Plant-and-payoff | Revealed through action, contradiction, or not at all | | Boone phone call | Plot device | Cut, or make it cost something | | Interrogation for info | Exposition delivery | Let Meg infer from evidence | | Villain POV codas | Tension technique | Full commitment or cut | | Lily is smart and brave | Idealized child | Let her be scared, regressed, imperfect | | Ruiz negotiates-threatens-pleads | Default villain arc | Subvert it, or make it specific | | Hospital resolution | Bow on the box | End earlier, harder, messier | | Sequel hook | Fake ambiguity | Real ambiguity — no answer, just a moment | | "Violence is justified but never celebrated" | Moral instruction | Let the reader feel however they feel | | "The suburban setting should feel invaded" | Workshop abstraction | Just describe it. Let it be what it is. | --- ## Part 5: Final Thoughts The fundamental problem with the current plan is that it's *too good*. It's too organized. Too intentional. Too aware of its own themes. Human stories are messier than that. They're written by people who are trying to figure something out, not people who already know what they think. If you want to make this piece more human, you have to *let it be bad*. You have to let it be weird. You have to let it surprise you. You have to stop trying to control it and start trying to *listen* to it. That's the hardest thing for an LLM to do — and the most important thing for a human writer to remember.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention ## Core Premise **Meg Sawyer** is a dishonorably discharged Marine Raider who now works as a nanny in suburban San Diego. She is babysitting seven-year-old **Lily Chen** when a cartel crew breaks in to kidnap the girl — leverage to force her prosecutor father to drop charges against a cartel boss. They beat Meg, break her arm, take Lily, and burn the house down around her. They should have made sure. What follows is one night of ugly, exhausted, unglamorous violence as Meg crawls out of the fire and hunts them down, one at a time, until she gets Lily back. The cartel fucked with the wrong babysitter. That's the story. Everything else is decoration. ## Voice & Style - **First person, past tense, Meg's voice.** Not "limited third." *Her*. Her cadence, her opinions, her blind spots, her way of noticing things and not noticing others. First person is harder to fake than third, which is exactly why it's the right choice here. - **Pulp energy through *rhythm*, not adjectives.** Short sentences. Fragments. Repetition. A voice that moves because it doesn't have time to stop. Think Elmore Leonard's economy, not a movie trailer's punch. - **Dark humor comes from *Meg*, not just the villains.** She's tired. She's in pain. She's doing something absurd. She knows it. That self-awareness is what makes her human — and it's what keeps the story from being a revenge fantasy. - **Emotional core: guilt, exhaustion, and a stubbornness that isn't noble.** Meg failed to save a child before. She's not doing this because she's good. She's doing it because she can't do anything else. The reader should feel that, not be told it. - **No moral instruction.** The story doesn't tell you how to feel about Meg or about violence. It just shows you. You decide. - **Restraint on exposition.** Meg's past comes out sideways — a flinch, a joke, a lie, a scar she doesn't explain. The reader assembles her from fragments. Some fragments don't fit. That's fine. - **Avoid:** purple prose, one-liners, workshop abstractions ("defamiliarize the suburban setting"), moralizing, neat resolutions, over-explaining, and the impulse to make Meg *likable*. ## Tone Targets - *Jack Reacher* by way of *Winter's Bone* — grounded, regional, unromantic. Violence is quick and mostly happens off the page or in the corner of the eye. - The suburban setting is *not* defamiliarized. It's just a place. That's the point. Bad things happen in nice neighborhoods because nice neighborhoods are where people live. - Violence is *consequential* — Meg gets hurt, gets slower, gets sick. The story tracks the cost. - Humor is dry, situational, and often at Meg's expense. She's not cool. She's a mess who happens to be dangerous. ## Themes - **Found family** — but not sentimental. Meg and Lily's bond is real and also a projection of Meg's guilt. Both things are true. - **Pasts that won't stay buried** — but the past isn't a secret; it's just a fact Meg lives with. She doesn't need to confront it. She needs to survive it. - **Protective rage** — but rage isn't noble. It's just what's left when everything else is gone. - **Underestimation** — the villains dismiss Meg because she's a woman, a nanny, a "nobody." The story doesn't celebrate her proving them wrong. It just shows what happens. ## Key Choices Locked In | Element | Decision | |---|---| | Babysitter | Meg Sawyer, 34, ex-Marine Raider, dishonorably discharged, first-person narrator | | Child | Lily Chen, 7, scared, imperfect, not precocious | | Villains | Ruiz (leader), Marco, Diego, Vince, and a driver — cartel enforcers, professionals | | Setting | Suburban San Diego, one night, roughly eight hours real time | | Structure | Linear chronology, 8 chapters, ~8000 words | | POV | First person, Meg, throughout. No villain POV. | | Ending | Meg and Lily survive. The story ends before the bow. | ## Structural Decisions - **No villain POV.** The story stays in Meg's head. We learn about the villains the way she does — through evidence, bodies, and the things they leave behind. Their fear is *inferred*, not shown. That's more human and more frightening. - **No Boone phone call.** No interrogation scene. Meg figures things out from what she finds. - **No hospital resolution.** The story ends at the boatyard, or just after. The bow is not tied. - **Chapter endings are not all cliffhangers.** Some end on a thought. Some end on a silence. Some end mid-action. Variety is human. - **At least one thing goes wrong in a way that isn't fixed.** Meg makes a mistake she can't undo. The story carries it. --- # Chapter Planning ## Chapter 1 — "The Girl Who Was Supposed to Die" **POV:** Meg, first person | **Setting:** The Chen house, evening A real scene, not a setup checklist. Meg is putting Lily to bed. Lily is being difficult — not cute-difficult, actually difficult. She doesn't want to sleep. She asks Meg a question Meg doesn't want to answer. Meg lies. The lie is small and human. We learn, through the texture of the evening, that Meg has been doing this for a few months, that she likes it, that she's good at it, and that she is also *waiting* for something — she doesn't know what. There's a moment where Meg catches herself checking the locks and doesn't know why. Lily notices. Meg makes a joke. Lily doesn't laugh. The phone rings. It's Lily's father, working late. He's tense. He doesn't say why. Meg doesn't ask. She hangs up. She reads Lily a story. Lily falls asleep. Meg sits in the dark living room and doesn't turn on the TV. She just sits. Then the power cuts. Then the front door opens. **End on:** the sound of boots on hardwood, and Meg's voice, flat: *"Lily. Get under the bed."* ## Chapter 2 — "Bad Night for Bad Men" **POV:** Meg | **Setting:** The Chen house, night The break-in, from inside Meg's body. She fights — and she's good, but there are five of them and they're professionals and she's been out of the game for three years. She takes down one. She hurts another. Then Ruiz puts a gun to Lily's head and Meg stops. She has to. She hates it. Ruiz is not a monster. He's a businessman. He tells Meg this isn't personal. He tells her she should have picked a different job. He has one of his men break her arm — not for good measure, just because it's easier to leave her if she can't follow. Meg doesn't scream. She bites through her lip. Lily is crying. Meg tells her it's okay. It's not okay. They take Lily. They set the fire. They leave. **End on:** Meg on the floor, one arm useless, smoke filling the room, and the sound of Lily's voice somewhere outside, getting smaller. ## Chapter 3 — "The Wrong Babysitter" **POV:** Meg | **Setting:** The burning house, then the street Meg escapes the fire. It's not heroic. It's slow and stupid and she almost doesn't make it. She crawls. She vomits. She passes out in the yard and wakes up because the grass is on fire. She kills the man Ruiz left behind to confirm the body — not cleanly, not quickly, with a piece of the broken banister and a lot of swearing. It's the first time she's killed anyone since Afghanistan. She doesn't feel anything about it. That scares her more than the killing. She pats herself down. She has: a broken arm, a kitchen knife she grabbed on the way out, Lily's stuffed rabbit (found in the yard), and a phone with 3% battery. She calls the one number she swore she'd never call. A man named **Boone** answers. He doesn't ask why. He gives her an address. She doesn't thank him. She hangs up before he can say anything else. She walks. She doesn't have a car. She doesn't have shoes. She walks anyway. **End on:** Meg, barefoot, on the shoulder of a road, the knife in her belt, the rabbit in her good hand, and a thought she doesn't finish: *I should have*— ## Chapter 4 — "Nothing to Lose" **POV:** Meg | **Setting:** A cartel stash house on the edge of the city Meg finds the stash house. She doesn't interrogate anyone. She watches. She waits. She learns the plan from a phone left on a table and a map on a wall: Lily is at a boatyard near the harbor. Transport to Mexico at dawn. She takes out two of the crew — **Diego** and **Vince** — and the kills are not clean. Diego begs. Vince doesn't. Meg doesn't say anything to either of them. She doesn't have anything to say. She takes Vince's gun, his phone, and his car keys. She sits in his car for a minute before she starts it. She looks at her hands. They're shaking. She doesn't know if it's the pain or something else. She decides it doesn't matter. **End on:** Meg driving toward the harbor, one hand on the wheel, the other arm in a sling she made from a curtain, and the radio playing something she doesn't recognize. ## Chapter 5 — "Little Girl Lost" **POV:** Meg | **Setting:** The road, then the boatyard perimeter This chapter is not Lily's POV. We stay with Meg. She's running on empty. She pulls over once to throw up. She pulls over again to cry, briefly, and then stops because it's not helping. She talks to herself. She talks to Lily, who isn't there. She says things she wouldn't say if Lily could hear. She reaches the boatyard. She scouts it. She counts guards. She counts exits. She makes a plan and then immediately has to change it because there are more guards than she thought. She's not sure she can do this. She's going to do it anyway. That's the whole chapter. **End on:** Meg, crouched behind a shipping container, watching the lights of the boatyard, and a thought that isn't a thought: *Lily. I'm coming. I'm coming. I'm coming.* ## Chapter 6 — "The House of the Dead" **POV:** Meg | **Setting:** The boatyard The longest, ugliest chapter. Meg infiltrates the boatyard. She uses the environment — boats, chains, fuel, a flare gun — but nothing goes according to plan. She gets hurt again. She gets cornered. She kills **Marco** in a way that's not clever, just brutal, and it costs her. She loses the knife. She loses the gun. She's down to her hands and her teeth. She finds the storage room. She opens the door. **End on:** Lily, alive, tied to a chair. And **Ruiz**, standing behind her, with a gun. ## Chapter 7 — "Kill Them All" **POV:** Meg | **Setting:** The boatyard, storage room The confrontation. It's not a monologue. It's not a negotiation. It's two exhausted people in a small room, one of whom is holding a gun to a child's head. Ruiz tries to talk. Meg doesn't listen. She waits. She takes her opening. Ruiz dies badly — not cleanly, not heroically, just badly. Meg doesn't watch him die. She unties Lily. She picks her up with one arm. She carries her out. **End on:** Meg and Lily in the parking lot, the sun starting to come up, Lily's arms around Meg's neck, and Meg's voice, hoarse: *"I've got you. I've got you."* ## Chapter 8 — "What Comes After" **POV:** Meg | **Setting:** The road, dawn The story ends before the bow. Meg and Lily are in Vince's car, driving away from the boatyard. Lily is asleep in the back seat. Meg is bleeding. She doesn't know where she's going. She doesn't know what happens next. She doesn't know if she'll be arrested, or if the cartel will come for her, or if she'll ever be able to do anything again except this. She pulls over at a gas station. She buys a bottle of water and a bag of chips. She sits in the car and eats the chips with one hand. Lily wakes up and asks if she can have some. Meg gives her the bag. They sit there. Lily asks if Meg is still going to babysit her. Meg doesn't answer. Not because she doesn't want to. Because she doesn't know. Because she's not sure she's the kind of person who gets to do that anymore. Because she's not sure she ever was. **End on:** Meg looking at Lily in the rearview mirror. Lily looking back. Neither of them saying anything. The sun coming up. The story just stopping — not resolving, just stopping — because that's how it works.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Meg Sawyer ## Background, Personality, Idiosyncracies, Flaws Meg grew up in Barstow, California — a desert town that exists mostly because people need somewhere to stop between Los Angeles and Las Vegas. Her father was a Marine who was gone more than he was home. Her mother worked at a diner and smoked two packs a day and loved Meg in a way that was real but not warm. Meg enlisted at eighteen because it was the only thing she could think of that would get her out of Barstow and because she wanted her father to look at her the way he looked at his buddies. He didn't. He died before she got back from her first deployment. She doesn't talk about him. She was good at the Marines. Not because she loved it — she didn't — but because she was good at being told what to do and good at doing it better than anyone else. She made Raider. She deployed four times. She killed people. She was fine with it. That's the part she doesn't explain to anyone, because there's no way to say it that doesn't make her sound like a monster: she was fine with it. It was a job. It was a thing she could do that other people couldn't. She didn't enjoy it. She didn't hate it. She just did it. The discharge happened in Afghanistan. Her unit was clearing a compound. There was a man in one of the rooms with three children — two girls and a boy, all under ten. The man was known to be a trafficker. He was unarmed. Meg's commanding officer told her to leave him for the intel team. Meg shot him in the face. She doesn't regret it. She regrets that she did it in front of the children. She thinks about that a lot. Not the man. The children. She got a general discharge under honorable conditions — a bureaucratic middle ground that means "we're kicking you out but we're not going to say why." She drifted for a while. She did security work. She did some things she doesn't list on resumes. Then she got a job as a nanny through a friend of a friend, because she needed something that didn't involve violence and because she thought — correctly — that she would be good at it. She's been doing it for three years. She has a reputation among the families she works for as reliable, unflappable, and a little strange. She doesn't talk much. She doesn't ask questions. She's always early. She always has a bag packed, just in case. **Personality:** Meg is not warm. She's not cold either. She's *flat* — a woman who has learned to keep her feelings in a box because the box is the only way she can function. She's funny in a dry, self-deprecating way that surprises people who assume she's humorless. She's patient with children in a way she isn't with adults. She's good at listening and bad at sharing. She has a temper she keeps on a very short leash. When it gets off the leash, it's not explosive — it's quiet and precise and terrifying. She has never hit a child. She has never hit a partner. She has hit men who deserved it and some who didn't. **Idiosyncrasies:** She always sits facing the door. She checks locks twice. She can't sleep in a bed that's against a wall. She eats fast, like someone might take her food. She has a habit of touching her left forearm — where the scar is — when she's thinking. She doesn't like being touched from behind. She's a good cook but doesn't enjoy it. She reads the same four books over and over — a dog-eared paperback of *The Things They Carried*, a biography of Ulysses S. Grant, a book about the history of the Marine Corps, and a romance novel she'd never admit to owning. She has a sweet tooth she suppresses. She's a terrible liar and knows it, so she avoids lying when she can. **Flaws:** Meg's flaw isn't that she's violent. It's that she doesn't think she deserves anything else. She's not suicidal — she's just *resigned*. She doesn't expect to live past fifty. She doesn't expect to have a family. She doesn't expect to be happy. She thinks she's already used up whatever good she had coming. This makes her dangerous in a way that's hard to explain: she's not afraid to die, and she's not afraid to kill, and the only thing she has left to lose is a child who isn't hers. ## Physicality Meg is five-eight, lean, and built like someone who used to be an athlete and still mostly is. She has a swimmer's shoulders and a runner's calves. Her hair is dark brown, cut short and practical — she trims it herself with kitchen scissors and it shows. Her face is plain in a way that's hard to describe: not pretty, not ugly, just *there*. A strong jaw. A nose that's been broken once. Eyes that are gray-green and flat when she's not paying attention and startlingly direct when she is. She has a scar on her left forearm, a long one, from a knife. She has a smaller scar on her chin from a fall when she was twelve. She has a tattoo on her right shoulder — a small, faded globe and anchor she got at nineteen and regrets. She wears loose clothes: jeans, plain T-shirts, a hoodie that used to be black and is now mostly gray. She doesn't wear jewelry. She doesn't wear makeup. She carries herself like someone who is always aware of where the exits are. When she's not working, she's still. Very still. She can sit in a chair for an hour without moving and not seem restless — just *waiting*. When she's working — when she's doing something physical — she's economical. No wasted motion. No flourishes. She moves like someone who has been trained to move and has never quite stopped being trained. When she's angry, she gets quieter. When she's scared, she gets calmer. This is not a conscious choice. It's what the Marines did to her. ## Motives, Allegiances, Relationships Meg's motive is not revenge. It's not justice. It's not even really Lily, although she tells herself it is. Meg's motive is that she has spent her entire adult life failing to protect people she was supposed to protect, and she cannot do it again. Her father died while she was overseas. The children in Afghanistan watched her shoot a man in the face. Every family she's worked for has eventually let her go, not because she did anything wrong but because she's *strange*, because she doesn't fit, because there's something in her that people can sense and don't want in their homes. Lily is the first child in years who hasn't been afraid of her. Meg doesn't know how to say that. She doesn't even know how to think it. But it's true. **Allegiances:** Meg doesn't have many. She has Boone, a former Raider who got out before she did and now runs a security consulting firm in San Diego. They were in the same unit for two years. They were never friends — Meg doesn't have friends — but they trust each other in the way that people who have been shot at together trust each other. Boone is the only person Meg has ever called for help. She has called him twice. Both times, he answered. She has no family. Her mother died of lung cancer four years ago. Meg went to the funeral and left early. She has no partner. She has no close friends. She has a cat named Duke who lives with her in a one-bedroom apartment in National City and who is, by Meg's own admission, an asshole. She loves him anyway. **Relationship with Lily:** Meg has been babysitting Lily for four months. She was hired through an agency after Lily's father — David Chen, a federal prosecutor — went through a divorce and needed reliable childcare. Meg was not the first nanny. She was the fourth. The first three quit because Lily was "difficult." Lily is not difficult. Lily is a seven-year-old whose parents split up and whose mother moved to Seattle and whose father works eighty hours a week, and she is angry about it in the way that seven-year-olds are angry, which is to say loudly and constantly and without any ability to articulate why. Meg understood this immediately. She didn't try to fix it. She just sat with Lily while Lily was angry and didn't leave. That's all it took. Lily loves her now, in the way that children love people who don't abandon them. Meg doesn't know what to do with that. She's trying to figure it out. ## Voice **Internal monologue:** *The thing about kids is they can tell when you're lying. Not about the big stuff — they don't know enough to know what the big stuff is. But the small stuff. The "I'm fine." The "it's okay." They can smell it on you. Lily can smell it on me. I don't know what she smells. I don't want to know.* *I'm not doing this because I'm good. I'm doing this because I'm not good at anything else. That's not the same thing. I know it's not the same thing. I'm going to do it anyway.* **Dialogue:** *"Lily. Get under the bed. Don't come out until I say. Don't come out for anyone else. Not even your dad. Not even if they say I sent them. You understand? Good. Go."* *"I don't want to hurt you. I'm going to, but I don't want to. That's the best I can do right now. I'm sorry."* *"You think I'm a person who's going to stop. That's the problem. I'm not. I'm not a person right now. I'm just the thing that's coming for you."* --- # Lily Chen ## Background, Personality, Idiosyncracies, Flaws Lily is seven years old. She was born in San Diego and has lived in the same house her whole life. Her parents divorced eighteen months ago. Her mother moved to Seattle for a job and sees her twice a year. Her father — David Chen, an assistant U.S. attorney — is a good man and a distracted one, a man who loves his daughter and also doesn't know how to talk to her. Lily has learned to be angry at him in ways that are safe, because the alternative is being angry at him in ways that are not. Lily is not precocious. She's not a genius. She's not wise beyond her years. She's a seven-year-old who is scared and confused and tired, and who has learned that the world is not a safe place and that the people who are supposed to protect her sometimes don't. She's smart in the way that all children are smart — she notices things, she remembers things, she understands more than adults give her credit for. But she's also seven. She still sleeps with a stuffed rabbit. She still cries when she's frustrated. She still thinks that if she's good enough, bad things won't happen. **Personality:** Lily is watchful. She doesn't talk much to strangers. She talks a lot to people she trusts — Meg, her father, her teacher — but even then, she edits herself. She's learned that some things make adults uncomfortable. She's learned to read a room. She's learned that being quiet is safer than being loud. She has a temper that comes out in bursts — screaming, crying, throwing things — and then disappears, leaving her exhausted and ashamed. She doesn't know why she does it. She doesn't know how to stop. **Idiosyncrasies:** She has a stuffed rabbit named Mr. Bun. She's had him since she was two. He's missing an eye and one ear is chewed down to the nub. She can't sleep without him. She counts things when she's anxious — stairs, ceiling tiles, cars on the street. She hates the dark. She hates loud noises. She hates being alone. She likes apples but not apple juice. She likes being read to but not reading herself. She has a habit of biting her nails that her father has given up trying to break. She asks questions constantly — *why, why, why* — not because she wants answers but because she wants to hear a voice. **Flaws:** Lily's flaw is that she's seven. She doesn't have the vocabulary to explain what she's feeling, so she acts out instead. She doesn't understand that her father is doing his best, so she punishes him for not doing better. She doesn't understand that her mother left because of things that had nothing to do with her, so she assumes it was her fault. She's not a bad kid. She's a kid in a bad situation, doing what kids do. That's the whole thing. ## Physicality Lily is small for her age — she hasn't hit her growth spurt yet — and thin, with knobby knees and elbows that seem too big for her body. She has black hair, straight and fine, that her father tries to brush and mostly fails. She has her mother's eyes — brown, wide, expressive — and her father's stubborn jaw. She's missing her two front teeth. She has a scab on her knee from a fall at school that she keeps picking at. She wears clothes that are too big for her because her father buys them a size up so she'll "grow into them," and she hates it. When she's comfortable, she's physical — she climbs on things, she hangs off Meg's arm, she sits too close. When she's scared, she goes still. Very still. She makes herself small. She watches. She waits. This is the version of Lily that the cartel sees. This is the version that survives. ## Motives, Allegiances, Relationships Lily's motive is simple: she wants her parents back together. She knows this is impossible. She wants it anyway. She wants her mother to call more. She wants her father to be home more. She wants Meg to stay. She wants Mr. Bun to be real. She wants the world to make sense. **Allegiances:** Lily's allegiance is to whoever is there. Her father is there most nights, even if he's tired. Meg is there four days a week, and Meg doesn't leave, and Meg doesn't get frustrated with her when she's angry, and Meg reads her the same book over and over without complaining. Lily loves her father. She loves her mother, too, in a complicated way she doesn't understand. She loves Meg in a way that's simpler, because Meg doesn't ask her to be anything other than what she is. **Relationship with Meg:** Lily doesn't know what Meg is. She knows Meg is a babysitter. She knows Meg was in the Marines, because Meg told her once, in passing, and Lily has never forgotten. She knows Meg has a scar on her arm that Meg won't explain. She knows Meg is sad sometimes, in a way that's different from her father's sadness, and she knows Meg doesn't talk about it. Lily doesn't ask. She's learned not to ask. But she watches. She's always watching. **Relationship with her father:** David Chen is a good man who is not good at being a father. He loves Lily. He doesn't know how to show it in ways she can understand. He buys her things. He works late. He tells himself he's doing it for her. He's not entirely wrong and not entirely right. Lily knows this. She doesn't have words for it. She just knows that when he's home, she feels better, and when he's not, she feels worse, and she doesn't know why those two things can't be the same thing. ## Voice **Internal monologue:** *I don't like the dark. I don't like it. I don't like it. I don't like it. If I count to a hundred, maybe it will be morning. If I count to a hundred, maybe Meg will come. If I count to a hundred — one, two, three —* *Meg said she would come. Meg said. Meg doesn't lie. Meg said she would come.* **Dialogue:** *"Are you going to leave?"* *"Why do you have that scar? Did someone hurt you? Did you hurt them back?"* *"I don't want to sleep. I'm not tired. I'm not. I'm not."* *"Mr. Bun says you're nice. He doesn't like most people. He likes you."* --- # Ruiz ## Background, Personality, Idiosyncracies, Flaws Ruiz is forty-three years old. He was born in Sinaloa, the son of a schoolteacher and a nurse, and he was supposed to go to university. He didn't. He got involved with the cartel when he was nineteen because his brother was already involved and because it was the only thing in his town that paid. He has been doing this for twenty-four years. He is good at it. He has killed people. He has ordered people killed. He has never killed a child. He has never ordered a child killed. He tells himself this makes him different. He knows it doesn't. Ruiz is not a monster. He's a professional. He has a wife in Culiacán and two daughters, ages sixteen and twelve. He calls them every night. He sends money. He has not seen them in eight months because he is in the United States on business and cannot cross the border without risking arrest. He misses them in a way that is real and also irrelevant. He is not a good man. He is not a bad man. He is a man who made a choice a long time ago and has been living with it ever since. **Personality:** Ruiz is calm. Almost unnervingly calm. He doesn't raise his voice. He doesn't threaten. He doesn't need to. He speaks softly and carries himself with the confidence of a man who has been in dangerous situations before and has always come out on top. He's polite. He says please and thank you. He apologizes when he has to. He's not sadistic. He doesn't enjoy violence. He just doesn't mind it. That's worse. **Idiosyncrasies:** He wears a wedding ring he never takes off. He has a photo of his daughters in his wallet that he looks at when he thinks no one is watching. He drinks tea, not coffee. He doesn't smoke. He doesn't drink. He has a habit of cleaning his glasses when he's thinking, which he does a lot. He speaks English with almost no accent — he learned it deliberately, because it made him better at his job. He calls his wife every night at nine o'clock. He has never missed a call. Not once. **Flaws:** Ruiz's flaw is that he thinks he's still in control. He's been doing this for twenty-four years and he's never been seriously challenged. He's forgotten what it feels like to be afraid. He's forgotten that the world is full of people who don't play by his rules. He looks at Meg — a woman, a nanny, a nobody — and he doesn't see a threat. That's his flaw. That's what kills him. ## Physicality Ruiz is five-ten, solid, with the build of a man who was athletic in his youth and has kept most of it. He has gray at his temples that he doesn't dye. He wears glasses — wire-rimmed, expensive — and cleans them with a handkerchief he keeps in his pocket. His hands are soft. He's never done manual labor. He has a small scar on his chin from a fight when he was seventeen. He dresses well but not flashily — dark slacks, a button-down shirt, a jacket that conceals a shoulder holster. He moves slowly. Deliberately. He doesn't waste motion. He doesn't waste words. When he's in control, he's relaxed. When he's not, he gets very still. Very quiet. His eyes stop moving. He becomes a man who is calculating, and the calculation is always the same: *how do I get out of this alive?* He's never had to answer that question before. He's about to. ## Motives, Allegiances, Relationships Ruiz's motive is simple: he wants to go home. He wants to see his wife. He wants to see his daughters. He wants to stop sleeping in safehouses and eating takeout and looking over his shoulder. He took this job — kidnapping the daughter of a federal prosecutor — because it was supposed to be easy. In and out. A few hours. A leverage play to get his boss's brother out of prison. He was told the house would be empty except for the child and the nanny. He was told the nanny was a nobody. **Allegiances:** Ruiz is loyal to the cartel because the cartel pays him and because leaving the cartel is not an option. He's loyal to his family because they're the only thing he has left. He's not loyal to his men — not really. He's responsible for them, in the way that a manager is responsible for his employees. He doesn't love them. He doesn't even like most of them. He'll mourn them if they die, but he'll mourn them the way you mourn a broken tool: with annoyance, not grief. **Relationship with Meg:** Ruiz doesn't think about Meg. She's a detail. She's a problem he solved — a woman he beat and left to burn. He doesn't hate her. He doesn't fear her. He doesn't think about her at all. That's the point. That's what makes her dangerous. ## Voice **Internal monologue:** *The nanny. The nanny is the problem. I don't know how. I don't know why. But she's the problem. I should have made sure. I should have made sure. I should have —* *I'm going home. I'm going to see my wife. I'm going to see my daughters. I'm going to —* **Dialogue:** *"This isn't personal. I want you to know that. It's just business. You picked the wrong house to work in. That's all."* *"You're making a mistake. You don't have to do this. We can work something out. We can —"* *"Who are you? What are you? What are you?"* --- # Marco ## Background, Personality, Idiosyncracies, Flaws Marco is thirty-one. He's Ruiz's second-in-command, not because he's the smartest or the strongest but because he's the most reliable. He does what he's told. He doesn't ask questions. He doesn't complain. He's been with the cartel for eight years and has never risen higher because he doesn't want to. He doesn't want responsibility. He doesn't want to be in charge. He wants to do his job, get paid, and go home. He has a girlfriend in Tijuana he's been seeing for three years. He thinks he loves her. He's not sure. He's not sure about a lot of things. Marco is not a bad man. He's a man who has done bad things because it was easier than doing good things. He doesn't think about it. He doesn't let himself think about it. He's learned to turn his brain off when he's working. It's a skill. It's the only skill he has. **Personality:** Marco is quiet. Not calm — quiet. There's a difference. He's anxious. He's always anxious. He chews his fingernails. He taps his foot. He can't sit still. He's not afraid of violence — he's seen too much of it for that — but he's afraid of everything else. He's afraid of getting caught. He's afraid of getting killed. He's afraid of being alone. He's afraid of the dark, which he would never admit to anyone. He's the kind of man who checks the back seat of his car before he gets in. He's the kind of man who sleeps with a gun under his pillow. He's the kind of man who will die badly, because he'll see it coming and won't know what to do. **Idiosyncrasies:** He carries a rosary in his pocket that he doesn't use. He hasn't prayed since he was a kid. He doesn't know why he keeps it. He drinks too much coffee. He smokes when he's nervous, which is always. He has a tattoo on his neck that he got when he was nineteen and now regrets. He can't remember the last time he laughed. He has a scar on his hand from a knife fight in a bar in Tijuana that he lost. He doesn't talk about it. **Flaws:** Marco's flaw is that he's a coward. Not a physical coward — he'll fight if he has to — but a moral one. He's never made a decision in his life. He's never stood up for anything. He's never said no. He's drifted through his life like a leaf in a river, and the river is going to take him somewhere bad, and he knows it, and he can't stop it. He's going to die in a boatyard in San Diego, and he's going to know it's coming, and he's going to do nothing to prevent it. That's who he is. ## Physicality Marco is five-eleven, wiry, with the build of a man who was skinny as a kid and never quite filled out. He has dark hair, slicked back, and a thin mustache he's proud of. He has nervous eyes — brown, quick, always moving. He looks like he's about to be caught doing something he shouldn't. He wears jeans and a leather jacket that's too heavy for the weather. He has a gold chain around his neck that he touches when he's anxious. He chews his fingernails down to the quick. His hands are always moving — tapping, fidgeting, reaching for something that isn't there. When he's working, he's focused. He can be focused. He can be professional. He can do what he's told. But there's always a part of him that's watching, waiting, calculating the distance to the nearest exit. He's never fully in the room. He's always halfway out the door. ## Motives, Allegiances, Relationships Marco's motive is survival. He doesn't care about the cartel. He doesn't care about the money. He cares about getting through the day without getting killed. He's been doing this for eight years and he's still alive and he doesn't know how much longer that's going to last. He thinks about quitting. He thinks about running. He thinks about going back to Tijuana and marrying his girlfriend and getting a job at his uncle's auto shop. He thinks about it every day. He never does it. **Allegiances:** Marco is loyal to Ruiz because Ruiz is the only thing standing between him and the chaos. He's loyal to the cartel because leaving the cartel is a death sentence. He's loyal to his girlfriend because she's the only person who's ever looked at him like he was worth something. He doesn't know if he loves her. He doesn't know if he loves anyone. He's not sure he's capable of it. **Relationship with Meg:** Marco sees Meg at the house. He sees her fight. He sees her take down one of his men. He sees Ruiz break her arm. He sees her go down. He thinks she's dead. He doesn't think about her again until she starts killing his crew. And then he thinks about her constantly. He thinks about her the way you think about a storm that's coming for you: with dread, with disbelief, with the growing certainty that you're not going to make it. ## Voice **Internal monologue:** *She's dead. She's dead. She has to be dead. I saw her. I saw her go down. She's dead. She's dead. She's —* *I should have left. I should have left when I had the chance. I should have —* **Dialogue:** *"You said she was a nanny. You said she was nobody. You said —"* *"I don't want to die here. I don't want to die in this fucking boatyard. I don't —"* *"Please. Please. I have a girlfriend. I have —"* --- # Diego ## Background, Personality, Idiosyncracies, Flaws Diego is twenty-six. He's the youngest of the crew. He's been with the cartel for two years. He's not good at it. He's not bad at it either — he's just young. He's still excited by the violence. He still thinks it makes him a man. He hasn't learned yet that it doesn't. He hasn't learned yet that it just makes you tired. He'll learn. Or he won't. Diego grew up in a small town in Michoacán. His father was a farmer. His mother was a teacher. He was supposed to go to university. He didn't. He got involved with the cartel because his cousin was involved and because it was the only thing in his town that paid. He sends money home. He tells his mother he's working construction. She believes him. He doesn't know why she believes him. He doesn't know why anyone believes anything he says. **Personality:** Diego is loud. He talks too much. He laughs too much. He's the kind of person who fills silence because silence makes him uncomfortable. He's not stupid — he's just young. He thinks he's invincible. He thinks he's the main character. He thinks the world is a movie and he's the star. He's going to die in a boatyard in San Diego, and he's going to be surprised, and that's the saddest thing about him. **Idiosyncrasies:** He wears a cross around his neck that he touches when he's nervous. He has a photo of his mother in his wallet. He chews gum constantly — he goes through a pack a day. He can't grow a beard, which bothers him more than it should. He has a tattoo of a snake on his forearm that he got when he was eighteen and now thinks is stupid. He listens to music on his phone without headphones, which annoys everyone. He's never been in love. He's never been in a fight he couldn't win. He's never been afraid for his life. He's about to be. **Flaws:** Diego's flaw is that he doesn't understand consequences. He's never had to face them. He's never had to deal with the aftermath of anything he's done. He's never had to look at a body and know that he made it that way. He's about to. He's about to learn that violence isn't a game. He's about to learn that the world doesn't care if you're young. He's about to learn that there's always someone bigger, someone meaner, someone who will do to you what you've done to others. He's about to learn all of this in the space of a few seconds. And then he's going to die. ## Physicality Diego is five-nine, stocky, with the build of a man who was chubby as a kid and turned it into muscle. He has dark hair, cut short, and a face that's still boyish despite the tattoos and the swagger. He has a wide smile that he uses too much. He wears clothes that are too expensive for his paycheck — designer jeans, a gold chain, a watch that's probably fake. He walks like he owns the world. He walks like he's never been afraid. When he's scared, he doesn't know what to do. He's never been scared before. He doesn't have the equipment for it. He freezes. He stares. He says something stupid. And then he dies. ## Motives, Allegiances, Relationships Diego's motive is money. He wants to send more home. He wants to buy his mother a house. He wants to prove to his father that he made the right choice, that the cartel was a better path than the farm, that he's not a failure. He doesn't know that his father is ashamed of him. He doesn't know that his mother cries when she gets his money. He doesn't know anything. **Allegiances:** Diego is loyal to the cartel because the cartel is his family now. He's loyal to Ruiz because Ruiz is the boss. He's loyal to Marco because Marco is his friend — or as close to a friend as he has. He doesn't have real friends. He doesn't have real anything. He's a kid playing at being a man, and he's about to find out what that costs. **Relationship with Meg:** Diego sees Meg at the house. He's the one who breaks her arm. He does it because Ruiz tells him to. He doesn't think about it. He doesn't think about her at all. She's a detail. She's a problem. She's a thing that needs to be dealt with. He doesn't know that she's going to kill him. He doesn't know that she's going to look at him while she does it. He doesn't know that he's going to beg. He doesn't know anything. ## Voice **Internal monologue:** *This is easy. This is so easy. I don't know why everyone was so worried. It's just a kid. It's just a nanny. It's just —* *Wait. Wait. What is she — what is she doing — what is —* **Dialogue:** *"You want me to do it? For real? Okay. Okay. I'll do it."* *"Hey. Hey, lady. You should have picked a different house. You know? You should have —"* *"No. No. No. Please. Please. I don't want to — I don't —"* --- # Vince ## Background, Personality, Idiosyncracies, Flaws Vince is thirty-eight. He's the oldest of the crew besides Ruiz. He's been with the cartel for fifteen years. He's seen everything. He's done everything. He's tired. He's not afraid of dying — he's afraid of dying for nothing. He's afraid that his life has been a waste. He's afraid that when he dies, no one will remember him. He's afraid that he's already dead and no one has told him. Vince grew up in Los Angeles. His father was a mechanic. His mother was a nurse. He was supposed to go to community college. He didn't. He got involved with a gang when he was sixteen and graduated to the cartel when he was twenty-three. He's been doing this for fifteen years. He has a daughter in Fresno he hasn't seen in six years. He sends money. He doesn't call. He doesn't know why. He doesn't know anything. **Personality:** Vince is quiet. Not calm — quiet. He's a man who has learned to keep his mouth shut because keeping his mouth shut is how you survive. He doesn't talk unless he has something to say. He doesn't laugh. He doesn't smile. He just watches. He's the kind of man who has seen too much and has decided that the only way to keep going is to feel nothing. He's good at it. He's very good at it. **Idiosyncrasies:** He carries a photo of his daughter in his wallet. He looks at it when he thinks no one is watching. He doesn't know why. He doesn't know what he's looking for. He drinks whiskey, but only when he's alone. He doesn't smoke. He doesn't do drugs. He has a scar on his neck from a knife fight in a bar in Phoenix that he won. He doesn't talk about it. He doesn't talk about anything. He has a habit of rubbing his thumb against his index finger when he's thinking. He's always thinking. **Flaws:** Vince's flaw is that he's given up. He's not fighting for anything anymore. He's not even fighting to survive — he's just going through the motions, waiting for the end. He's been waiting for fifteen years. He's about to get what he's been waiting for. He's about to die in a boatyard in San Diego, and he's going to know it's coming, and he's not going to fight it. He's going to let it happen. That's who he is. ## Physicality Vince is six feet, lean, with the build of a man who was strong as a young man and has stayed strong out of habit. He has gray hair, cut short, and a face that's weathered and lined. He has dark eyes that don't give anything away. He wears plain clothes — jeans, a T-shirt, a jacket. He doesn't care about his appearance. He doesn't care about anything. He moves slowly. Deliberately. He doesn't waste motion. He doesn't waste words. When he's working, he's focused. He's always focused. He's a professional. He's been doing this for fifteen years. He's never been caught. He's never been hurt. He's never been afraid.
