# Chapter 1: The Girl Who Was Supposed to Die The kid didn't want to go to sleep. That was the whole thing. That was the night. I'd been sitting on the floor next to her bed for forty minutes, my back against the wall, my legs stretched out in front of me, reading from a book about a mouse who lived in a motorcycle. She'd heard it a hundred times. She could recite it. She still made me read every word. "Again," she said. "No." "Again." "Lily. It's nine-forty." "So?" "So you have school." "I don't care about school." "I know. But I care about you going to school, because if you don't go to school, your dad fires me, and then I have to find another job, and the only other job I'm qualified for is hauling trash." "You'd be good at that." "Thanks." She smiled. She had a gap where her front teeth used to be. She was seven years old and she smiled like she'd invented it. I put the book down. She watched me do it. She had a way of watching that was different from other kids — not hungry, not needy, just *present*. Like she was taking notes. I don't know what she was writing down. I don't know what she saw. "Meg." "Yeah." "Are you going to leave?" It wasn't the first time she'd asked. It was maybe the tenth. She asked it every few weeks, like she was checking the locks. I'd learned to answer it the same way every time, because the same way every time was what she needed. Kids don't want the truth. They want the thing that stays the same. "No," I said. "I'm not going to leave." "Promise?" "Promise." She thought about it. She had a way of thinking about things that took a long time — longer than most kids her age, longer than most adults. Her father called it "processing." Her teachers called it something else. I called it what it was, which was *paying attention*. "Mom left," she said. "I know." "She promised too." I didn't have anything for that. I never did. It was the one question I couldn't answer, because she was right, and I wasn't going to lie to her, and the truth was that sometimes people promise things and then they leave anyway and there's nothing you can do about it. I'm not good at the truth. I'm better at the lies that keep things moving. But she wasn't asking for a lie. She was asking for something I didn't have. "Your mom's a different thing," I said. "Why?" "Because." "That's not a reason." "No," I said. "It's not." She looked at me for a second. Then she nodded, like I'd passed a test. She reached under her pillow and pulled out Mr. Bun — the rabbit, missing an eye, one ear chewed down to nothing — and held him against her chest. It was a surrender. It was the closest thing she had to saying *okay, I'll go to sleep now*. "Read it again," she said. "No." "Please." "No." "Please." I read it again. She was asleep before I got to the part with the hill. I closed the book and sat there for a minute, listening to her breathe. The house was quiet in a way that houses are quiet at night — not silent, just *settled*. The refrigerator hummed. The furnace clicked. Outside, somewhere down the block, a dog was barking at something and then stopped. I got up. My knees cracked. I'm thirty-four years old and my knees crack like I'm sixty. That's what four deployments will do to you. That's what a lot of things will do to you. I checked the front door. Locked. I checked the back door. Locked. I checked the windows in the living room, one by one, the way I always did, and I couldn't have told you why. It wasn't a habit. It was something underneath the habit. It was the thing that made me sit facing the door in restaurants and sleep with my back to the wall and keep a bag packed in the closet. It was the thing I couldn't name and didn't try to. I sat down on the couch. I didn't turn on the TV. I just sat there in the dark, in the house that wasn't mine, in the life that wasn't mine, and I thought about nothing. I'm good at thinking about nothing. It's a skill. The phone rang at ten-fifteen. It was David — Lily's father. He was at the office. He was always at the office. He asked if everything was okay. He asked if Lily had gone down okay. He asked if I needed anything. He sounded tense. Not tired — tense. There's a difference. Tired is when you've been working too long. Tense is when you're waiting for something. I've heard both. I know the sound. I told him everything was fine. He was quiet for a second. Then he said he'd be home by midnight. He said it like he was asking a question. "Okay," I said. "Okay," he said. "Goodnight, Meg." "Goodnight." I hung up. I sat there with the phone in my hand for a minute. Then I put it down and went to the kitchen and got a glass of water, and I stood at the sink and looked out the window at the backyard, which was dark and empty and had a swing set in it that Lily never used. The power went out at ten-forty. Not a flicker. Not a brownout. It just went. The refrigerator stopped humming. The furnace clicked off. The little red light on the microwave died. The house went dark and quiet in a way that felt wrong, and I stood there in the kitchen with the glass of water in my hand and I knew. I didn't know *what*. I just knew. The front door opened. It didn't break. It didn't get kicked in. It just opened, the way it opens when someone has a key, and the sound of it was so ordinary that for a second I thought it was David, home early, and then I heard the boots. More than one. Heavy. Deliberate. I set the glass down. I walked to the hallway as quietly as I could. I stopped at Lily's door and put my hand on it. "Lily," I said. Not loud. Just enough. She was awake. Of course she was awake. She'd never been asleep. She was sitting up in bed with Mr. Bun against her chest, and her eyes were wide, and she looked at me the way she always looked at me — like she was taking notes. "Get under the bed," I said. "Don't come out until I say. Don't come out for anyone else. Not even your dad. Not even if they say I sent them. You understand?" She nodded. "Good. Go." She went. I heard her hit the floor. I heard the rabbit hit the floor after her. I didn't look back. I walked down the hallway toward the front of the house, toward the boots, toward whatever was coming, and I didn't have a weapon and I didn't have a plan and I didn't have anything except the thing I always have, which is the certainty that I'm going to do what needs to be done, and the fear that comes with knowing I might not be able to. The boots stopped. A voice said, "Check the bedrooms." And then I was moving.

The voice is consistent and controlled throughout — Meg's first-person narration has the flat, economical quality the plan calls for, and it never tips into self-congratulation or sentimentality. The dialogue feels earned rather than constructed. Lily reads as a real seven-year-old: stubborn, watchful, not precocious in the annoying way, and the detail of her smiling "like she'd invented it" is one of the chapter's few genuinely poetic moments that actually lands. The chapter follows its plan faithfully. The lock-checking, the phone call from David (tense, not tired — a distinction Meg makes that reveals character), the power cut, the boots on hardwood — all present and executed in the right order. The ending lands on the right note: not a cliffhanger exactly, but a threshold moment. "And then I was moving" is a clean, effective close. Where the chapter is slightly weaker: some of the self-commentary edges toward telling rather than showing. "I'm good at thinking about nothing. It's a skill" is a line that works once but the chapter uses this pattern — Meg explaining herself to the reader — a few times too many. "That's what four deployments will do to you. That's what a lot of things will do to you" is the most egregious example: it's Meg editorializing about herself in a way that undercuts the restraint the prose otherwise maintains. The plan specifically calls for the past to come out "sideways — a flinch, a joke, a lie, a scar she doesn't explain," and this line is too direct, too explanatory. The David phone call is functional but thin. The plan calls for him to be "tense" and for Meg to notice it without asking — this is executed, but the scene doesn't quite do the work of establishing David as a person with stakes. It's a setup beat, and it reads like one. The violence setup at the end is handled well — the power cut, the door opening "the way it opens when someone has a key" is a nice, unsettling detail. The instruction to Lily is clean and character-consistent: no wasted words, no sentiment, just the operational necessity. "Good. Go." is exactly right. The Mr. Bun detail is used well — it's introduced naturally, it pays off in the ending (the rabbit hitting the floor after Lily), and it doesn't feel forced. The motorcycle mouse book is a nice, specific touch that grounds the scene without over-explaining. Overall, this is a confident, well-executed opening chapter. It's not a masterpiece — the self-commentary occasionally undercuts the restraint, and the David scene is underdeveloped — but it establishes voice, character, and stakes with economy and genuine skill. The darkness is earned, the lightness is dry and appropriate, and the chapter ends exactly where it should. # Chapter 2: Bad Night for Bad Men There were five of them. I counted in the first three seconds, because that's what I do, because that's what I've always done, because when you walk into a room you count the people and you find the exits and you figure out which one you're going to use before you need to use it. Five men. Front door and back door. Two in the living room, two in the hall, one in the kitchen. All of them armed. All of them moving like they knew the house. They knew the house. I didn't have time to think about what that meant. I came around the corner fast and low and took the first one by surprise — the one in the hall, the one closest to Lily's room — and I hit him in the throat with the heel of my hand and then I hit him again in the temple and he went down. Not dead. Down. I didn't have time to finish it. I grabbed his gun out of his hand and I turned and I fired twice at the man behind him and I missed both times because I'm not as good as I used to be and because my hands were shaking and because I hadn't held a gun in three years. The man I hit was named Diego. I didn't know his name then. I learned it later, from his wallet, which I took out of his pocket after I killed him. But that's later. That's not now. Now there was a man in the living room with a pistol pointed at me, and a man in the kitchen coming around the other way, and a man in the hall behind the man in the living room, and I was standing in the middle of the hallway with a gun I didn't know how to use and nowhere to go. The man in the living room said, "Put it down." I didn't put it down. He said, "We have the girl." I looked at him. He was older than the others. Fifties, maybe. Glasses. Calm. He wasn't sweating. He wasn't excited. He was just standing there with a gun in his hand like he'd done this a hundred times, because he had. He said, "My name is Ruiz. I'm not here to hurt anyone. I'm here to take the girl. If you put the gun down, this goes easy. If you don't, it goes hard. That's the whole thing. That's the whole choice. I'd like you to make the easy one." I said, "You're not taking her." He said, "I am." And then one of them hit me from behind. I don't know which one. Doesn't matter. What matters is that I went down, and the gun went flying, and then they were on me. Not beating me — *holding* me. Two of them. One on each arm. They hauled me up off the floor and held me in the middle of the living room, and Ruiz walked over and looked at me the way you look at a piece of furniture you're thinking about moving. "You're the nanny," he said. I didn't say anything. "You're the nanny," he said again, "and you put my man on the ground. That's interesting. That's a problem. Do you want to tell me why that's interesting?" I didn't say anything. "Okay," he said. "We'll do it the other way." He nodded at the man on my left. The man on my left was Diego, the one I'd hit, and he was holding his throat and he was angry, and he grabbed my arm and he twisted it and he broke it. I heard it before I felt it. That's a thing people don't know — you hear it first. It sounds like a green branch snapping. Then the pain comes. Then the pain comes and it's so big you can't see for a second and you can't hear and you can't think and you can't do anything except stand there and not scream, because if you scream you give them something, and I wasn't going to give them anything. I bit through my lip. I tasted blood. I didn't scream. Ruiz watched. He didn't smile. He didn't frown. He just watched, the way you watch a clock. "Take her to the bedroom," he said. "Find the girl." They took me to the bedroom. Lily was under the bed. Of course she was. She'd done exactly what I told her, because she was seven years old and she trusted me, and that was the worst thing that had ever happened to me. I could see her under there. I could see her eyes. I could see Mr. Bun. I could see her hands over her mouth, holding in the sound, because she'd learned how to be quiet and I hated that she'd learned that and I hated that I was the reason. One of them — the one from the kitchen, the one who'd been quiet, the one I'd learn later was named Vince — reached under the bed and pulled her out. She didn't scream. She didn't fight. She just went limp, the way kids go limp when they've decided there's no point in fighting, and Vince picked her up and carried her out to the living room, and I followed because they made me follow, because Ruiz wanted me to watch. He wanted me to watch. That's the thing about Ruiz. He's not a sadist. He doesn't enjoy it. He just wants you to understand the situation you're in. He wants you to know exactly how much you've lost. It's not cruelty. It's *business*. It's worse than cruelty. Cruelty has a reason. Business doesn't. Lily looked at me from Vince's arms. She didn't say anything. She didn't cry. She just looked at me with those eyes, the ones that were always taking notes, and I looked back at her, and I tried to tell her something with my face. I don't know what. I don't know if it worked. Ruiz said, "You should have picked a different house." I said, "Where are you taking her." He said, "That's not your concern." I said, "Where." He said, "Somewhere you won't find her. Because you won't be looking. Because you'll be dead." He nodded at Diego. Diego took the gun out of his waistband and pointed it at my head. I looked at the barrel. I looked at the way his hand was shaking. I looked at the way he was trying not to look at me. I said, "You don't have to do this." He said, "I do." I said, "No. You don't." He looked at Ruiz. Ruiz shook his head. *No*. Diego lowered the gun. Not because he was merciful. Because Ruiz had a better idea. Ruiz said, "Burn it." They set the fire in the kitchen. They used lighter fluid, the kind that's in every house, and they poured it on the floor and they lit it with a match and they walked out the front door and they didn't look back. I heard them leave. I heard the car start. I heard Lily's voice somewhere outside, small and distant, saying *Meg*. Just once. Just that. Then the car drove away and it was just me and the fire and the house that wasn't mine. I was on the floor. My arm was broken. The smoke was filling the room. I got up.

# Chapter 3: The Wrong Babysitter There's a thing they teach you in training about fire. They teach you to stay low, because the smoke rises, and because the heat is worse up high, and because the air near the floor is the only air you're going to get. They teach you to cover your mouth with something wet. They teach you to find a door, to touch it with the back of your hand before you open it, to crawl if you have to. They don't teach you what to do when your arm is broken and you can't crawl on it and the house is filling up with smoke and the only person you've ever loved is somewhere in the dark outside. I got up. That was the first thing. I got up off the floor and I stood, and my arm screamed at me, and I put my good hand over my mouth and I started moving toward the front of the house. The fire was in the kitchen. It hadn't spread yet. It was going to. I had maybe a minute. Maybe less. I made it to the living room. I made it to the front door. I put my hand on the knob and it was cool and I opened it and I fell out onto the porch and I lay there on the concrete and I breathed. Just breathed. The air was cold and wet and it smelled like grass and it was the best thing I'd ever tasted. I stayed there for four seconds. I counted them. I don't know why I counted them. Then I got up. I went back in. I don't know if that was smart. It wasn't smart. It was the opposite of smart. The house was burning and I went back in, because I'd seen them leave a man behind — I'd seen it, when they were walking out, the one in the hall, the one I'd hit, the one called Diego, staying behind to make sure the job was done — and I wanted to talk to him. I wanted to ask him some questions. He was in the living room when I came back in. He was standing by the window, watching the fire, waiting. He had a gun in his hand and he wasn't holding it like he knew how to use it. He turned when he heard me and he said, "What the —" And I hit him. I hit him with the lamp. The lamp was brass and heavy and it was the first thing my hand found and I swung it one-handed and I caught him in the side of the head and he went down and the gun went off and the bullet went into the ceiling and I hit him again. And again. And again. I don't remember how many times. I remember stopping. I remember standing over him and looking at what I'd done and feeling nothing. That's the part that scares me. Not the hitting. The nothing. I looked at a man I'd just killed and I felt exactly the same as I felt when I was folding laundry. I took his wallet. I took his phone. I took his gun. I took his jacket, because it was cold outside and I wasn't wearing one. I took his keys. Then I got out. The fire was in the hall by then. The fire was everywhere. I went out the front door and I didn't go back in. I made it to the yard and then I sat down. I didn't decide to sit down. My legs decided for me. I sat in the grass and I looked at the house — at the house that wasn't mine, full of things that weren't mine, burning — and I thought about Lily. About her eyes. About the way she'd looked at me from Vince's arms. About the rabbit, still under the bed, still on the floor where she'd dropped it. I went back for the rabbit. I don't know why. I went back in through the front door, which was an insane thing to do, and I crawled into the bedroom through smoke so thick I couldn't see, and I found Mr. Bun under the bed by touch, and I grabbed him, and I got out again. I don't know how. I don't remember it. I just remember lying in the yard afterward with the rabbit in my hand and the house behind me and the sky above me, and the sound of a siren somewhere far away. The sirens. Right. The sirens. I got up. If the police came, I was done. I knew that. I'd killed a man. I'd broken into a burning house. I had a gun that wasn't mine and a wallet that wasn't mine and a jacket with someone else's blood on it. If the police came, they'd take me in, and they'd ask me questions, and I'd answer them, and then I'd be in a cell while Lily was on a boat to Mexico. So I didn't let the police come. I walked. I walked into the dark on the shoulder of the road with my arm in a sling I'd made out of a curtain I'd torn off a window, and I walked away from the sirens, and I walked toward the only person in the world who might be able to help me. His name was Boone. He'd been in my unit. He'd gotten out two years before I did. He ran a security consulting firm in San Diego now, and he had a wife and a kid and a mortgage, and he'd told me once, at a bar, four years ago, that if I ever needed anything — anything at all — I should call him. He'd said it because he was drunk. He'd said it because it was the kind of thing you say when you're drunk. But he'd meant it. I'd known he'd meant it. That was the kind of man he was. I pulled out the phone I'd taken off Diego's body. I dialed Boone's number from memory. It rang twice. "Hello?" "Boone. It's Meg." Silence. Then: "Meg. It's two in the morning." "I know." "Are you —" He stopped. He was hearing something in my voice. He was hearing the thing that people hear when they've been in the same war as you. "Where are you?" "I don't know. Somewhere off the 805. A road. I don't know the name." "Are you hurt?" "My arm's broken. It's fine." "It's not fine. Meg. What happened?" I told him. Not all of it. Just the shape of it. A house. A kidnapping. A girl. He listened. He didn't interrupt. When I was done, he was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "I can't help you." "I know." "I have a family. I can't —" "I know, Boone. I'm not asking you to come. I'm asking you to tell me where they are." Another silence. Longer this time. I could hear him breathing. I could hear him thinking. I could hear him deciding whether the woman on the phone was the same woman he'd served with, or whether she was something else now. "There's a house in National City," he said. "On Commercial. A safehouse. The cartel uses it. If they took her, that's where they'd take her first. Before they move her." "Okay." "Meg. If you go there —" "I know." "Meg." "Thank you, Boone." I hung up before he could say anything else. I stood on the side of the road for a minute, in the dark, with the rabbit in my good hand and the gun in my belt, and I looked at the lights of the city in the distance, and I thought about the girl under the bed with her hands over her mouth. I thought about the man I'd killed in the living room. I thought about Diego, who broke my arm, and Vince, who carried her out, and Ruiz, who told me I should have picked a different house. I started walking.

# Chapter 4: Nothing to Lose I walked for an hour and twenty minutes before I found a gas station. It was one of those twenty-four-hour places with a fluorescent light that buzzed and a clerk behind bulletproof glass who didn't look up from his phone when I came in. I went to the bathroom and locked the door and sat down on the toilet and looked at myself in the mirror. I looked like something that had crawled out of a fire. Which I had. My face was gray with smoke. There was blood on my chin from my lip and blood on my shirt from Diego and there was a purple bruise spreading up my neck that I hadn't noticed until right then. My arm was in the curtain sling and it was swollen so bad the sleeve was cutting into it. I took the sling off. I took my shirt off. I looked at my arm. It was bad. The bone wasn't through the skin — thank God — but the whole forearm was the wrong shape. I'd seen breaks before. I'd set breaks before. I'd never set my own. I sat on the toilet and I put my arm on the edge of the sink and I braced my feet against the wall and I pulled. The sound I made wasn't a scream. I don't know what it was. I bit down on my own wrist and I pulled and something ground back into something like a place and the pain went white and then it went away and then it came back worse, and I sat there for a while just breathing. Then I made a new sling out of what was left of the curtain and I put my shirt back on and I washed my face in the sink and I looked at myself again. Better. Not good. Better. I bought a bottle of water and a bag of chips and a roll of duct tape and paid with cash I'd taken out of Diego's wallet. The clerk didn't look at me. I don't know what he thought. I don't care. Outside, I sat down on the curb and I ate the chips with one hand and I looked at Diego's phone. There was nothing useful in it. Texts in Spanish I could mostly read. Contacts with first names and no last names. A photo of a woman and a kid on a beach somewhere. I looked at the photo for a second. Then I kept scrolling. There was a text thread with a number saved as *R*. The last message had come in at nine that night: *Commercial. 2 a.m. Bring her.* That was it. That was all I needed. I got up. I started walking again. — National City is a place that doesn't look like anything. It's strip malls and tire shops and apartment buildings with bars on the windows, and I walked through all of it, and nobody looked at me. That's the thing about being invisible. Once you've been beaten half to death and set on fire, you stop being a person that people notice. You become a thing that's happening. People look away from things that are happening. The house on Commercial was a two-story with peeling paint and a chain-link fence and a carport that had a boat in it that hadn't moved in a decade. There was a light on in the kitchen. There was a car out front — a black Tahoe, the same one they'd driven away in, the same one I'd heard starting up while I was on the floor of a burning house. I stood on the corner for a while. Then I crossed the street and I went around the back. The back door wasn't locked. That's the thing about people who think they're the hunters. They don't lock the door. They don't check the windows. They don't think about the person they left for dead, because in their minds that person is dead. That's the mistake. That's always the mistake. I went in. There were two men in the kitchen. One was Vince — the quiet one, the one who'd carried Lily out. He was sitting at the table with a cup of coffee and a phone in his hand. The other one I didn't know. He was younger, maybe twenty, and he was standing at the counter making a sandwich, and he had a gun in his waistband and he wasn't paying attention to anything. Vince saw me first. He didn't shout. He didn't reach for anything. He just looked at me — this woman in a torn shirt with a curtain for a sling and a gun she didn't know how to use — and something went across his face that I recognized. Not fear. Recognition. Like he'd been waiting for me. He said, "You." I said, "Where is she." The younger one turned around. He said, "Who the —" I shot him in the chest. The gun was louder than I remembered. The whole house shook with it. The kid went back against the counter and slid down with his hand on his chest and his mouth open like he was going to say something and then he didn't say anything, ever again. He was nineteen. I found out later he was nineteen. He had a driver's license from Bakersfield and a photo of a dog in his wallet. Vince was still sitting at the table. He hadn't moved. I said, "Where is she." He said, "You shouldn't have come here." I said, "Where." He looked at me for a long time. He looked at me the way I've looked at people. Like I was a thing he'd been expecting his whole life. He said, "Boatyard. Pier Four. They move her at dawn." I said, "Who's there." He said, "Marco. Ruiz." He paused. "Three others." I said, "Is she okay." He said, "She's scared. She's not hurt." He paused again. "She asked for you." That was the thing that almost broke me. Not the fire. Not the arm. That. *She asked for you.* I said, "Thank you." He nodded. He didn't beg. He didn't try to convince me. He just sat there with his coffee and looked at me and waited. I shot him in the head. — I found the map on the wall in the hallway. I found a phone on the table with a text thread that confirmed it. I found a set of car keys on a hook by the door and a jacket that fit me and a first aid kit in the bathroom that I used to wrap my arm properly, with the duct tape, ugly but tight. I sat in the Tahoe for a minute before I started it. I looked at my hands on the wheel. They were shaking. I didn't know if it was the pain or the cold or something else. I decided it didn't matter. I decided a lot of things didn't matter, right then. That was going to be my whole strategy. Decide things don't matter. Keep moving. I started the car. The radio came on. It was the end of some song I didn't know, something slow and sad, and I turned it off, and I pulled out of the driveway, and I drove toward the harbor.

# Chapter 5: Little Girl Lost The boatyard was on the water, south of the airport, where the city runs out of land and turns into docks and cranes and shipping containers stacked like Legos. I parked the Tahoe two blocks away and walked the rest of it, and the whole time I could hear planes taking off overhead, one every ninety seconds or so, that low rumble that starts in your chest and moves up into your teeth. I found a spot behind a stack of containers and I sat down and I looked at the place. It was bigger than I'd expected. That was the first problem. I'd been picturing a dock and a shed and a few guys standing around. It wasn't that. It was a working yard — cranes, forklifts, a couple of buildings, a long pier with boats tied up along it, a chain-link fence with razor wire on top that ran the whole perimeter. There were lights on poles, and there were lights in the buildings, and there were men. I counted four. Then I counted again and got five. Then I stopped counting because counting wasn't helping. My arm was throbbing. I'd wrapped it tight with the duct tape and it was holding, but it was holding the way a tourniquet holds — it was keeping me upright, not making me better. Every time my heart beat I could feel it in the bone. I'd taken two of the painkillers from the first aid kit. They weren't doing anything. They were doing the thing where they make you think they're going to work and then don't. I sat there for a while and watched. The men moved in patterns. That's the thing about professionals — they have patterns. One of them walked the fence line every twelve minutes. One of them stood by the main building and smoked. Two of them were on the pier, near a boat that was tied up at the end, a white cabin cruiser with its lights off. And one of them — I couldn't see him, but I could feel him — was somewhere I couldn't see. Inside the building, maybe. Or on the boat. Or behind me. I didn't like that last one. I sat there and I made a plan. Then I threw the plan away, because the plan was stupid. The plan was: go in through the fence on the north side, take out the fence walker, move along the containers to the pier, take out the two on the pier, get to the boat. That was the plan. The plan assumed I could move fast and quiet and not get seen, and I couldn't. I had one arm. I had a gun I barely knew how to use. I had a body that had been beaten and burned and broken in the last three hours, and it was starting to send me messages. The messages were: *stop. lie down. sleep.* I sat there and I listened to the planes and I watched the men and I thought about Lily. She was in there. Somewhere in there. She was seven years old and she was scared and she'd asked for me, and I was sitting behind a shipping container with a broken arm, doing math. I thought about the compound in Afghanistan. I thought about the room with the three children. I thought about the man I shot in the face. I thought about the way the kids looked at me afterward — not scared, not grateful, just *blank*, like they'd already gone somewhere inside themselves where no one could reach them. I thought: *not again.* I got up. I don't know what I was going to do. I think I was going to do something stupid. I think I was going to walk through the front gate and start shooting and hope for the best, because I didn't have anything better. That's the truth. I was going to die in that boatyard, and I knew it, and I was going to do it anyway, because the alternative was sitting behind a container while a seven-year-old waited for me. And then the fence walker came around the corner and saw me. He was young. Younger than Diego. He had a flashlight and he swung it at me and the beam caught me in the face and he said, "Hey —" And I shot him. I don't remember deciding to do it. I remember the sound. I remember the way his body folded. I remember the flashlight hitting the ground and rolling and the beam spinning around and around like something out of a movie. I remember thinking, *that's it, that's the plan, that's the whole plan now*, and then I was moving. I ran. Or I did the thing I could do that was like running. I went along the fence and through the gap where the gate was open and into the yard, and I heard shouting behind me, and I heard a car engine start somewhere, and I heard a man's voice — Marco's voice, I'd learn later — yelling something in Spanish, and I kept moving. I got to the containers. I got behind one. I stopped and I leaned against it and I breathed and I listened. The shouting had stopped. That was worse than the shouting. Shouting means people are confused. Silence means people are organized. Silence means people are coming. I looked around the corner of the container. The two men on the pier were gone. The man by the main building was gone. The yard was empty. The lights were still on. The boat was still there. And then I heard it. Small. Thin. Coming from the building on the left, the one with the light in the window. A girl's voice. "Meg." Just that. Just once. Just the way she'd said it outside the burning house. I started walking toward the building. I didn't run. I didn't have it in me to run. I just walked, one foot in front of the other, across the open yard, in the light, in the open, with a gun in my hand and a broken arm in a duct-tape sling and a dead man's jacket on my back, and I didn't care who saw me. I didn't care about the men. I didn't care about Ruiz. I didn't care about anything except the voice. *Meg.* I'm coming. I'm coming. I'm coming.

WEAKNESSES: The chapter has a few moments that don't fully land. "Stacked like Legos" is a slightly tired simile for shipping containers. The shooting of the fence walker is handled well in terms of Meg's dissociation, but the line "I don't remember deciding to do it" is a familiar beat in this genre. The emotional vulnerability of those roadside stops — talking to Lily who isn't there, saying things she wouldn't say if Lily could hear — is missing. This is a real loss; it was supposed to be the chapter's emotional core before the action begins. DARKNESS AND LIGHTNESS: The darkness is well-earned. The violence (the fence walker's death) is handled with appropriate brevity and consequence. There's no glorification. The humor is absent from this chapter, which is appropriate given the circumstances, though the plan did note Meg's dry self-awareness — there are traces of it ("counting wasn't helping") but the chapter is grimmer than some others in the sequence. OVERALL: A competent, often effective chapter that executes its action beats well and maintains voice consistency. The missing road section is the most significant deviation from the plan. The prose is clean and controlled, occasionally reaching for effect in ways that don't quite pay off, but never embarrassing itself. # Chapter 6: The House of the Dead The building was a maintenance shed. Concrete floor, metal walls, a workbench along one side with tools hanging above it, a coffee maker, a radio playing something soft and Mexican. There was a door at the back that led to a smaller room — an office, maybe, or a break room — and there was a light under it. I didn't go straight to the door. I'd learned that much. I went along the workbench and I took a hammer off the wall and I put it in my belt, and I took a box cutter and I put it in my pocket, and I took a length of chain off a hook and I wrapped it around my good hand, and I stood in the middle of the room and I listened. Nothing. No footsteps. No voices. Just the radio. They'd heard the shot. They'd heard the shouting. They'd organized. And now they were waiting. I looked at the door with the light under it. *Meg.* I walked to it. I put my hand on the knob. I turned it. The room was small. A desk, a chair, a filing cabinet, a window with the blinds down. And in the middle of it, tied to the chair with zip ties around her wrists and her ankles, was Lily. She looked up when I came in. She'd been crying — I could see the tracks on her face — but she wasn't crying now. She was just looking at me. Taking notes. I said, "Hey, kid." She said, "Meg." I said, "I told you I'd come." She said, "I know." I crossed the room and I knelt down in front of her and I took the box cutter out of my pocket and I cut the zip ties off her wrists. She didn't move. She just sat there and looked at me and I looked back at her, and I wanted to say something. I wanted to say something that would make it okay. I didn't have anything. There was nothing to say. I got the ankle ties. I stood up. I picked her up with my good arm and I held her against my hip and she put her arms around my neck and her face against my shoulder and she was shaking. Not crying. Just shaking. I could feel it through her whole body. I said, "We're going." She said, "Mr. Bun." I said, "What?" "Mr. Bun. He's —" And then the door behind me opened and Marco came in with a gun. He was breathing hard. He had his gun up and his hands were shaking and he was looking at me the way a man looks at something he's been told isn't real. He said, "Put her down." I didn't put her down. He said, "Put her down. Put her down or I'll —" I said, "You'll what." He didn't answer. He just stood there with the gun pointed at me and his hands shaking and his eyes moving between me and Lily and the door and back again. He was trying to figure out how this had happened. He was trying to figure out how a nanny had walked into a cartel safehouse and killed his crew and come out the other side. He couldn't. You could see it on his face. He couldn't make it make sense. I said, "Where's Ruiz." He said, "He's — he's on the boat. He's waiting. He's —" I said, "Is he alone." He said, "No. There's — there's two more. On the boat. With him." I said, "Okay." And then I moved. I don't know how to describe it. I was holding a seven-year-old girl in one arm and I had a length of chain wrapped around the other hand and I moved toward him, and he fired, and the bullet went past my head and into the wall behind me, and I hit him with the chain. I hit him in the face. Once. Twice. He went down and the gun went off again and the bullet went into the floor and I hit him again and then I stopped. I don't know how long I hit him. I know that when I stopped, he wasn't moving, and Lily was crying into my shoulder, and my hand hurt from the chain, and there was blood on the wall and on the floor and on my face. I stood there for a second. I looked at what I'd done. I felt nothing. I turned around. I walked out of the room. I walked through the shed and out the front door and into the yard. The yard was empty. The men from the pier were gone. The man from the building was gone. They were all on the boat. That was the only place left. I looked at the boat. The white cabin cruiser, tied up at the end of the pier, lights off, dark against the dark water. Somewhere in there was Ruiz. Somewhere in there were two more men. Somewhere in there was the end of this. Lily said, "Meg." I said, "Yeah." She said, "I'm scared." I said, "I know." She said, "Are you scared?" I said, "Yeah." She said, "Okay." I don't know why that made her feel better. Maybe it was the truth. Maybe she just wanted the truth. Maybe she'd been waiting her whole life for someone to tell her the truth. I walked down the pier. One foot in front of the other. The boat got bigger. The water moved under the boards. Somewhere behind me, a plane took off, and the sound went through my chest, and I kept walking. At the end of the pier, I stopped. The boat had a name painted on the back. *La Reina.* The Queen. I stepped aboard. The deck was empty. There was a door at the back of the cabin, and there was a light on inside, and I could see a shape moving behind the glass. I set Lily down on the deck. I knelt in front of her and I put my hand on her face and I looked at her. I said, "Stay here. Don't move. Don't make a sound. Not for anything." She said, "Okay." I said, "I'll be right back." I'd like to know what you are." I said, "I'm the babysitter." He looked at me for a long time. Then he nodded, slowly, like I'd told him something he'd been trying to figure out. He said, "Yes. I suppose you are."

I parked in the emergency lot and I sat there and I looked at the doors and I thought about what was going to happen when I walked through them. They'd call the police. They had to. He asked me questions. I answered them. Some of them. I told him I was the nanny. I told him men broke in. I told him I got Lily out. I didn't tell him the rest of it. He came in with his tie loose and his eyes red and he stood at the foot of my bed and he looked at me for a long time and he didn't say anything. Then he said, "Thank you." I said, "Okay." He said, "You saved my daughter." I said, "Yeah." He said, "I don't know how to thank you." I said, "You don't have to." He left. I lay there and looked at the ceiling and listened to the machines beep and thought about nothing. I'm good at thinking about nothing. Lily came the next day. She said, "Are you coming tomorrow?" I said, "Yeah." She said, "Promise?" I said, "Promise." I went the next day. I made her dinner and I read her the book about the mouse on the motorcycle and I sat on the floor next to her bed and I listened to her breathe until she fell asleep. And then I sat there for a while in the dark with the rabbit on my lap, the one she'd given me, the one she'd said wanted to stay with me. I don't know what happens next. I don't know if the cartel comes for me. I don't know if the FBI figures out what I did. Final Piece Evaluation

Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a confident, propulsive piece of pulp revenge fiction that largely succeeds at what it sets out to do. The author has a strong, distinctive voice — clipped, declarative, Hemingway-adjacent — and deploys it with considerable consistency across eight chapters. Let me examine the piece critically across multiple dimensions. VOICE AND STYLE: The prose style is the story's greatest strength. The short sentences, the repetition for emphasis ("I'm coming. I'm coming. I'm coming."), the dry self-awareness ("My knees crack like I'm sixty. That's what four deployments will do to you. That's what a lot of things will do to you.") — these work well and feel earned rather than affected. The voice is consistent throughout, which is a genuine achievement in a piece this long. However, the style occasionally tips into self-parody. The repetitive sentence structure, while effective in moderation, becomes a tic. "I said X. He said Y. I said X. He said Y." — this pattern is used so relentlessly in the dialogue scenes that it starts to feel mechanical rather than stylistically intentional. CHARACTER: Meg is a compelling protagonist. Her military background is revealed economically, her competence is demonstrated rather than merely stated, and her emotional core — the relationship with Lily — is genuinely touching. The detail of going back into the burning house for Mr. Bun is excellent character work. Lily is well-drawn for a seven-year-old: the "taking notes" quality, the gap-toothed smile, the way she checks locks by asking the same question repeatedly. These feel observed rather than invented. Ruiz is the weakest character. He's given a humanizing speech ("I have daughters...") that the story immediately undercuts, which is fine, but his decision to shoot his own man to save Meg is poorly motivated. The story gestures at "I want to understand" as his reason, but this doesn't hold up. A cartel boss who has been doing this for 24 years doesn't shoot his own enforcer out of intellectual curiosity. This is the story's most significant logical failure. PLOT AND ACTION: The action sequences are competent but strain credulity. A woman with a freshly broken arm who has been beaten, burned, and is bleeding from a gunshot wound kills six armed cartel members across multiple locations over the course of a few hours. The story acknowledges this is improbable ("I don't know where the strength came from") but acknowledgment isn't the same as earning it. The pulp genre gives some latitude here, but the accumulation of physical punishment Meg absorbs while remaining functional pushes past even pulp conventions. The self-setting of a broken arm is a particularly egregious moment — she pulls the bone back into place alone, in a gas station bathroom, and then continues operating at high capacity. This is not how broken bones work, and the story doesn't earn this with sufficient mythologizing of Meg's toughness. DIALOGUE: The dialogue is the piece's most significant weakness. The "I said / He said" pattern strips all texture from conversations. Real dialogue has interruptions, misunderstandings, people talking past each other. Here, every exchange is perfectly turn-taking and on-the-nose. The Ruiz confrontation on the boat — which should be the dramatic and thematic climax — is particularly flat. His philosophical musings ("I want to understand") feel like a device to delay action rather than genuine character revelation. PACING: The pacing is generally strong. The story moves quickly, chapters are well-sized, and the escalation from babysitting to boatyard feels appropriately propulsive. The final chapter (the aftermath) is the right length and the right tone — it doesn't overstay its welcome. EMOTIONAL ENGAGEMENT: The Meg-Lily relationship is genuinely affecting. The moment where Lily says "She asked for you" is the story's emotional peak, and it lands. The ending — Lily giving Meg Mr. Bun, Meg returning to work the next day — is quietly moving. The circular structure (ending where it began, with the kid not wanting to sleep) is effective. FORCED POETRY: There are moments where the style reaches for profundity and misses. "Business doesn't" (as opposed to cruelty having a reason) is a bit too neat. The repeated "I'm coming" is effective the first time and overwrought by the third. The "just the sun" ending of Chapter 7 is the kind of thing that sounds meaningful but is actually vague. WORLD BUILDING: Minimal but functional. The San Diego/National City setting is used well — it's specific enough to feel real without becoming travelogue. The cartel context is sketched rather than developed, which is appropriate for the genre. UNEARNED TRANSFORMATIONS: Ruiz shooting his own man is the clearest example of an unearned transformation — a character acting against established motivation for plot convenience. The story also somewhat rushes past the psychological weight of Meg killing six people; she notes she "felt nothing" but this is presented as a character trait rather than something the story interrogates. OVERALL: This is a well-executed piece of pulp fiction with a strong voice, a genuinely affecting central relationship, and significant craft on display. Its weaknesses — the mechanical dialogue, the implausible physical endurance, the one major plot logic failure — prevent it from being exceptional, but it's solidly above average for the genre. # Brainstorming ## Character Ideas **The Narrator / Protagonist:** - A cab driver who works the graveyard shift, sees the city's underbelly, has a noir-appropriate job that allows for observation and isolation - A bartender at a dive bar who's seen too much and stopped caring—until someone makes them care again - A burned-out private investigator, but make them younger, more vulnerable, less Bogart and more broken - A night-shift nurse who patches up criminals off the books - A trans man who fled his hometown and reinvented himself in the city, working some job that keeps him invisible - A femme fatale's target rather than the detective—someone being pursued rather than doing the pursuing - A former academic (literature professor, art historian) who lost their career to scandal or addiction and now works some menial night job **The Love Interest ("cigarette smoke and bad ideas"):** - A small-time criminal—not a kingpin, but someone who runs scams, boosts cars, does B&Es. Dangerous but not powerful. Desperate. - A woman with a secret—maybe she's hiding from an abusive ex, maybe she's a con artist, maybe she's both victim and perpetrator - A nonbinary person who exists in the margins, survives by being adaptable, morally grey - An ex-con trying to go straight but failing - Someone with a connection to the narrator's past—an old flame, a former friend, someone who knew them "before" - A journalist chasing a story that will get them killed - A poet or artist who romanticizes danger and self-destruction - Someone who is literally dying (terminal illness, addiction) and therefore has nothing to lose **Supporting Cast:** - A best friend / confidant who warns the narrator away (the "you're going to get hurt" voice) - An antagonist: a crime boss, a corrupt cop, an abusive ex, a rival criminal - A neutral party: a bar owner, a neighbor, someone who provides information but stays out of the fray - The city itself as a character—rain-slicked streets, neon signs, 3am diners ## Setting Ideas - **Contemporary urban:** A mid-sized American city with a decaying downtown, a gayborhood, industrial outskirts. Think rust belt meets noir. - **New York:** The classic. But which era? The 70s/80s grit (Cruising, Taxi Driver), or contemporary? - **A coastal city:** Miami, San Francisco, Seattle—rain, fog, water as metaphor - **A fictional city:** Allows for more control over geography, politics, atmosphere - **Seasonal:** Late autumn into winter—cold, dark, the holidays as backdrop (loneliness amplified) - **Time period:** The 1950s (classic noir, but harder to write queer joy without historical trauma), the 1970s (post-Stonewall but pre-AIDS, a window of freedom and danger), contemporary (more freedom but different dangers) ## Tone & Style - **Hardboiled first person:** Short sentences, sardonic observations, emotional restraint that occasionally cracks - **Lyrical but controlled:** Poetic without being purple. Think Denis Johnson, James Baldwin, Patricia Highsmith - **Dual timeline:** Alternating between "then" (how they met) and "now" (how it's falling apart)—creates tension, foreshadowing - **Second person:** "You walk into the bar and you see him..."—puts the reader in the narrator's shoes, creates intimacy - **Epistolary elements:** Letters, texts, voicemails interspersed - **Present tense:** Immediacy, urgency - **The "bad idea" is self-aware:** The narrator knows this is a mistake and does it anyway. The tension is not "will they get together" but "how badly will this end" ## Plot Possibilities **Option A: The Heist Gone Wrong** - Narrator meets love interest, gets pulled into a crime - The crime goes wrong, someone dies, they go on the run - The climax is a confrontation with the antagonist - Ending: ambiguous—they survive but lose each other, or they escape but are forever changed **Option B: The Abusive Ex** - Love interest is hiding from someone dangerous - Narrator falls for them, wants to protect them - The ex finds them, violence ensues - Ending: they survive, but the narrator realizes they can't save anyone; or the love interest goes back; or the love interest kills the ex and they bury the body together (dark romance) **Option C: The Con** - Love interest is running a scam, and the narrator is the mark - But the love interest falls for real, complicating the plan - The antagonist is the person the love interest is working for - Ending: they turn the tables on the antagonist, or they go down together, or the love interest betrays the narrator and the narrator lets them **Option D: The Slow Burn** - Less plot-driven, more character-driven - The "bad idea" is the relationship itself—two self-destructive people enabling each other - The antagonist is internal: addiction, mental illness, self-sabotage - Ending: one of them gets sober/gets help and the other doesn't, and they have to part; or they both spiral; or they find a way to be broken together **Option E: The Murder** - Love interest is involved in a murder (as perpetrator or witness) - Narrator gets pulled into covering it up - The tension is external (will they get caught?) and internal (can the narrator live with this?) - Ending: they get away with it but are haunted; or one confesses; or they turn on each other **Option F: The Past Returns** - Narrator and love interest have history—maybe they were lovers before, maybe the narrator did something unforgivable - They reunite, and old patterns reassert themselves - The "bad idea" is revisiting something that already failed - Ending: they finally get it right, or they finally let each other go, or they destroy each other for good ## Story Beats (Generic 8-Chapter Structure) 1. **The Meet:** Establish narrator's world, voice, loneliness. Love interest enters. Immediate chemistry, immediate warning signs. 2. **The Pull:** They spend more time together. The narrator is drawn in despite themselves. First kiss / first intimate scene. Warning from a friend. 3. **The Complication:** The love interest's dangerous side becomes clear. The narrator is asked to do something, or witnesses something, that crosses a line. 4. **The Point of No Return:** The narrator is fully in. They commit to the love interest, knowing it's a mistake. The antagonist becomes a clear threat. 5. **The False Calm:** A moment of happiness, or the illusion of it. They play house. But the seeds of destruction are already planted. 6. **The Turn:** The betrayal, the violence, the revelation. Everything falls apart. The narrator realizes how bad this is. 7. **The Climax:** Confrontation with the antagonist, or with each other. A choice must be made. Someone gets hurt. 8. **The Aftermath:** Resolution—tragic, bittersweet, or ambiguously hopeful. The narrator reflects on what they've learned (or haven't). Final image that echoes the opening. ## Pacing Considerations - Chapters 1-2: Slow, atmospheric, character-building - Chapters 3-4: Increasing tension, plot kicks in - Chapter 5: Breather, false sense of security - Chapters 6-7: Rapid escalation, violence, climax - Chapter 8: Denouement, reflection, emotional payoff ## Tone References - *The Long Goodbye* (1973) — noir with emotional depth - *Inherent Vice* — stoner noir, confusion as aesthetic - *Carol* (2015) — queer romance with noir elements, longing, restraint - *Bound* (1996) — queer neo-noir, tension, desire - *The Talented Mr. Ripley* — obsession, identity, moral decay - *Killing Eve* — toxic queer romance, violence and desire intertwined - *Disco Elysium* — voice, failure, self-destruction - *The City and the Pillar* — queer loneliness, desire, tragedy - *Giovanni's Room* — queer love, shame, self-destruction ## "Bad Ideas" Brainstorm What makes the love interest a "bad idea"? - They're a criminal - They're married / unavailable - They're an addict - They're emotionally unavailable / avoidant - They're violent - They're using the narrator - They're related to the narrator's enemy - They're dying - They're a cop (and the narrator is a criminal) - They're the narrator's ex's sibling - They bring out the worst in the narrator—old addictions, old violence, old patterns - The narrator is the "bad idea" for them—the relationship is mutually destructive - They're underage (no—too problematic, skip) - They're the narrator's therapist / doctor / someone with power over them (ethically fraught, interesting but complicated) - They're a ghost / hallucination (unreliable narrator)—maybe too experimental for this scope ## Queer Specificity - The queerness should be present but not the conflict—the conflict is the noir plot and the bad romance - Homophobia can exist in the background (a slur from a passerby, a wary look from a landlord) but shouldn't be the central tension - The relationship should feel specific to queer experience: the intensity, the chosen family, the secrecy (even in a world where they don't have to be secret, there's a shadow of it) - Consider trans identity: does the narrator or love interest being trans add to the noir themes of identity, reinvention, being seen/not seen, danger in intimacy? - The "bad idea" romance can be coded as the past (self-destruction, internalized shame) vs. the future (self-love, the possibility of something better) ## Title Ideas - *Cigarette Smoke and Bad Ideas* - *The Last Bad Decision* - *Neon and Ash* - *What We Do in the Dark* - *A Good Reason to Ruin Everything* - *The Shape of a Mistake* - *All the Wrong Reasons* - *Smoke Gets in Your Eyes* - *Bad Idea, Sweetheart* - *The Long Fall* --- # Reflection ## What Works **The core tension is strong.** "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas" immediately establishes a dynamic: the narrator knows this is a mistake, and is doing it anyway. That self-awareness is key to noir and to compelling romance. The reader is not waiting to see *if* this goes wrong, but *how* and *why*. **Queer neo-noir romance is a rich space.** Noir has always had a queer subtext (the femme fatale, the homosocial detective, the coded villain), and explicitly queer neo-noir (Bound, Killing Eve, The Last of Us Part II) shows there's an audience for stories where desire and danger are intertwined. The queerness shouldn't be the *problem*—it should be the *texture*. **The 8-chapter structure fits a novella/short story well.** It allows for a compressed arc: introduction, escalation, climax, aftermath. Each chapter can be a discrete scene or moment, and the transitions between chapters can carry as much weight as the scenes themselves. **First person past tense feels right.** It allows for reflection (the narrator looking back, knowing what's coming) and intimacy. The narrator can editorialize, can warn the reader, can acknowledge their own stupidity. It's the voice of someone telling you a story about a time they fucked up. **The "bad idea" is flexible.** It could be the love interest, the relationship, or the narrator's own choices. The ambiguity gives room to play. ## What Doesn't Work (Or Is Risky) **Too many plot elements can overcrowd 8,000 words.** A heist, a murder, an abusive ex, *and* a romantic arc is a lot. Better to pick one external plot (the threat) and focus on the relationship. The external plot should be simple—it's the pressure cooker, not the meal. **The "abusive ex" plot is familiar.** It's been done (and done well) many times. It risks veering into torture porn or trauma tourism if not handled carefully. It also can make the love interest seem passive (a victim) rather than an agent of their own destruction. Works better if the love interest has some responsibility, some complicity in their own danger. **The "con artist" plot is great but tricky.** It requires a reveal, a betrayal, which can feel like a twist for twist's sake. If the love interest is conning the narrator, the love story becomes a lie, which can retroactively sour the whole thing. Unless the con is *emotional* rather than financial—the love interest is using the narrator for comfort, for escape, for a place to crash, without realizing they're falling for real. That's messier and more interesting. **The "terminal illness" angle can be maudlin.** "I'm dying so let's have a tragic romance" is a well-worn path. It can work, but it risks feeling manipulative. **The "unreliable narrator / ghost" angle is probably too experimental** for this scope. It requires a lot of setup and can frustrate readers if not done perfectly. **The "we're both broken" angle is strong but needs external stakes.** If the conflict is purely internal (addiction, mental illness), the story risks being a mood piece without momentum. Better to have an external threat that forces the internal conflict to manifest. **The "1950s" setting is historically complicated.** Queer people existed and loved and fucked in the 50s, but the threat of violence, imprisonment, and social death is a lot to carry. It can be done (Carol, The Price of Salt), but it requires care. Contemporary setting avoids this, allows the queerness to be unremarkable, and lets the noir elements come from other sources (crime, class, addiction, violence). ## What I'm Leaning Toward (Without Deciding) **Setting:** Contemporary, unnamed American city. Late autumn/winter. Industrial, rainy, neon. The city is a character—hostile, beautiful, indifferent. **Narrator:** A trans man, late 20s/early 30s. He fled his hometown, transitioned in the city, works a night job (I'm thinking cab driver or bartender). He's isolated, observant, self-deprecating, smart. He's not a detective, but he *sees* things. He's been hurt before and thinks he's learned his lesson. He hasn't. **Love Interest:** A woman or nonbinary person, also late 20s/early 30s. They're a small-time criminal—not a mastermind, just someone who does what they need to survive. Charming, magnetic, reckless. They're in danger from someone (an ex, a partner, a boss). They're not a victim, but they're not innocent either. They smoke. They have bad ideas. They're the kind of person who makes you feel alive and then sets your life on fire. **The "Bad Idea":** The relationship itself. The narrator knows this person is trouble. The love interest knows they're trouble. They do it anyway. The bad idea is also the narrator's *return* to something—maybe he used to be like this, maybe he used to date people like this, maybe he thought he was done with this kind of chaos. Falling for this person is a relapse. **The External Plot:** The love interest is in trouble. Someone is after them—a former partner, a employer, a mark they scammed. The narrator gets pulled in. The question is not "will they survive" (they will) but "what will it cost them" and "will they stay together." **The Ending:** Bittersweet. They survive the external threat, but the relationship is damaged. Maybe they stay together, but we know it's not forever. Maybe they part, but with love. Maybe one of them leaves the city. The final image should echo the opening—the narrator alone, smoking, thinking about the person they can't forget. **Voice:** First person past tense. Hardboiled but vulnerable. Short sentences. Concrete details. Occasional moments of lyricism. The narrator is telling this story to someone (maybe a friend, maybe a therapist, maybe the reader). **Chapter Structure:** Each chapter should be a discrete scene or moment, with a clear setting and a turn. The chapters should escalate in tension and intimacy. By Chapter 4, the narrator should be in too deep. By Chapter 6, everything should be falling apart. By Chapter 8, we should have resolution—not necessarily happy, but earned. ## What I Need to Decide - Is the love interest a woman, a nonbinary person, or a trans woman? (This affects the dynamics, the stakes, the specificities.) - What is the external threat? (An ex? A boss? A mark? A cop?) - What is the narrator's specific job? (Cab driver, bartender, night nurse, etc.) - Does the narrator have a friend/confidant, or is he completely isolated? - What is the "bad idea" specifically? Is it the person, or the return to a pattern, or both? - How explicit is the romance? (Sex scenes? Fade to black? Emotional intimacy without physical?) - What is the tone of the ending? (Tragic? Bittersweet? Ambiguously hopeful?) - What is the final image? (The narrator alone? The narrator with someone new? The narrator looking at a photograph? A cigarette burning down to nothing?) These are the questions I'd want to answer before drafting. The brainstorming has given me a lot to work with. Now I need to narrow.

Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention ## Core Concept A queer neo-noir romance about a trans man named **Vic**, a night-shift cab driver in a rust-belt city, who falls for **Rook**—a magnetic, self-destructive small-time criminal who is all cigarette smoke and bad ideas. The story is told in first-person past tense, looking back, with the narrator aware of his own stupidity and telling the story anyway. The romance is the bad idea. The external plot is simple: Rook is in danger from a former partner named **Marla**, and Vic gets pulled in. The ending is bittersweet—they survive, but the relationship doesn't, and Vic is left with the knowledge that he'd do it again. ## Plot - **External plot:** Rook owes money to Marla, a more dangerous criminal who was once Rook's lover and partner. Rook has been hiding, but Marla finds them. Vic gets caught in the middle. The climax is a confrontation where Vic has to choose between his own safety and Rook's. - **Internal plot:** Vic thought he was done with this kind of chaos. He transitioned, moved cities, built a quiet life. Falling for Rook is a relapse into old patterns—dating dangerous people, confusing intensity with intimacy, mistaking being needed for being loved. The story is about Vic learning (or not learning) that he can't save anyone, and that love isn't the same as rescue. - **Romance arc:** Meet, attraction, warning signs ignored, intimacy, escalation, betrayal (of a kind), climax, aftermath. They don't end up together. But the love was real. That's the tragedy. ## Voice - **First person past tense.** Vic is telling this story after the fact. He's sardonic, self-aware, occasionally poetic. He knows how it ends. He's telling you anyway. - **Hardboiled but vulnerable.** Short sentences. Concrete details. Emotion expressed through action and image rather than direct statement. Occasional moments of lyricism that crack the hardboiled surface. - **The narrator addresses the reader occasionally**—"You'd think I'd know better. I didn't."—but this is used sparingly. No more than once per chapter. - **Avoid:** purple prose, over-explaining emotions, therapy-speak, quirkiness, sentimentality. The tone should be controlled, restrained, and let the emotion emerge from the gaps. ## Style - **Setting as character:** The city is unnamed but specific—rust belt, industrial, rainy, neon, 24-hour diners, dive bars, empty streets at 4am. Late autumn into winter. Cold. - **Sensory detail:** Cigarette smoke, wet asphalt, cheap coffee, the hum of the cab's heater, the flicker of a broken neon sign. The physical world is vivid and concrete. - **Dialogue:** Sparse, loaded. What's not said matters as much as what is. Rook is charming, evasive, a little cruel. Vic is dry, observant, self-deprecating. - **Sex and intimacy:** Present but not explicit. The focus is on emotional intimacy—the vulnerability of being seen, the danger of being known. A kiss that means too much. A night spent together that Vic narrates around rather than through. - **Queerness:** Present but not the conflict. Vic is trans; this is established early and treated as fact, not plot. Rook is queer; this is unremarkable. Homophobia and transphobia exist in the background (a look, a comment, the threat of violence that all queer people carry) but are not the source of the story's tension. The story is about two queer people being messy and human and self-destructive. - **Avoid:** coming-out narratives, trauma porn, tragedy that punishes queerness. The tragedy is about two people who can't save each other, not about queerness itself. ## What I'm Aiming For - **Tension:** Constant, low-grade tension that escalates. The reader should feel the pull of the bad idea, the inevitability of the fall. - **Ambivalence:** Rook should be genuinely magnetic and genuinely dangerous. The reader should understand why Vic falls for them, even as they want to scream at him to run. - **Earned emotion:** The ending should feel inevitable and devastating, but not nihilistic. There should be love in it, even if there's loss. - **Specificity:** The city, the job, the small details of these people's lives should feel real and particular. - **Restraint:** The story should trust the reader. No explaining what can be shown. No telling the reader how to feel. ## What I'm Avoiding - **Melodrama:** No soap-opera twists, no amnesia, no secret twins. The plot is simple; the emotion is complex. - **Moralizing:** The story shouldn't judge Vic or Rook. It should present them as people, not cautionary tales. - **Clichés:** No "I can fix them" arc, no redemption, no neat resolution. The love is real, but it's not enough. - **Overcrowding:** One external plot, one relationship, one arc. Keep it tight. - **Romanticizing abuse:** Rook should be dangerous and chaotic, but not abusive to Vic. The bad idea is their own self-destruction, not cruelty toward each other. Their love should be genuine, even if it's doomed. --- # Chapter Planning ## Chapter 1: The Pickup **Setting:** 3am, a rain-slicked street outside a dive bar called The Rusty Nail. November. **Summary:** Vic picks up Rook as a fare. Rook is bleeding from a cut above their eyebrow, smiling like it's nothing. They ask to go to an address on the other side of town. Vic should say no. He doesn't. They talk. Rook is charming, evasive, flirty. Vic is drawn in despite himself. The chapter ends with Rook getting out, leaving a smear of blood on the seat and a phone number on the back of a receipt. Vic knows he should throw it away. He doesn't. **Voice notes:** Introduce Vic's voice—dry, observant, self-aware. He tells the reader he should have thrown the receipt away. He didn't. "You already know how this ends." **Beats:** 1. Vic's cab, the rain, the lonely rhythm of the night 2. Rook gets in—the crackle of danger, the smell of smoke 3. The drive, the conversation, the pull 4. Rook gets out, leaves the number 5. Vic's late shift ends, he goes home, he looks at the receipt **Tone:** Atmospheric, slow, seductive. Establish the city, Vic's loneliness, the charged space between them. --- ## Chapter 2: The Call **Setting:** Vic's apartment—small, spartan, a place to sleep. The next day. **Summary:** Vic calls the number. Rook answers like they were expecting him. They meet for coffee at a 24-hour diner. Rook tells half-truths about themselves—claims they're a "consultant," makes jokes about being trouble. Vic doesn't believe them, doesn't care. They banter. Rook asks about Vic—the first person in a long time who has. Vic is guarded but wants to be seen. The chapter ends with Rook asking Vic for a favor: a ride somewhere at 2am. Vic says yes. **Beats:** 1. Vic's apartment, morning, the receipt on the kitchen counter 2. He calls Rook, the first conversation 3. The diner, the meeting, the chemistry 4. Rook deflects questions, turns them back on Vic 5. The favor, the yes **Tone:** Warmer than Chapter 1, but with an undercurrent of unease. The reader should see the warning signs Vic is ignoring. --- ## Chapter 3: The Favor **Setting:** The cab, various stops across the city, 2am–5am. A parking lot, an alley behind a pawn shop, a bridge with a view of the river. **Summary:** Vic drives Rook around. He doesn't ask what Rook is doing. He picks up on clues—a duffel bag, a phone call Rook takes in the parking lot, a manila envelope exchanged in the alley. Rook is a criminal, or something close to it. Vic should pull over and kick them out. He doesn't. Afterward, they park by the river. Rook kisses him. It's a bad idea. Vic kisses back. **Beats:** 1. The drive, the errands, the clues Vic ignores 2. The pawn shop exchange—Vic sees too much 3. A moment of danger—someone watching them? 4. The river, the quiet, the kiss 5. Vic drives home, alone, knowing he's in trouble **Tone:** Tense, electric. The kiss should feel earned but ominous. The reader should feel the line being crossed. --- ## Chapter 4: The Pull **Setting:** Vic's cab, Rook's apartment (a sublet, barely furnished, signs of impermanence), a bar where Rook's friend works. **Summary:** Vic and Rook spend more time together. Vic learns more—Rook is running from something, someone. They don't say who. Vic doesn't push. They fall into a routine: Vic drives, Rook accompanies him on shifts, they sleep at Vic's place. Vic's friend **Dez**, a fellow cab driver, warns him. "You're gonna get burned." Vic ignores her. The chapter ends with Vic at Rook's apartment, finding a gun in a drawer. Rook tells him it's for protection. Vic believes them. **Beats:** 1. The new routine, the intimacy of shared nights 2. Dez's warning, Vic's dismissal 3. Rook's apartment—the emptiness, the impermanence 4. The gun, the lie, Vic's willful ignorance 5. Ending: Vic lying awake, Rook asleep beside him **Tone:** Slow burn, domestic intimacy undercut with dread. The reader should see the danger building. --- ## Chapter 5: The Threat **Setting:** A parking garage, a bar, Vic's cab. **Summary:** Marla finds them. Vic comes back to the cab to find Rook talking to a tall woman with cold eyes. Rook is scared—the first time Vic has seen them scared. After Marla leaves, Rook tells Vic part of the truth: Marla is an ex, a former partner in crime, and Rook owes her money. Rook promises to handle it. Vic wants to help. Rook says no. Vic insists. The chapter ends with Vic agreeing to help Rook with one last job—a pickup, a drop-off, nothing more. He's in now. **Beats:** 1. Vic's shift, returning to the cab, seeing Rook with Marla 2. The tension, Marla's coldness, Rook's fear 3. After—Rook's partial confession 4. The argument, Vic insisting on helping 5. The agreement, the point of no return **Tone:** Escalation, danger becoming real. The chapter should feel like a door closing. --- ## Chapter 6: The Job **Setting:** A warehouse on the outskirts of the city, a stretch of empty highway, a motel room. **Summary:** Vic drives Rook to the job. It goes wrong. There's a man, a gun, a struggle. Vic doesn't see everything—he's in the car, engine running, heart pounding. Rook comes back with blood on their hands and a duffel bag. They drive. They don't talk. At the motel, Rook cleans up, shakes, finally breaks down. Vic holds them. Rook says, "I'm sorry." Vic says, "I know." They don't say what they're sorry for. They both know. **Beats:** 1. The drive to the job, the silence, the tension 2. Vic waiting in the car, the sounds from inside 3. Rook returning—the blood, the bag, the silence 4. The motel—Rook's breakdown, Vic's comfort 5. Ending: Vic watches Rook sleep, knows they can't go back **Tone:** Climactic, violent, intimate. The violence should be implied rather than graphic. The emotional fallout is the focus. --- ## Chapter 7: The Choice **Setting:** Vic's apartment, Rook's apartment, a meeting with Marla. **Summary:** Marla wants more. The job wasn't enough—Rook still owes her. She gives them a choice: one more job, or she tells the police what Rook did. Rook wants to run. Vic wants to stay and fight. They argue. Rook says Vic doesn't understand—Marla won't stop, she'll never stop. Vic says he doesn't care. Rook says, "You should." The chapter ends with Rook leaving in the middle of the night. Vic wakes up alone. Rook has taken the cab. **Beats:** 1. The aftermath of the job, the new normal 2. Marla's ultimatum 3. Vic and Rook's argument—run or fight 4. Rook's confession: "I'm not worth this" 5. Vic waking up alone, the empty space, the missing cab **Tone:** Emotional climax. The argument should be raw, honest, the first time they've really said what they mean. The abandonment should feel inevitable and devastating. --- ## Chapter 8: The Aftermath **Setting:** The city, weeks later. Vic's apartment. A bar. A street corner. A bus station. **Summary:** Vic looks for Rook. He doesn't find them. He learns from Dez that Marla was arrested—someone tipped off the police. Vic knows it was Rook. He doesn't know where they went. The chapter is about aftermath, about the slow process of letting go. Vic drives his new cab (the old one was found abandoned). He thinks about Rook. He knows he'd do it again. The final scene: Vic at a diner at 3am, months later. A new fare gets in. Someone with a bruise, a smile, a bad idea. Vic hesitates. Then he says, "Where to?" The story ends with the engine starting, the city ahead, the possibility of another mistake. Vic knows better. He does it anyway. **Beats:** 1. The search, the not-finding 2. Learning about Marla's arrest, Rook's goodbye 3. The slow return to normal—driving, sleeping, surviving 4. A memory of Rook—a specific, small moment 5. The final scene: the new fare, the choice, the engine starting **Tone:** Bittersweet, earned, ambiguous. The ending should feel like a cycle beginning again, but with the knowledge of what it costs. Vic isn't healed. He's not saved. But he's still here.

They'd have a song or a film or a book that they're trying to capture the feeling of. They'd write the first chapter and then realize it's wrong and start over. The specificity comes from lived experience and idiosyncratic taste, not from an averaged-out sense of what "noir" and "queer romance" typically look like. Human writers also make weird choices. They might decide the story is told in second person because it feels right. They might include a chapter that's just a list of things the narrator remembers about the love interest. They might end on a line that doesn't wrap anything up but just sits there, unresolved, because that's how it felt. The love interest is dangerous *but* vulnerable. The ending is tragic *but* hopeful. The narrator is hardboiled *but* sensitive. They want to cover all bases. The result is a story that feels like it was written by a committee trying not to offend anyone. **2. The "just enough" problem.** LLMs are good at calibrating. They'll write a sex scene that's just explicit enough, a violent scene that's just graphic enough, an emotional scene that's just vulnerable enough. This calibration is often the enemy of art. Human writers overshoot. They write something too raw, too weird, too much. Then they edit. The overshooting is where the life is. LLMs skip the overshooting and go straight to the "appropriate" version. **3. The "summarizing" problem.** LLMs love to summarize. They'll write a paragraph of scene and then a paragraph of reflection that tells you what the scene meant. They'll have a character say something and then have the narrator explain what it meant. They don't trust the reader. They don't trust the scene. They want to make sure you got it. Human writers often do the opposite—they under-explain, they leave gaps, they trust the reader to fill in the blanks. The gaps are where the reader lives. **4. The "impressive" problem.** LLMs want to impress. They'll reach for a metaphor that's too clever, a sentence that's too well-crafted, a structure that's too neat. They want you to notice how good they are. Human writers often want you to forget they're there. They want the prose to disappear. They end in the middle of a thought, a feeling, a moment. They let the reader sit with the ambiguity. This is especially true in noir, where resolution is often a lie—the case gets solved, but the world is still broken. **6. The "safety" problem.** LLMs are trained to be safe. They avoid uncomfortable content, ambiguous morality, characters who do bad things without being punished. They want the story to be "responsible." Human writers often write irresponsible stories. They let bad things happen. They let characters be unlikable. They let the ending be sad without a lesson. The "just enough" problem would make the intimacy too tasteful, the violence too controlled, the emotion too managed. This story needs to be a little messy. It needs moments of too much. It needs to risk sentimentality in order to earn the emotional payoff. The "summarizing" problem would kill the story. Noir is a genre of implication, of things unsaid.
