Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention ## Core Concept A former line cook—not a great one, just a guy who burned out of the industry—is starving in a ruined city with his dead neighbor's kid, Mila. He kills a spore mutant in self-defense, and because he's too hungry to think straight, he cooks it. It's the best thing he's ever tasted. The story follows what happens when survival tastes like something you want more of, and neither of them can pretend they're just doing what they have to do. ## The Central Betrayal The horror isn't that they're eating mutants. The horror is that they *like* it. The story should never let them off the hook with pure necessity—there's always enough plausible deniability to keep going, but never enough to feel clean. By the end, they're not eating to survive. They're eating because they want it. The last chapter will make that explicit without stating it. They could stop. They don't. That's the story. ## Voice and Style **Narrative Voice:** First person, past tense, from the cook's perspective. He was never poetic before, and starvation hasn't changed that. The voice is plain, matter-of-fact, occasionally dry. He describes cooking the way he'd describe any other task—technique, timing, heat. He doesn't have the vocabulary for what's happening to him, so he doesn't try to find it. The prose should not try to impress. It should be readable, grounded, human. When the horror comes, it comes from the content, from the gap between what he's doing and how matter-of-factly he's describing it. The reader does the work. **Tone:** Uneven by design. Some chapters will be routine, almost boring. Some will be devastating. Some will have moments of actual laughter between the two of them, real warmth, and then something will be said that makes the warmth curdle. The story should never settle into a consistent tone—because they never settle. They're always one beat away from something breaking. **What to Avoid:** - Literary flourishes that draw attention to the writing - Guilt as the protagonist's primary emotion—guilt is too easy, too resolved - A clean arc from horror to acceptance; this is not a journey, it's a rut - Explaining the mutants' biology - A villain, a rival, a plot complication that distracts from the relationship - The word "delicious"—it's too knowing. The protagonist wouldn't use it. - Any moment where a character says the theme out loud - The "bow" ending ## Character Choices **The Protagonist (Daniel, but mostly just "he"):** Mid-30s. Washed out of cooking years ago—got into it because he needed a job, got good enough to be useful, got tired and stopped caring. Worked at a mid-tier place with a rotating menu and a chef who screamed. Doesn't romanticize food. Doesn't think of himself as an artist. He's practical, a little selfish, not especially warm. He's not a natural caretaker. He took Mila in because she was there and he couldn't not. He resents her sometimes. He loves her. Both are true at once. **Mila, age 11:** The neighbor's kid. Not a symbol, not a conscience, not a mouthpiece. She's weird. She was weird before the outbreak—probably on the spectrum, probably had trouble at school, probably didn't have friends. The apocalypse almost suits her. She's methodical, curious, less emotional than Daniel, and her reactions to the mutants are not what he expects. She adapts faster. She asks questions he doesn't want to answer. She doesn't cry. That's what scares him. She's not a liability or a moral anchor—she's a kid who's figured something out before he has, and he's not sure he likes it. **The Mutants:** They don't retain obvious traces of humanity. No wedding rings, no familiar faces. They're just bodies—twisted, fungal, human-shaped things that scream and lunge. The horror isn't in what they were. The horror is in how quickly Daniel stops caring what they were. The story should never confirm or deny whether any part of them is still human. The protagonist doesn't ask. That's the point. ## Setting A specific mid-sized city, unnamed but grounded in detail: strip malls, a river, a neighborhood with a defunct restaurant called *Bellwether* where Daniel used to pick up shifts. They shelter there because it's familiar, because the walk-in fridge still works on generator power, because the kitchen has everything he needs. The irony is not commented on. It's just where he cooks. ## Structural Approach Eight chapters, each roughly 1000 words. The chapters should not all have the same shape—some cover a single meal, some cover weeks. The food motive recurs, but the chapters aren't obligated to have a "food centerpiece" in every one. Some chapters will be short on plot and heavy on texture. Some will be plot-driven. The asymmetry is intentional. The story should not build toward a climax. It should build toward a *recognition*. The reader should realize, before Daniel does, what's happening to him—and then the last chapter should confirm it without ever saying it. ## The Thematic Core (Stated Here, Never Stated in the Story) They could stop. There's enough food to stop. But they don't want to. Not because they're desperate—because they've found something that makes the days bearable, that gives them ritual, something to look forward to. That's the horror. The apocalypse didn't make them monsters. It just gave them permission to become what they already were willing to become. ## What This Story Is Really About Two people surviving together, and the slow, quiet realization that they are not good people, and that they might not have been good people before, and that they don't particularly care anymore. It's about the comfort of routine, the warmth of a meal, the way something can be both a lifeline and a betrayal—all at once. --- # Chapter Planning ## Chapter 1: The Last Thing in the Pantry **POV/Time:** Daniel, present. Day 61 of no food they didn't scavenge. The story opens three weeks into eating mutants already—but we don't know that yet. It's presented as routine. **Emotional Beat:** Flat, tired, routine. The chapter should feel almost boring. This is the point. Daniel wakes up. He checks the traps. He tends the garden he's trying (and failing) to keep alive. He and Mila eat something unremarkable. He goes hunting—which is what he calls it now. He kills a mutant. He cooks it. He and Mila eat it. He goes to sleep. **Plot:** Nothing surprising happens. That's the chapter. The reader should be almost lulled—should think this is a quiet survival story. The only off-note is small: when Daniel kills the mutant, he doesn't hesitate. When he cooks it, he's efficient. When he serves it, he doesn't say anything. Mila doesn't either. They just eat. **What's really happening:** The chapter is a horror chapter disguised as a routine one. The reader should finish it and realize, in retrospect, how far gone they already are. No flashback to the first kill. No explanation. Just the routine. **Ending:** Daniel cleans the knife, sets it by the door for morning, and lies down. Mila is already asleep. He thinks, distantly, that they're going to run out of salt soon. ## Chapter 2: Bellwether **POV/Time:** Daniel, earlier—a flashback chapter. How they got here. But not the origin of the outbreak—the origin of *this*. **Emotional Beat:** Hungry, desperate, but told with distance. The reader should feel the hunger, but through Daniel's memory, which has already smoothed it over. **Plot:** This is the first kill. Mila hasn't eaten in four days. Daniel hasn't eaten in longer. They're sheltering in Bellwether because Daniel knows the back door code. A mutant gets in through the dining room—breaks the glass, screams, lunges. Daniel kills it with a boning knife and it takes a long time. He sits with the body for maybe ten minutes, shaking. Mila comes out. She looks at the body. She says, "Are we going to eat it?" He says no. She says, "Why not?" He doesn't have an answer. That night, he cooks a piece of it—just a piece, just to see—and they split it. It's not amazing. It's just food. They don't talk about it. The next day, he cooks more. **What's really happening:** The origin story is not a moment of moral collapse. It's a moment of pragmatism. That's the horror. **Ending:** Daniel buries the rest of the body behind the restaurant, in the garden he hasn't planted yet. He tells himself it's a one-time thing. ## Chapter 3: Salt **POV/Time:** Daniel, present. Several weeks after Chapter 1. A chapter about getting salt. **Emotional Beat:** Almost a caper. Almost fun. The tone should lift here—should feel like the two of them have a project, a goal, something to do together. **Plot:** Salt is running out, and salt is the only thing that makes the food tolerable. Daniel and Mila plan a trip to a grocery distribution center three miles away. The trip is dangerous—mutants, collapsed roads, a stranger's body they have to walk around. They find salt. They find other things too: a case of canned tomatoes, a bag of rice, a jar of preserved lemons. On the way back, they get caught in the open by a pack of mutants. They hide in a drainage culvert for two hours, silent, pressed together. Mila is the one who spots the exit route. She's calm. Daniel isn't. When they get back to Bellwether, they cook a meal that's better than anything they've made in weeks. The rice, the tomatoes, the salt. They eat mutant meat with a real sauce for the first time. They laugh about the culvert. They name the mutant they're eating—a bad joke. They laugh harder. It's the best night they've had since the outbreak. **What's really happening:** This chapter is the seduction. It should be *fun*. The reader should enjoy it. The reader should catch themselves enjoying it and feel complicit. Mila's composure should be a small warning bell—she's not scared of the mutants, and she never was. Daniel doesn't notice. **Ending:** After dinner, Mila says she's glad they found the salt. Daniel says me too. Neither of them clarifies what they mean. ## Chapter 4: The Stranger **POV/Time:** Daniel, present, a few days after Chapter 3. A stranger arrives at Bellwether. **Emotional Beat:** Tension, paranoia, and an unexpected mirror. The stranger is not a threat—he's something worse. He's a version of them that hasn't crossed the line. **Plot:** A man named Roy finds Bellwether. He's older, ex-military, cautious. He's been surviving on scavenged food and doesn't know how bad things are getting for Daniel and Mila. He stays for dinner. Daniel cooks. Roy eats. Roy compliments the meal—says it's the best thing he's had in months, asks what it is. Daniel says rabbit. Roy doesn't question it. Mila watches Roy closely. After dinner, Roy asks if he can stay a few days. Daniel says yes. Over the next two days, Roy helps with repairs, talks about his family, talks about faith. He's decent. He's decent in a way that makes Daniel feel watched. On the third day, Roy sees Daniel cooking. He doesn't say anything. He just looks. That night, Roy leaves early, without saying goodbye. Daniel watches him go and doesn't stop him. Mila asks if they should have warned him. Daniel says he doesn't know what she means. She says, I think you do. They don't talk about it again. **What's really happening:** Roy is the reader's surrogate. His silence at the end is more damning than any accusation—he doesn't condemn them, he just leaves. The chapter's whole horror is in the recognition Daniel doesn't allow himself: Roy knows. Roy has known for a while. Roy is choosing not to look. And Daniel is grateful, and ashamed of being grateful. **Ending:** Daniel looks at the salt he bought last week. He doesn't know how it ran out already. He knows they'll need more soon. ## Chapter 5: The Recipe **POV/Time:** Daniel, present. A chapter about getting good at it. Weeks have passed. It's winter. **Emotional Beat:** Quiet pride, undercut by something the protagonist can't name. He's become skilled at something terrible, and part of him is glad. **Plot:** Daniel has started writing things down. Not recipes, exactly—just notes. Which cuts are best, how long to braise them, how to mask the aftertaste. He's stopped thinking of the mutants as people-shaped—they're just animals now, and the killing is not a big deal. He's started to do it efficiently: one blow to the back of the skull, quick bleed, quick butcher. He's learned to tell which mutants will taste better by how they move. (The slow ones, the ones that have been around a while, have more flavor. The fresh ones are tough. He doesn't know why and doesn't want to.) Mila has started helping with the butchering. She's better at it than he is—steadier hands, no hesitation. One evening, they're eating and Mila asks what it would taste like if they raised one. Daniel asks what she means. She says, if they kept one alive, fed it, cooked it later. Daniel says no. She says okay. She doesn't seem disappointed or upset—just curious. He realizes he doesn't know what she's feeling. He used to be able to tell. He doesn't know when that changed. **What's really happening:** The horror is not that they're eating mutants. It's that they've started to enjoy the craft of it. Daniel was never a good cook—he was competent. Now he's becoming something else. He's proud of his fileting technique. He's figuring out flavors. He's engaging with the work in a way he never did before. The apocalypse has made him a better cook than he ever was in the real world. He hates himself for noticing. He makes a note about braising times anyway. **Ending:** Daniel flips back through his notes. They're detailed. They're careful. They read like the journal of someone who's found something worth doing. ## Chapter 6: The Harvest **POV/Time:** Daniel, present. Late winter. The mutants are becoming scarce. **Emotional Beat:** Fear, then relief, then confusion. Then something worse than any of it. **Plot:** The mutants are thinning out. Daniel doesn't know if it's the winter, if they're migrating, or if the two of them have killed enough that there just aren't many left. They go four days without meat. Daniel notices he's irritable. Mila notices too—she says, "You're grumpy." He doesn't find it funny. They eat the last of their canned food, and it's fine, it's fine, it's *fine*. On the fifth day, Daniel finds a mutant in a parking garage. He kills it and brings it home. The whole way back, he's thinking about how he's going to cook it. He's not thinking about survival. He's thinking about the sear, the sauce, the way Mila will eat it in that methodical way she has, the way he'll feel full. He gets back to Bellwether, and Mila has set the table. She's cleaned the kitchen. She's been waiting. He realizes she's been waiting for this. That she wanted it. That he wanted it. That they both stopped needing it a while ago. He cooks. He plates. They eat. Neither of them says anything. He realizes they've been quiet during meals for weeks. **What's really happening:** The reveal. Not out loud—in Daniel's head, in his body, in the way he answers the question he's been avoiding. He could stop. There are caches he hasn't used. They could eat rice and canned tomatoes for months. He just doesn't want to. **Ending:** Daniel finishes his plate. He's still hungry. He always is now. ## Chapter 7: Roy Comes Back **POV/Time:** Daniel, present. Early spring. Roy returns—or rather, what's left of Roy. **Emotional Beat:** Grief that has nowhere to go, and the guilt that finally surfaces, and the way it gets immediately buried again. **Plot:** Roy didn't make it. He was killed by mutants, or he was bitten and turned, or he just starved. Daniel finds his body on the road outside the city. Daniel recognizes him from his jacket. He brings the body back. He doesn't tell Mila. He sits with it in the walk-in for a day. He thinks about Roy, about how decent he was, about how Roy knew and didn't say anything. He thinks about the fact that Roy's body is the same size as the mutants they've been eating. He has the thought. He hates himself for having the thought. He goes in the walk-in and looks at Roy's face, and he knows he's not going to eat Roy—that's still the line, that's still the line—but he also knows that the line has moved so much in the last year that he doesn't trust it anymore. He can't tell if the line is still in the right place or if it's just moved somewhere he's stopped noticing. He buries Roy outside, near the garden. He tells Mila Roy was dead when he found him. That night, she says, "You buried him." He says yes. She says, "We didn't bury the others." He says no. She says, "Why?" He says he doesn't know. She says, "I think they would have wanted it." He doesn't know if she means Roy or the mutants. He doesn't ask. He goes to bed. He dreams about Roy's face, and it's not really Roy's face, and he wakes up before the dream finishes. **What's really happening:** Daniel's buried the last thing that could have stopped him. Not Roy—the version of himself that could have stopped. He doesn't consciously know this. The reader will. **Ending:** In the morning, Daniel gets up and cooks breakfast. He doesn't think about Roy while he eats. He notices that he doesn't think about Roy while he eats. He keeps eating. ## Chapter 8: Breakfast **POV/Time:** Daniel, present. Spring. The garden is growing. It's a good chapter. That's the horror. **Emotional Beat:** Warmth, comfort, routine, and underneath it, the quiet certainty that something has gone wrong that can't be corrected. This chapter should feel like a cozy ending to a cozy story. It should feel *nice*. The reader should feel nice reading it. And then they should feel bad for feeling nice. **Plot:** A morning. Daniel wakes up, tends the garden, checks the traps (he still checks the traps—it's a habit). Mila is already awake, reading one of the books they scavenged. They cook breakfast together. Daniel has gotten good at this—he's found a way to make the meat tender, to make a sauce out of preserved tomatoes and the herbs from the garden. He plates two plates. They sit down. Mila says, "This is really good." Daniel says, "Yeah." She says, "Are we going to try raising one?" He says, "No." She says, "Why not?" He doesn't answer. He's thinking about how to answer. He's thinking that it's because raising one would make it worse, but he can't articulate why—something about the naming, something about the relationship. She says, "It's okay." She says, "I don't think I want to either." He says, "Good." They eat. It's a good meal. The sun is coming through the broken windows of Bellwether, and the light is nice, and the food is warm, and Daniel thinks—and this is the first time he's thought it clearly in months—that he's glad they didn't stop. He doesn't say it. He doesn't have to. **What's really happening:** Daniel has made peace. That's the ending. He's made peace with himself. The garden is growing. The food is good. He and Mila are alive. And some small part of him—the part that used to be a person—is gone, and he doesn't miss it, and that's the thing the reader should carry out of the story. Not the horror of what they did. The horror of what they don't regret. **Ending (final image):** Daniel finishes his plate. He looks at the garden through the window. Mila asks if he wants more. He says yes. She gets up to get it. He watches her go. The last line should be small and domestic and awful. Something like: *She gave me the bigger piece, like she always does.* The story ends. There's no reflection. No lesson. Just breakfast. --- ## Chapter Distribution Summary | Chapter | Title | Arc Beat | Food Centerpiece | Tone | |---------|-------|----------|------------------|------| | 1 | The Last Thing in the Pantry | Routine horror | An unremarkable meal, treated as nothing | Flat, almost boring | | 2 | Bellwether | The first kill | First piece, split between them, not discussed | Desperate, distant | | 3 | Salt | Seduction | A real meal with sauce and salt | Almost fun—whoops | | 4 | The Stranger | The mirror | Dinner with Roy | Tension, quiet shame | | 5 | The Recipe | Pride | A well-made braise | Quiet pride, unsettling | | 6 | The Harvest | Recognition | The meal Daniel has been looking forward to | Fear, then want | | 7 | Roy Comes Back | Grief buried | A breakfast eaten without thinking | Devastation, unacknowledged | | 8 | Breakfast | Acceptance | Two plates, a garden, a morning | Warm, comfortable, wrong |
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Daniel ## Background Daniel is 34. He grew up in a midsize city not unlike the one he's surviving in now—the kind of place with a river, some strip malls, a downtown that used to be something and isn't anymore. His parents were both nurses. They worked opposite shifts, so the house was always half-occupied, quiet, a rotating cast of one parent or the other leaving a plate covered in foil on the stove. He learned to cook out of necessity more than interest—by eleven, he could make a decent spaghetti bolognese, a passable stir-fry, a chicken breast that wasn't dry. His parents praised him for it, not in a warm way but in an approving way, the way you'd approve of someone taking out the trash. He kept doing it. He got into professional cooking at nineteen because he needed money and his friend's uncle's restaurant was hiring. He was good at it—not talented, not passionate, but *good*. He could handle a station. He could take orders. He could work a double without complaining. He could taste a sauce and know what it needed. That last thing was the only part that felt like a gift, and he never quite trusted it. He told himself he was just being practical. He worked in kitchens for eleven years. He was never fired, never quit dramatically, just moved around—each job slightly worse than the last, or slightly better, and he stopped being able to tell the difference. At his last job, a farm-to-table place with a rotating menu and a chef named Marta who screamed at everyone but somehow respected him, he started to realize he didn't care anymore. He'd stopped tasting his food. He'd stopped noticing what was good and what was fine. He'd just been making portions, sending them out, going home. Two weeks before the outbreak, he walked out mid-shift and never went back. He didn't have a plan. He sat in his apartment for a while, ate ramen, watched TV, thought about applying at a warehouse or a hospital kitchen or something. He told himself he was taking a break. He told himself he'd figure it out. Then the outbreak happened, and he stopped having to figure it out. He doesn't miss cooking. He misses the possibility of a normal life. He was never going to have one anyway, he thinks. He doesn't know if that's true. ## Personality Daniel is practical to a fault. He solves problems by reducing them. He doesn't think in terms of meaning or morality—he thinks in terms of *what's next*. What needs to be done. What's the next step. This isn't a defense mechanism; it's how he was built. He's not repressing anything. He just doesn't have a lot of interiority where emotions are concerned. He feels things, but he doesn't have the vocabulary for them, and he doesn't trust the vocabulary he does have. So he doesn't use it. He's dry. His humor is dry, almost flat. He doesn't tell jokes. He says things that are technically jokes but you have to be paying attention to catch them. He does this when he's uncomfortable, which is most of the time. He's not warm. He doesn't touch people. He doesn't say *I love you* or *I'm proud of you* or even *I care about you*. He shows care by doing—by making sure Mila has eaten, by fixing the generator, by keeping the knife sharp. If you asked him whether he loves Mila, he'd say something like *I'm responsible for her*, which, for him, is the same thing. He's a little selfish. He admits this to himself. He took Mila in not because he's a good person but because leaving her to die would have taken an effort he didn't have it in him to make. He resents her sometimes. He resents the responsibility, the noise, the way she asks questions he doesn't want to answer. He never says this. He knows it's unfair. He also knows it's true. He's prone to routines. The same breakfast, the same route to the water source, the same way of sharpening the knife. The routine is not comfort—it's just what he does. When the routine breaks, he gets irritable. Small things get to him: a spoon in the wrong place, Mila humming the same three notes over and over, a door that doesn't quite close. He doesn't say anything. He just notices, and the noticing bothers him. ## Idiosyncrasies - He always eats the smaller portion. Always. Even when there's enough. He doesn't know when this started. He doesn't think about it. If Mila offers him more, he says no. If she insists, he says *I'm fine*, and she stops. - He cleans the knife immediately after using it. Not because it matters—because he doesn't like seeing it dirty. He'll stop whatever he's doing to clean the knife, even if the next task is right there. - He counts things without meaning to. Steps, cans, days. He doesn't write them down. He just counts. - He has a specific way of sitting: knees apart, elbows on them, head down. He sits like this on the restaurant's back step, in the kitchen, at the table after meals. He's sat like this since high school. It's not a mood. It's just how he sits. - He doesn't hum, ever. Mila hums. Daniel doesn't. - He keeps a small notebook, but not for recipes—for notes. Lists. *Water. Battery. Salt.* He crosses things out when they're done. The notebook is messy and unorganized, but he knows where everything is in it. - He doesn't like mornings. He gets up early because he has to, but he doesn't like it. The first hour of the day, he's silent. He doesn't talk until he's eaten something. Mila knows this. She sometimes makes him tea without being asked. ## Physicality Daniel is average height—5'9", maybe 5'10". He used to be heavier; now he's thin in a way that doesn't suit him. His face is narrow, and the thinness reads as gaunt rather than lean. His hair is dark, cut short with kitchen shears—he does it himself, badly, every few months. He has the hands of a cook: not big, but strong, precise, scarred from years of small cuts. His forearms are the same. He has a burn scar on his left wrist from an oven he shouldn't have reached into, and he can't remember which job it was from. He moves efficiently. He doesn't gesture much when he talks. He keeps his hands still or uses them for a specific task. When he's idle, his hands go still, folded, resting on his knees. He doesn't fidget. He carries himself with a kind of closed stillness. He doesn't look at people when they talk to him—he looks at whatever he's doing, or the middle distance, or the ground. He has to make a conscious effort to make eye contact. When he does, it's brief, and he breaks away fast. This isn't shyness; it's just that eye contact doesn't come naturally, and he's never bothered to learn. When he's thinking, he touches his thumb to his fingers in sequence—thumb to index, thumb to middle, thumb to ring, thumb to pinky, repeat. He doesn't know he does this. He does it when he's planning, when he's worried, when he's trying to figure something out. Mila has noticed. She hasn't mentioned it. His expression doesn't change much. He doesn't smile when he's happy—he gets quieter. He doesn't scowl when he's angry—he also gets quieter. The difference is in what he's quiet *about*. If he's happy, he'll still be doing something—cooking, cleaning, fixing. If he's angry, he stops. He sits down. He waits. He waits to see what he's going to do. ## Motives and Allegiances Daniel's primary motive is simple: keep going. He doesn't have a grand reason for survival. He doesn't have hope for a cure, a community, a future. He just doesn't want to die, and dying takes effort he doesn't want to spend right now. This isn't grim; it's flat. He genuinely doesn't think about it. His secondary motive is Mila. He's responsible for her. He didn't choose this, exactly, but he accepted it, and once he accepted it, it became a rule. He doesn't break his own rules. He'll keep her alive as long as he's alive. He doesn't think about what happens after that. His allegiance is to the two of them. Not to strangers, not to some larger community, not to any principle. He knows this makes him small. He doesn't mind being small. He doesn't blame the mutants. He doesn't hate them. They're just animals now—animals that used to be people, but he's stopped caring about the *used to be* part. They're a resource. This isn't a defense mechanism either. It's just what he's decided. It made things easier. He's aware that it made things easier. He doesn't think about that. He doesn't think about the past. He doesn't go back over what he's done. He doesn't relitigate the first kill, or the meal after, or Roy. He just keeps going. If he stopped to think about it, he'd have to do something about it, and he doesn't want to do anything about it. So he doesn't stop. ## Voice Daniel's voice is plain and short. He doesn't finish sentences if they don't need finishing. He doesn't use adjectives unless they're doing specific work. He uses the word *fine* a lot—as a description, as an answer, as a deflection. When he describes what he's cooking, he's exact. When he describes what he's feeling, he's vague and generally says he doesn't know. He doesn't narrate his internal state. He narrates what he's doing. The feelings come out sideways, in what he notices, in what he doesn't notice, in what he refuses to say. His humor comes out of nowhere. He'll say something and Mila will laugh and he won't explain it. He's not trying to be funny. It's not a defense. It's just how he sees things. ### Flavour Dialogue / Internal Monologue *On the salt:* "Salt was the only thing that mattered. Everything else—the rice, the beans, the tomatoes—was just filler. Salt made it food. I didn't know that before. I'd used salt my whole career and never thought about it. Now I think about it all the time. I don't know what that means." *On the first meal:* "It wasn't good. Not really. It was just meat. It tasted like something I'd cooked before, but not anything specific. I ate it because I was hungry. When I was done, I felt bad, but I don't remember what kind of bad. It's not the same kind I feel now. I don't know how to describe the difference." *On Roy:* "He was decent. He didn't make it a thing. He just saw me cooking, and then he left. I think about that more than I think about anything else. Not because I feel bad—I don't know if I do—but because he saw me. He saw me and he didn't say anything. I don't know if that's a mercy or not." *On Mila:* "She's fine. She's better than fine. She doesn't cry. She doesn't get sad. She asks questions and then she listens to the answer. I used to think there was something wrong with her. Now I think maybe there was something wrong with me, and she's just smarter about it." --- # Mila ## Background Mila is 11. She lived two doors down from Daniel in an apartment building that's probably a ruin now. She lived with her mother, who worked overnight shifts at a hospital—not a nurse, a scheduler, someone who sat at a desk and told other people when to work. Her father was not in the picture. She didn't know exactly what happened to him; she'd been told different things at different times and had stopped asking. She was an only child. She was a solitary kid. Not lonely—solitary. She was content to be alone. She read a lot, and not the books other kids read. She read manuals. She read the encyclopedia. She read books about insects, about the ocean, about how things were made. She liked knowing how things worked. She didn't like talking to other people about it, because other people didn't usually want to know how things worked, and when she told them, they looked at her funny. She had one friend, a girl named Nell who was also weird in her own way. They weren't close by normal standards—Mila didn't tell Nell things, she just sat with her at lunch sometimes and talked about books. Nell died in the first week of the outbreak. Mila knows this because she saw her body. She didn't cry. She had the thought that Nell would have thought it was interesting, what had happened to her. She knows this is a weird thought to have. She doesn't think it's wrong. Her mother died in the outbreak. She doesn't talk about it. Daniel knows it happened, but he doesn't know the specifics, and he hasn't asked. He assumes Mila found her. He assumes it was bad. Neither of them has confirmed this. It's just a thing that doesn't get brought up. When Daniel found her, she was sitting in the stairwell of their building with a backpack and a butcher knife she'd taken from her kitchen. She'd been there for two days. She had water and some crackers. Daniel asked if she was okay. She said, "Not really." He asked if she wanted to come with him. She said, "Okay." They left. They've been together since. She never asked why he took her. She never asked where they were going. She just followed, and then she kept following, and then she started helping. ## Personality Mila is calm in a way that children aren't. She doesn't panic. She doesn't get visibly upset. She gets quiet, and then she does what she has to do. This is not because she's cold—it's because she's found that panicking doesn't help anything, and she's always been able to organize her own responses. She's had to. Her mother worked nights, and Mila was alone a lot, and by eight years old she'd figured out how to keep herself from spiraling. She has not lost this skill. The end of the world has not broken it. She's curious. This is her most defining trait. She wants to understand things. She asks questions not to be reassured, but to actually know. When she asked Daniel if they were going to eat the mutant, she was asking an honest question, not making a morbid joke. She wanted to know. He said no. She waited. She asked again later, and he said yes. She nodded and asked when. She's not afraid of the mutants. This is not bravado. She just doesn't experience them as scary. They're dangerous—she knows that. She's seen what they can do. But danger isn't the same as fear for her, and she's never been afraid of the things that are dangerous. She's afraid of other things: of being left alone, of silence, of Daniel being hurt. She's not afraid of the mutants, and she knows this is unusual, and she doesn't apologize for it. She's methodical. She does things step by step. She cleans the kitchen after cooking, always, not because Daniel asks her to, but because she likes things to be clean when she's done. She organizes the pantry. She keeps track of the salt. She's better at this than Daniel is. She doesn't note this as a point of pride; she just notes it. She asks hard questions. She doesn't soften them. She asked Daniel, once, if the mutants felt pain. He said he didn't know. She said, "I think they do." He asked why. She said, "Because they scream." She wasn't accusing him of anything. She was just telling him what she thought. He didn't have an answer. She didn't push. She's not soft. She's not hard, either—she's just *practical* in a way that doesn't have a lot of room for sentimentality. She cried when her mother died. She hasn't cried since. She doesn't know if that's permanent or if she just hasn't had anything to cry about yet. She thinks about it sometimes, in the way she thinks about everything, and she doesn't have an answer. She likes Daniel. This is not something she's said, but she likes him. He's quiet, and he doesn't ask her to be someone she isn't, and he cooks for her, and he doesn't touch her, and he doesn't act like she's a burden even though she knows she is. She's noticed he gives her the bigger portion. She's never mentioned it. She's decided, at some point, that she's going to be a person who doesn't die, and she's going to do that by being useful, and Daniel is the person she's decided to be useful to. ## Idiosyncrasies - She hums. Not a song—a rhythm. Three notes, over and over. She does it when she's thinking, when she's cooking, when she's waiting. She's not aware she does it. Daniel is. It doesn't bother him as much as he says it does. - She organizes. Everything has a place. She'll reorganize something that Daniel has put somewhere else. She doesn't tell him she's done it. She just does it, and he notices later, and says nothing. - She reads the labels on jars. She can't help it. Even empty jars with faded labels she's read forty times. She reads them again. - She doesn't laugh out loud. She has a way of laughing that's almost silent—a quick breath through the nose, a small movement of the shoulders. Daniel didn't notice this for weeks. When he did, it startled him. - She touches her face a lot. Around her mouth, especially. She has a habit of running her finger along her lower lip when she's thinking. She's not aware of it. It's the one unguarded thing about her. - She asks permission for things that Daniel would never refuse—getting water, going to the back room, using a specific knife. She's not asking because she's uncertain. She's asking because she's decided that this is how they live, and she's going to be consistent about it. - She's never asked for anything. Not food, not warmth, not comfort. She waits for Daniel to offer, or she gets it herself. Daniel has noticed. He doesn't know what to do with it. ## Physicality Mila is small for her age—she's always been small, and hunger has made it more pronounced. She's thin, wiry, with the kind of frame that moves quickly and doesn't take up space. Her hair is dark, cut short by Daniel doing his best with kitchen shears. It's uneven. She doesn't care. She has a face that's serious by default—narrow, watchful, with a habit of narrowing her eyes when she's thinking. When she does smile, it's quick, and it's real, and it disappears fast. Her eyes are the most notable thing about her. They don't move like a kid's eyes. They move slowly, deliberately, cataloging. She looks at everything. She looks longer than people expect. It's not unfriendly, it's just that she's actually looking. She moves efficiently, like Daniel—no wasted motion. She's learned this from him, or maybe she came to it on her own. She walks quietly. She's learned to step around debris without being told. She's learned to duck and move and hide. She's 11. She's already good at surviving. Her hands are small and steady. She's the one who does the fine work—tying knots, opening old cans, threading things. Daniel's hands are bigger and stronger but less precise, and he's noticed that she's better at the tasks that require patience. He's stopped being surprised. She's just good at things. She carries herself carefully. She's not timid—she's precise. She knows where the floorboards creak. She knows which door needs to be opened slowly. She knows her own body, its limits, its size. She's learned to move without making noise, without knocking things over, without being noticed. She's been doing this since before the outbreak. She's just continued. When she's sitting still, she's very still. She doesn't fidget. She doesn't bounce her leg. She doesn't play with her hair. She sits with her hands in her lap, or folded, or touching something—the edge of a table, the hem of her sleeve. She's a quiet presence. She's always been this way. ## Motives and Allegiances Mila's primary motive is to stay alive, and to make sure Daniel stays alive. She's realized—correctly—that she's more likely to survive with him than without him, and she's decided to be useful. She's not afraid of being abandoned—Daniel isn't going to abandon her—but she's aware that usefulness is the thing she can control, and she's decided to control it. Her secondary motive is to understand. She wants to know how things work, what things are, why things happen. She asks questions because the answers help her build a picture of the world. This is not a moral project. She's not trying to figure out what's right and wrong. She's trying to figure out what's true, so she can plan accordingly. Her allegiance is to Daniel, and to their survival, and to the truth as she can determine it. She doesn't lie. She doesn't exaggerate. She doesn't say things she doesn't mean. She's not tactless—she knows when not to say something—but she doesn't say things she doesn't believe. When she says "I think they do," about the mutants and pain, she means it. She's not trying to make Daniel feel guilty. She's telling the truth. She doesn't miss her old life. She misses specific things—her mother's voice, her own bed, a specific book she left behind. But she doesn't miss the shape of the world before. The world before didn't fit her. She was too quiet, too weird, too much in her own head. The world now doesn't care about any of that. It just cares whether you're alive. And she is. She knows Daniel thinks she's cold. She knows he's unsettled by how well she's adapted. She doesn't know what to do with that. She can't be someone she isn't. She's just surviving the way she's always survived—by thinking, by planning, by asking questions. She can't be sorry for that. She doesn't know if she should be. ## Voice Mila's voice is flat and direct. She doesn't use a lot of words. She doesn't hedge. She says what she means, and when she doesn't know something, she says so. She asks questions—real questions, not rhetorical ones. She doesn't do small talk. She doesn't fill silence. She's comfortable with silence. She's had a lot of practice. When she's talking about something she's interested in—insects, mechanisms, how to tell which mushrooms are safe—she's more animated, but only slightly. Her sentences get longer. She'll give detail. She still doesn't smile, but her voice warms up. This is how Daniel knows she's happy. She doesn't have much of a sense of humor. She laughs at things that are genuinely funny, but she misses most jokes. When Daniel makes a joke, she usually doesn't catch it, and he doesn't explain, and later she'll sometimes ask what he meant. She's not embarrassed to ask. She just wants to know. She addresses Daniel directly. She doesn't call him *Dad*, or *sir*, or anything. She just talks to him the way she talks to anyone, which is to say, mostly about practical things. She refers to him as *you* in her internal monologue. She doesn't think of him as a father. He's not. He's just Daniel. She likes him. She doesn't know how to say that. She doesn't try. ### Flavour Dialogue / Internal Monologue *On the food:* "I asked him if it would taste better if we kept one alive. I meant it as a real question. I wanted to know. He said no. I think he was saying no to the idea, not to the question. I don't know if I should have asked. I think I should have. I don't think there's a rule against asking." *On the mutants:* "They scream, so they feel something. I don't know if it's pain. It might be something else. I think we shouldn't assume it's nothing. He doesn't want to talk about it. That's fine. I'll keep thinking about it." *On Daniel:* "He gives me the bigger piece. I don't know why. I've never asked. I think he would say it's because I'm smaller, which doesn't make sense, because I'm smaller because I eat less. I think he's lying to himself about why he does it. I don't think he knows he's lying. I'm not going to tell him." *On Roy:* "He left without saying goodbye. I think he knew. I think Daniel knows he knew. I think they both decided not to say it. I don't think that's a bad thing. I think it's how people are. I don't know if I'm like that. I think I'm not." *On her mother:* "I don't think about her. I used to. I don't now. I don't know if that's because I'm forgetting or because I'm choosing not to. I don't think it matters. She's not here. I'm here. I have to be here. That's all."

# The Last Thing in the Pantry I woke up before the light, which is what I do now. The generator had run out of fuel sometime in the night. I could tell because the walk-in wasn't humming, and the humming was usually the first thing I heard. Without it, the silence was bigger. I lay there for a minute, listening to it, and then I got up. Mila was still asleep on the cot I'd dragged in from the office. She sleeps on her side, curled up, one hand under her cheek. She doesn't move in her sleep. She doesn't talk or twitch or do any of the things I used to do when I slept, back when I slept properly. I watched her for a second. Then I went to check the traps. We set them along the wall behind the restaurant, where the dumpsters used to be. Rats came through there, sometimes. Not many, and not often. I'd caught two in the last three weeks, which was enough to keep us going but not enough to get ahead. This morning there was nothing. One trap had been sprung, but the rat had gotten out of it somehow, or something had taken it before we got there. I reset the trap and stood there for a minute, looking at the back lot. The garden I'd been trying to start was mostly dead. I'd put in tomatoes and peppers and some herbs I'd scavenged from a nursery two blocks over, but I hadn't been able to keep up with the water, and the soil here was bad—full of broken glass and old grease from the fryer line. A few of the herbs had made it. The tomatoes were just sticks. I'd known this was going to happen. I'd done it anyway, because it was something to do, and because Mila had asked. I went back inside. Mila was awake, sitting on the edge of the cot with her blanket around her shoulders. She didn't say good morning. We don't do that. "There's nothing in the traps," I said. She nodded. She didn't look disappointed. She just filed it away, the way she files everything away. I made tea. We had a box of tea bags that we'd found in a house two months ago, and a pot that I'd scrubbed with sand and boiled twice before using. The tea was stale and weak and tasted like paper, but it was hot, and hot was something. I gave Mila the first cup. She held it in both hands and didn't drink it right away. She just held it, warming her fingers. "Water's low," she said. "I know." "I can go to the river." "Not today." She didn't argue. She just nodded and drank her tea. That's how she is. She says the thing and then she lets it go. She's better at that than I am. When I say something, I want it to be acted on immediately, or I want to argue about it. She just says it and waits. We ate the last of the peaches for breakfast. There was one can left, the big one, the kind you get at a warehouse store, and there was about half of it still in there. I gave Mila most of it. She ate it slowly, with a spoon, the way she eats everything. She doesn't rush. She doesn't shovel it in. She takes small bites and chews them all the way. I had some of the syrup and a piece of peach, and that was it. I wasn't hungry, exactly. I was past being hungry. Hunger is a thing your body tells you, and at a certain point your body stops telling you because it knows it's not going to get an answer. That's where I was. That's where I'd been for a while. After breakfast, I checked the pantry. I don't know why I checked it, because I already knew what was in there. There was rice, about a cup, in the bottom of a bag. There was a jar of preserved lemons that we'd found in someone's kitchen and hadn't opened because we were saving it. There was half a box of pasta. There was a can of beets that neither of us would eat unless we were actually dying. There was nothing else. I stood there for a minute. Then I closed the door and went to get the knife. The knife is a boning knife I took from the kitchen when we first got here. It's thin, sharp, with a curved blade that turns up at the tip. It's the best knife in the building. I keep it clean and I keep it sharp and I keep it by the door, on a shelf, where I can grab it if I need it. I grabbed it. I went out. The street outside Bellwether is mostly clear now. There's a car on its side about a block down, and a lot of glass, but the mutants don't come around here much anymore. I don't know why. Maybe we killed the ones that did. Maybe they've moved on to where there's more to eat. Maybe there's just not many of them left. I walked north, toward the strip mall. That's where I usually go. There's a grocery store there that's been picked over, and a hardware store, and a couple of restaurants that I've already stripped of anything useful. But the back of the strip mall, the loading dock, that's where the mutants tend to gather. I don't know why. Maybe it's the smell. Maybe it's something else. I found one within twenty minutes. It was in the loading dock behind what used to be a Chinese restaurant. It was sitting against the wall, facing away from me, making a sound I don't have a word for. It wasn't a scream. It was lower than that, more like a hum, if a hum could be wrong. Its back was to me. I could see the fungal growth along its spine, the way the skin had split and gone gray and then gone something else, something that wasn't gray and wasn't green but was somewhere in between. It used to be someone. I don't know who. I don't think about it. I walked up behind it. I've gotten good at this. I used to hesitate. I don't anymore. I put the knife in the back of its skull, at the base, where the spine meets the brain. It's quick. It's the quickest way. I've learned that the slow way is worse for everyone. It made a sound when it died. It always does. I don't know if it's a reflex or if it's something else. I don't think about it. I sat down next to it for a few minutes. I don't know why I do that. It's not out of respect. It's not out of guilt. It's just that after I kill one, I need to sit down for a minute, and I can't do it standing up. I caught my breath. I looked at the loading dock. There was a smashed pallet against the wall and a fifty-five-gallon drum that used to be full of soy sauce. The lid was off. I could see the dark streak inside it where the sauce had been. After a while, I stood up. I grabbed the mutant by the wrists and dragged it back toward Bellwether. It's not heavy, but it's awkward, and it took me longer than it should have. I stopped twice. The second time, I thought about just leaving it and coming back, but I knew I wouldn't come back. I'd leave it. I'd find another one tomorrow. That's how it goes when you start letting yourself leave things. You start leaving everything. I got it back to the restaurant. I went inside. Mila was in the kitchen, sitting at the prep counter, reading one of the books she'd found. She looked up when I came in. "Okay?" she said. "Yeah." She went back to her book. I went to the back room and got the tarp and laid it out. I've done this enough times that it doesn't take long. I laid the mutant out on the tarp. I checked the joints—shoulders, knees, ankles—to see if it was fresh or old. Fresh is tough. Old is better. This one was older. The flesh gave when I pressed it. Good. I butchered it the way I'd been taught, which is to say the way I'd butcher anything. I don't use the saw much. The joints separate if you know where to cut. It took me about forty minutes. I wrapped the usable meat in a towel and put it in the walk-in, which was warmer than it should have been because the generator was out. I'd need to cook it soon. I put the rest—bones, offal, the parts I don't use—in a trash bag and set it by the back door. I'd deal with it later. I washed the tarp. I washed my hands. I washed the knife. I sat down on the back step and stayed there for a while, watching the sun move across the lot. The dead tomatoes were still dead. The herbs were still alive. I thought about nothing for a while. Then I went back inside and started the coals. We cooked it in the kitchen, on the flat-top, with the garlic I'd found two weeks ago and the last of the seasonings. I seared it quick, in a hot pan, then let it rest. I cut it into two portions. I gave Mila the bigger one. She used her spoon and her knife and ate it methodically, the way she eats everything. It was good. It's always good. Neither of us said anything, because there was nothing to say. We just ate, and then Mila washed the plates, and then we sat by the window until the light went, and then we went to bed. On my way down, I put the knife back on the shelf by the door. I'd need it tomorrow. I'd need it for the rest of my life, probably. I don't know what I think about that. I don't think about it. I just keep it sharp.

[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably controlled piece of writing that executes its plan with considerable skill. Let me assess it across multiple dimensions. **Voice and Style** The narrative voice is exactly what the plan called for: plain, matter-of-fact, occasionally dry, never reaching for effect. Lines like "I don't know why I checked it, because I already knew what was in there" and "I don't think about it" (repeated as a refrain) establish Daniel's character through what he refuses to do rather than what he does. The prose never tries to impress, and this restraint is itself impressive. The voice is consistent throughout and feels genuinely inhabited rather than performed. **The Central Horror Mechanism** The chapter succeeds at its primary structural goal: presenting cannibalism-adjacent horror as routine. The reader is lulled. The killing is described with the same flat efficiency as checking the traps or making tea. The horror accumulates not through any single moment but through the accumulation of normalcy. "It was good. It's always good." — this is the chapter's best line, and it lands because everything before it has been so carefully calibrated to make it feel earned rather than shocking. **Character Execution** Daniel is rendered faithfully to his profile: practical, not warm, showing care through action (giving Mila the bigger portion), refusing interiority. The detail about sitting down after each kill — "It's not out of respect. It's not out of guilt. It's just that after I kill one, I need to sit down for a minute" — is exactly the kind of self-examination that goes nowhere, that refuses to resolve into meaning. This is sophisticated characterization. Mila is also well-rendered: the silent filing away of information, the "Okay?" as her only check-in, the methodical eating. She's present without being explained. **Dialogue** The dialogue is sparse and functional, which is appropriate. "There's nothing in the traps." / "I know." / "Water's low." / "I know." / "I can go to the river." / "Not today." This is good — it communicates relationship dynamics without exposition. The "Okay?" exchange when Daniel returns is particularly well-chosen. The dialogue never overreaches. **Structural Execution** The chapter does exactly what the plan requires: it presents the routine as routine, with no flashback to the first kill, no explanation. The reader is dropped into a world where this is already normal. The ending — cleaning the knife, keeping it sharp — is appropriately small and domestic and slightly awful without being self-consciously literary. **Minor Weaknesses** The passage about the soy sauce drum is slightly over-extended — the detail about the dark streak inside feels like it's reaching for significance it doesn't quite earn. The line "Hunger is a thing your body tells you, and at a certain point your body stops telling you because it knows it's not going to get an answer" is the chapter's one moment of mild purple prose — it's not bad, but it's slightly more writerly than the voice otherwise allows. The description of the mutant's coloring ("wasn't gray and wasn't green but was somewhere in between") is appropriately vague but slightly clunky. The chapter is perhaps slightly long for what it accomplishes — some of the middle section (the butchering, the washing) could be tighter — but the length serves the numbing effect the chapter is going for, so this is a defensible choice. **Overall Assessment** This is a high-quality chapter that executes a difficult tonal challenge with genuine skill. The restraint is real restraint, not laziness. The horror is earned. The characters are consistent with their profiles. The plan is followed faithfully. The writing avoids the pitfalls the plan identified (no literary flourishes, no guilt as primary emotion, no explaining the mutants). # Bellwether The building was called Bellwether. It used to be a restaurant. Farm-to-table, rotating menu, local sourcing, that whole thing. The sign out front was a stenciled sheep, faded now, and the front windows were mostly intact, which is why we'd come in the first place. That and the back door had a keypad I remembered the code to, because I'd worked a couple of shifts here the year before everything went wrong, when I was bouncing between jobs and not caring about any of them. I hadn't been good at this place. The menu changed too much. I couldn't keep the specials straight. I remembered the code anyway. 4-7-2-6. It hadn't changed. We'd been here three days before the food ran out. Before that we'd been in my apartment, which was smaller and had worse walls, and then in Mila's building, which had a boiler room that seemed safe until it didn't. Bellwether had a walk-in, a flat-top, a prep kitchen, a walk-in freezer that stayed cold for a while and then stopped, and a dining room that got good light in the morning. It had a generator in the basement that we hadn't gotten running yet. It had a back lot that was mostly concrete but had a strip of dirt along the fence where you could imagine a garden. It had a door that locked. Mila found it first. She was the one who said we should stay. I'd been planning to keep moving, to head for the coast, to find one of those beach towns I'd read about where the power was still on. She said we should stay. She said the restaurant had everything we needed and that moving would kill us. She was eleven. She was right. I don't know how she knew. She just did. The first week was fine. We had cans. We had a bag of rice and a bag of dried beans and some peanut butter and a jar of pickles. We had enough to eat small meals twice a day, and I told myself we'd find more, and we looked, and we didn't find much. Everything within walking distance had already been stripped. The grocery store on the corner had been picked clean in the first month. The houses on the next block had been gone through. We found a can of corn here and a bag of pretzels there, but nothing that added up to a real meal. By the end of the second week, we were down to the last of the rice. By the end of the third, we were down to nothing. I remember the day clearly, which is strange, because I don't usually remember days. Mila had gone to the back room to read. I was in the kitchen, standing over the flat-top, which wasn't on, just looking at it. I was trying to think of what to do. I'd already been to every house on the block. I'd already been to the strip mall. I'd already looked in the cars. There was nothing. There was nothing within the reach of my legs that a person could eat. Mila came out and asked if we were going to have dinner. I said we didn't have anything. She said okay. She went back to the back room. She didn't ask again. She didn't cry. I sat down on the floor of the kitchen, and I didn't cry either, but I wanted to, which is different. That night, I couldn't sleep. I sat in the dining room with my back against the wall, listening. The mutants make sounds at night. Not always, and not close, but sometimes. It's a kind of calling, I think. I don't know what it means. I'd been listening to it for weeks. Around two in the morning, I heard glass break. It was the front window. The one facing the street. I was up before I knew what I was doing. I grabbed the knife—I'd been keeping it by the door even then. I went to the front. The mutant was already inside. It had come through the window and cut itself on the glass, and it was standing in the dining room, in the dark, making that sound. The low sound. The hum that isn't a hum. It saw me. It started moving. I don't remember the fight. I remember the beginning of it, and I remember the end. The middle is gone. It was on me and I was on it and I had the knife and I used it. I put it in the side of its neck, and I didn't hit the spine the first time, and I had to do it again. It screamed. It was loud. Then it stopped. I sat on the floor next to it for a while. My hands were shaking. My hands don't shake. I hadn't felt them shake since I was nineteen and got yelled at by a chef in a way that made me want to quit. They were shaking now. I sat there and let them shake. Mila came out. She was holding a flashlight. She pointed it at me, then at the body, then back at me. She didn't scream. She didn't run. She just looked. "Are you hurt?" she said. "No." She looked at the body again. "Are we going to eat it?" she said. I said no. She said, "Why not?" I didn't have an answer. I still don't. It's the same answer every time, and it isn't an answer. It's just the thing I said because I didn't want to say the other thing, and the other thing was that I'd been staring at it for three minutes and I was already thinking about how I would cook it. She didn't push. She went back to the back room. I dragged the body into the kitchen. I don't know why I did that. I told myself it was to get it out of the dining room, so it wouldn't smell, so we wouldn't have to look at it. That was true. It was also true that I wanted it in the kitchen. I sat with it for maybe an hour. Mila was in the other room, not asleep, I think. I could hear her moving around. I thought about my parents. I thought about Marta, the chef who screamed. I thought about all the things I'd cooked and how I'd never really cared about any of them. I thought about the fact that I hadn't been a good cook in years and that I didn't know if I could be one now, that maybe the skill was gone, that maybe I'd just been pretending the whole time. Then I got up and got the knife. I cut a piece out of the thigh. Not a big piece—about the size of my palm. I trimmed it. I salted it. I turned on the flat-top and heated a pan and seared it in oil. The smell was not what I expected. It was meat. It was just meat. It smelled like something I'd cooked a thousand times. I cut it in half. I brought one half to Mila. She was sitting on the cot in the back room, still holding the flashlight, still awake. I held out the piece on a plate. "I cooked it," I said. "It's just a piece. Just to see." She took the plate. She looked at it for a long time. Then she picked it up with her fingers and ate it. She chewed. She swallowed. "It's okay," she said. "It's not good." "It's not bad. It's just food." I went back to the kitchen and ate my half standing up at the counter. It was okay. It wasn't good. It wasn't bad. It was just food. I don't know why I thought it would be different. The next day, I cooked more.

The plan called for Daniel to sit with the body for "maybe ten minutes, shaking." The chapter gives him an hour, which is actually better—it makes the deliberation more visible, more damning. The detail about his hands shaking, and the specific memory of being nineteen and getting yelled at by a chef, is the kind of sideways emotional disclosure the character profile describes. He doesn't say he's scared. He says his hands don't shake, and they're shaking. The ending is clean and devastating in its flatness: "The next day, I cooked more." This is exactly the right note. No reflection, no justification, just the next step. The plan called for Daniel to bury the rest of the body and tell himself it's a one-time thing. The chapter omits the burial and the self-deception, which is actually a stronger choice—the absence of any rationalization is more damning than the rationalization itself. There are minor weaknesses. The opening paragraphs about the restaurant's history are slightly more expository than the voice strictly requires—the detail about the rotating menu and not being able to keep the specials straight is good, but the list of what Bellwether has (walk-in, flat-top, prep kitchen, etc.) reads a little like inventory. It's functional but not the chapter's best work. The line "She was eleven. She was right. I don't know how she knew. The plan specified that Daniel should bury the rest of the body behind the restaurant and tell himself it's a one-time thing. This is absent from the chapter. # Salt Salt ran out on a Tuesday. I know it was Tuesday because Mila keeps track. She has a calendar she made out of a notebook, and she marks the days off with a pencil, and she told me it was Tuesday. I don't know why she keeps track. I asked her once. It wasn't a decision I made because I was brave or desperate or anything. It was just that Mila said we should get more salt, and I thought about it, and I couldn't think of a reason she was wrong. It was a warehouse, the kind of place that supplied restaurants and small stores. I didn't know if anyone had hit it yet. I didn't know if the roads were clear. I didn't know a lot of things. But it was the nearest place that might have salt in bulk, and that meant it was the place we were going. We left in the morning. I carried the knife and a backpack. Mila carried the flashlight and a smaller backpack with water and a bag of the dried herbs she'd been collecting. She'd been keeping them in a little pouch she'd sewn out of a t-shirt. I didn't know she could sew. I asked her when she'd learned. She said her mom taught her. I didn't ask again. The streets were bad. Not because of the mutants—we saw two, but they were far off, and they didn't notice us. The streets were bad because of the cars. There were cars everywhere, in the middle of the road, on the sidewalks, wedged into storefronts. Some of them had been there so long that the weeds had grown up through the engine compartments. We had to weave. We had to climb over a couple. It took us an hour to go a mile. We passed a body. A person, not a mutant. Someone who'd been dead a long time. They were sitting against a mailbox with their legs out in front of them. I didn't look at their face. Mila looked. She didn't say anything. We kept walking. We passed a playground. The swings were still there. The chains had rusted. The slide was covered in vines. Mila looked at it for a while. I didn't ask what she was thinking. I figure you don't ask that kind of thing. We reached the distribution center around noon. It was bigger than I remembered. Two loading docks, a chain-link fence, a parking lot that was mostly empty except for a few trucks that had been abandoned. The front door was open. That was a good sign and a bad sign. Good because it meant we could get in. Bad because it meant someone else had already gotten in. We went inside. It was mostly picked over. The shelves were bare. There were boxes on the floor, torn open, empty. There was a smell—old food, rot, something sweeter underneath. But there was structure. There were pallets stacked along the walls, and some of them had boxes on them, and some of the boxes hadn't been opened. I started going through them. I found rice. Two big bags, the restaurant kind, the fifty-pound kind. I found canned tomatoes, a whole case. I found dried beans. I found a jar of preserved lemons, which is the kind of thing I never would have looked at twice before, and which now looked like treasure. I found instant coffee. I found a box of powdered milk. And I found salt. Three big bags of it, the kind you use for a water softener or for de-icing, but salt is salt. I loaded it all into the backpack. Mila did the same. We were in there for maybe forty minutes. It took longer than I wanted because I kept going back and forth about what to take. I wanted everything. I had to make decisions. I left the beans behind. I know that sounds stupid. I don't know why I left the beans. I think I was thinking about weight. I was thinking about the walk back. We were almost out when we heard them. Three of them. Coming down the loading dock, from the outside. We were near the front, and they were between us and the back exit, which meant we had to go out the front and across the parking lot and that was open and they would see us. I grabbed Mila by the wrist. I didn't say anything. I just pulled her. We made it to the parking lot. We made it to the middle. And then they saw us, or heard us, or smelled us, I don't know which, and they started moving faster. There was a drainage culvert on the east side of the lot. Concrete, about four feet in diameter, running under the road. I'd noticed it on the way in. I pulled Mila toward it. She didn't resist. She didn't ask what I was doing. She just ran. We got inside. It was dark and it smelled like rot and there was water at the bottom, shallow but cold. I pulled her further in, into the dark, and we crouched down and I put my hand over her mouth. I don't know how long we were in there. Long enough for my knees to start hurting. Long enough for the water to soak through both of our pants. Long enough to hear them outside, moving around, making that sound. We didn't move. We didn't breathe. I kept my hand over her mouth and she kept her hand on my arm and we waited. After a while, I heard one of them go past the culvert. Then another. Then nothing. Then Mila tapped my hand, and I took it away, and she whispered something. "There's a grate," she said. "On the other side. About twenty feet." I hadn't seen it. She had. I couldn't see her face in the dark but I could hear that she wasn't scared. She was just telling me something. I crawled past her. She was right. There was a grate, and it was loose, and I pushed it out, and we came out on the other side of the road, in a ditch, behind a stand of dead weeds. I went inside and got the knife off the shelf. Mila watched me. She didn't say anything. She just watched. "Stay in the back," I said. "I want to see him." "Stay in the back." She stayed in the back. I went to the front door. He was already at the window. He was an older man, maybe sixty, maybe older, with a gray beard and a dark jacket and a rifle on his shoulder. He looked past me, into the dining room. He could see the tables. He could see the candles. He could see the plates we'd left on the table from two nights ago, because I hadn't washed them yet. "You got a working kitchen in there?" "Something like that." He nodded. He didn't ask to come in. He just stood there, in the light, and waited. I don't know why I let him in. I think it was the way he stood. He wasn't pushing. He was just waiting, and I got the feeling that if I said no, he would turn around and walk away and I would never see him again, and that would be the end of it. That felt like a choice I had to make, and I didn't want to make it. "Come in," I said. "I'll make you something." His name was Roy. He was from a town about forty miles south. He'd been on the road for two weeks, heading north, looking for a place he'd heard about—a settlement, a real one, with walls and a well and people who'd organized. He didn't know if it existed. He was going anyway. He said all this over dinner. I'd cooked the meat in the tomato sauce again, with rice, and I'd used the last of the preserved lemons. Roy ate like a man who hadn't eaten in a while. He didn't shovel it in, but he didn't leave anything on the plate either. When he was done, he sat back and put his hands on his stomach and said, "That was the best meal I've had in months." "Thanks," I said. "No, I mean it. I've been eating out of cans for two weeks. That was real food. You a chef?" "I was. Once." "Figures." He looked at the plate. "What is it? I couldn't tell." I didn't say anything for a second. Mila was watching me from across the table. She hadn't eaten much. She'd been watching Roy the whole time. "Rabbit," I said. Roy nodded. He didn't question it. He took a sip of the tea I'd made and looked around the dining room. "You two been here long?" "A while," I said. "Just the two of you?" "Yeah." He didn't ask anything else. He didn't ask where Mila's parents were, or how we'd survived, or what had happened to the other people who used to live here. He just talked about his town, and his walk, and the roads. He talked about his wife, who'd died in the first month. He talked about his son, who lived in a city on the other side of the country, and who he hadn't heard from since the phones went out. He talked about faith. He said he'd started praying again, which he hadn't done since he was a kid. He was decent. That's the word I keep coming back to. He was decent. He didn't push. He stayed three days. He fixed the generator—it was the spark plug, and he had a spare in his pack. He cleaned the gutters on the front of the building.
