# Chapter 1: The Summons The transfer vessel was old and the armrest was cracked. Arthur Neegan sat in the window seat and watched Mars turn below him. The planet was not beautiful from this distance. It looked like what it was: a cold, red, tired place. He had been living on it for thirty-one years. He had no feelings about it one way or another. The steward had been by twice. Neither time had she offered him anything. She was young, maybe twenty-five, and her uniform didn't fit properly, and she walked like someone who had only been aboard this class of vessel a handful of times. He noticed these things without meaning to. It was a habit. He had been in the window seat for four hours. He had not slept. His knee ached, the way it did when he sat still too long, and he had already shifted his weight three times to try to find a position that didn't hurt. There wasn't one. There had been a time when sitting for four hours would have been nothing. That time was over. He thought about the valve on his lander. It was still stuck. He had been meaning to fix it for two weeks and had been putting it off because it was a job that required him to take the housing apart and he didn't have the right gasket on hand and he didn't want to order one. Now he was here, four hundred kilometres above his homestead, and the valve was still stuck. He would come back to it. He always came back to it. He thought about the retinue's arrival instead. --- They had come on a Tuesday afternoon. He remembered it was Tuesday because Tuesday was the day the ration cartridge arrived and he had been waiting on it, and the retinue had arrived before the cartridge and the cartridge had arrived in the middle of everything, and he had been forced to sign for it with four strangers standing in his yard. There had been four of them. Two in front, two behind. Uniforms that Arthur didn't recognise until later, when Marta identified them for him—Antares diplomatic corps, she said, diplomatic in name only, and had laughed in a way that wasn't a laugh. The one in charge had been a woman, mid-thirties, with a scar across one eyebrow. She had waited while Arthur slid out from under his lander. He had taken his time. He had learned, over the years, that taking your time was one of the few things no one could take from you. He had stood up, wiped his hands on his trousers, and looked at her. She had asked, politely, if he would accompany them. He had asked if he had a choice. She had said yes, of course. He had looked at the four of them, at the scrubland behind them, at the Covenant's orbit visible in the evening sky. He had thought about the valve, which was still not fixed. He had thought about the ration cartridge, which he had not yet unpacked, and which he would now have to leave sitting in the yard, and which would probably be disturbed by the wind before he got back. He had thought about Marta, who would notice he was gone and would worry. He had thought about his knee, which was already hurting. He had said he would get his coat. He had gone inside. He had packed a small bag—toothbrush, spare shirt, the whisky flask that Helen had given him years ago and that he had never used for anything but whisky. He had stood in his kitchen for a moment, looking at the familiar room. Then he had gone back out to the yard, where the woman had been waiting, patient, and the other three had been waiting, less patient, and the ration cartridge had been sitting on the ground where the delivery had left it. He had followed them to the transport. He had climbed in. His knee had hurt more going up the ramp than it should have. --- On the vessel, he catalogued what he could see. The steward's name tag said KELLER. She was nervous. She had spilled water when she had poured it for the man two rows ahead of Arthur, and she had not spilled water for anyone since. The two other passengers—a man and a woman—had been careful not to look at him. They had boarded after him, sat behind him, and had not spoken since the vessel had left the surface. He could see their reflections in the window when the light was at the right angle. The man was reading something on a tablet. The woman appeared to be sleeping. Neither had looked at him once. They were with the retinue. He knew this the way he knew a machine was about to fail—from the small signs, the configuration, the way they held themselves. It didn't bother him. If they were going to do something to him, they would have done it already. The fact that they hadn't meant they wanted him somewhere specific. That was useful information. He filed it away. He thought about his wife. He didn't know why. She had been on his mind a lot lately. He had written her a letter three months ago, the seventeenth in the sequence, and he had not sent it, the way he had not sent the previous sixteen. He didn't know what the letters were for. He never read them back. He just wrote them, and put them in the drawer, and that was that. He thought about the vein under his land. He had known about it for three years. He had not told anyone. He had logged it in his private records, drawn up a rough survey, and then put the records in a drawer with the letters, in a way that he now recognised as his own version of a filing system—things he knew and did nothing about, all in the same place. He should have done something. He should have done it three years ago. He had not, because doing something would have changed things, and he had spent thirty years on Mars carefully doing nothing. He thought about whether he should have brought his tools. The valve was still stuck. He could have ordered a gasket. He had not ordered a gasket. A door opened at the far end of the cabin. Someone was coming. Arthur stood up, slowly, favouring his good leg, and waited. His knee hurt. It always hurt. He had stopped expecting it not to. The door opened the rest of the way.

# Chapter 2: The Offer The room was larger than Arthur had expected and emptier than it needed to be. A table, two chairs, a window that took up most of the far wall. Through the window, Mars was a curve of red-brown against black. From this altitude it looked less like a planet and more like a thing that had been left out in the weather for a long time. The woman was already seated when he came in. She was older than the soldiers who had collected him—sixties, maybe, though it was hard to tell; her face had the smoothness of someone who had paid for it. Grey hair cut short. A dark suit with no insignia anywhere on it. A cup of coffee on the table in front of her, half finished. Arthur had been expecting tea. "Mr. Neegan," she said. "Please sit." He sat. The chair was comfortable. He distrusted it immediately. "My name is Director Voss. I'm with Antares. I'd like to talk to you about your claim." She said this the way a doctor said the name of a disease—calmly, as though it were a fact that need not be frightening. "Would you like something to drink? Tea, coffee?" "Coffee," Arthur said, because she was drinking coffee and he wanted to see what she would do. She gestured to someone he couldn't see, and a moment later a cup appeared in front of him. He didn't drink it. He wrapped both hands around it and let the warmth soak into his knuckles. "You have a claim in the Elysium Planitia sector," Voss said. "Forty hectares. You've held it since 2145, free and clear. Before that, a lease, held under the standard indenture framework. You've worked it for thirty-one years." She paused. "You know what's under it." "Rock," Arthur said. She didn't smile. "Azra." "Some." "A lot. That's the problem." She turned her coffee cup a quarter-turn on the saucer. It was a deliberate gesture, Arthur thought, and also not—it was the kind of thing a person did without noticing, and it was also the kind of thing a person might do in front of someone they were trying to unsettle, and he couldn't tell which it was. That was the trouble with people like her. You could never tell. "Under your claim," she said, "is one of the largest Azra veins yet identified in the Elysium region. Perhaps the largest. It runs deep, it runs clean, and it's accessible from the surface with the kind of equipment you already own. There's enough there to shift the balance of several things I could name and won't. I'm telling you this because you already know it, and because I need you to understand that I know you know." "Alright," Arthur said. "I'd like to buy it." "How much." She named a figure. It was a large figure. It was not an insult. It was also not as large as it would have been if she thought he had more options than he did. He noted this. "I'd like to think about it," he said. "Of course." She picked up her cup and drank from it. "Take as long as you need. That said—I'd like to tell you a few things first, so that your thinking is well-founded." "Go on." "You're not the only one who wants it." She set the cup down. "Antares is one of several parties with an interest in the Elysium region, and the region is now of interest because of the vein under your claim. That was always going to happen eventually. You didn't cause it. You simply happen to be sitting on it." "Who else," Arthur said. "At least three corporations, one of which has already placed a prefab on your eastern boundary. The Federation, through the Mars Development Authority, though they'll work through intermediaries and claim they're doing no such thing. And a handful of smaller interests—settler organisations, independence groups, private buyers. Some of them want your claim. Some of them want to stop other people from getting your claim. Both kinds will contact you." "You're telling me this so I'll sell to you." "I'm telling you this," Voss said, "because the alternative is that you find out from someone with a worse offer. I don't mind being outbid on facts. I do mind being outbid on framing." Arthur turned this over. It was, he thought, one of the more honest things a person in her position had said to him. It might also have been a lie. With people like her, honesty was the cheapest thing you could buy. "What happens if I say no," he said. "That's your right." "That's not what I asked." She looked at him for a moment. Her eyes were grey-green, and whatever judgment she was making, she kept it to herself. "Someone else comes," she said. "Maybe several someone elses. They'll make their own offers. Some of them will be larger. Most of them will be worse in ways you won't see right away—the money will be in a form that's hard to spend, or the terms will have conditions on your existing equipment, or the buyer will be a shell for a party that can't legally hold the claim and will need to move it again within a year. If you refuse everyone, the Authority will find a reason for an administrative review, and you'll spend two years in filings while your equipment rusts, and eventually you'll take a settlement that's smaller than any of the offers. This isn't a threat. It's what happened to the Thoreson claim in 2151, and the Van der Merwe claim in 2154, and a dozen others. You can look those up. I'll give you the case numbers if you want." "I'll look them up," Arthur said. "I thought you might." She drank from her coffee. He still hadn't touched his. "There's one more thing," she said. "I should tell you that I don't particularly enjoy this. I've done it for thirty years and I'm good at it, and the fact that I'm good at it isn't the same as liking it. You can decide what you want to make of that." "Not much." "No," she agreed. "I didn't think you would." She stood, and the movement was smooth, and she picked up her cup and carried it to a side table, where she left it. "You'll be returned to your claim tomorrow morning," she said. "You'll have my offer in writing, with the case numbers for the claims I mentioned. You'll have my contact information." Arthur stood as well. His knee complained. He ignored it. "One question," he said. "Of course." "Why not just take it." She paused in the doorway. She didn't turn around for a moment. When she did, her expression was the same as it had been all along—patient, unreadable. "Because we're not the only ones who want it," she said. "And because this way, when you sign, you'll know you signed." She left. The door closed behind her with a soft click. Arthur stood in the empty room for a while, looking at the curve of Mars through the window. Then he picked up his cup of coffee and drank it, all of it, lukewarm and slightly bitter, and went back to his quarters to see if he could sleep.

# Chapter 3: Homecoming They brought him back on the morning shuttle and left him at the edge of his claim without ceremony. The transport lifted off before he had walked twenty metres. He didn't watch it go. The air was cold and thin and smelled of dust, and he stood still for a moment and let himself breathe it. He had been gone forty hours. It felt longer. It felt, in a way he couldn't account for, like coming back to a place that had moved while he was away. The ration cartridge was still in the yard. The wind had nudged it against the leg of his workbench. He picked it up and carried it inside, and put the cartridges away in the pantry, one by one, in the order he always put them in—protein, carbohydrate, the two vitamin packs, the one pack of coffee substitute he never drank because he didn't like the taste and ordered anyway out of habit. That was the first thing. Ration cartridges away. Then he went outside to the lander and looked at the valve. He had meant to fix the valve three weeks ago. He had meant to fix it again two weeks ago. Standing there, he understood that he was going to fix it now, not because he wanted to, but because it was the only thing in the world that was unambiguously his. The valve was stuck. The valve was going to be unstuck. He took the housing off and laid the parts out on a cloth, in order, the way he always did. It took him most of the morning. The gasket was worn. He could have gotten another year out of it with a patch, but he had been putting it off long enough. He cut a new gasket from the sheet stock he kept in the drawer, trimmed it, seated it, closed the housing back up. He bled the line. The valve moved. He cycled it three times to be sure, then a fourth time, then sat back on his heels and looked at it. It was fixed. He went inside and washed his hands. He ate a cold lunch. He checked the water reclaimer, which was still running hot, and decided he would deal with it tomorrow. He sat down at his desk and looked at the drawer where he kept the letters, and did not open it. He got up and stood in the middle of his kitchen, and could not think of a single thing he wanted to do. Then Marta knocked on the door. She had come with a jar of jam. She always came with a jar of jam. "Arthur," she said. "You're back." "I'm back." "Where were you." "Away." "Don't be clever." She came in without being invited, the way she always did, set the jam down on the counter, and looked at him with the directness of a woman who had known him for twenty years and had long since stopped being polite to him. "There are people on your land. Have you seen them." "I haven't." "On the western ridge. A prefab. They came yesterday morning, two of them, and then a third. Corporate boys. They say they're protecting your claim." Arthur looked past her, through the window, toward the western ridge. From this angle the ridge was hidden behind the corner of the habitat, but he could see the edge of a fresh cutting in the regolith where no cutting had been before—a track, running west, wide enough for a rover. "They've been on the neighbours too," Marta said. "Three of us. Two of them signed, and I signed, and the Fletchers wouldn't speak to them at all, so they didn't sign but they got a letter." "What did you sign." She was quiet for a moment. She turned the jam jar on the counter a quarter-turn, the way she did when she didn't want to answer something. "It was about water rights," she said. Arthur looked at her. She looked away. "Marta." "He was very patient," she said. "He explained it twice. Three times. Every time I asked, he explained it again, and he was so patient about it that I thought—" She stopped. She pressed her lips together, then went on. "I thought it was my fault for not understanding. He was doing me a favour, sitting there, being patient with an old woman, and I didn't want to waste his afternoon. So I signed it and said thank you." "Do you have the paper." "I have the copy he left." "Can I see it." She hesitated, and then she went home and got it, and came back, and gave it to him. He read it standing up, in his kitchen, in silence. The title was about water usage coordination. The body was about mineral rights—his neighbour's mineral rights, not water, the water language only in the recitals at the top, where it functioned more as atmosphere than as substance. Below the signature line, in small print, there was a clause about arbitration. He read it three times. He read the arbitration clause four times. "What does it say," Marta said. He turned the last page over. On the back, in fine grey print, there was a schedule of parcels, and one of them had her claim number on it, and another had a number he didn't recognise, and a third had a number that was very close to his own claim number—the western portion of it, up against the ridge, the part that ran toward where the prefab now stood. Arthur set the paper down on the counter. "It's not about water," he said. Marta looked at him. She didn't cry. Her face went quiet, and her shoulders drew in a little, and she stood in his kitchen with her hands folded and her eyes on the jam jar, and that was how it was. "What did I do," she said. "You signed a paper," Arthur said. "That's all." "Is it bad." "It's not good." "Arthur." "Go home," he said. "Make your tea. I'll look into it." She looked at him for a long moment. Then she nodded, once, and picked up her jar of jam and put it back in her hands and carried it out with her—she had brought it for him and she was taking it back, which was a thing she did when she was upset, and which she would be embarrassed about tomorrow—and Arthur stood in his kitchen a long time after she left, and looked at the copy of the paper she had left on his counter, and did not move. That evening he walked to the prefab on the western ridge. There were two men outside. He asked to speak to whoever was in charge. The officer who came out was young, maybe thirty, and polite in a way that Arthur recognised—the way Marta had described. Arthur showed him the copy of the paper. The officer read it, and nodded, and said it was valid. "Valid under what authority," Arthur said. "Mars Development Authority." "Which authority." The officer looked at him. He didn't have an answer to that. For a moment something flickered across his face, the expression of a man who had been handed a document by someone else and had not asked the same question—and Arthur saw it, and the officer saw him seeing it, and neither of them said anything. "Have a good evening, Mr. Neegan," the officer said. Arthur walked home. His knee hurt. It was colder now, and the stars over the eastern ridge were very bright, and the Covenant was a faint point of light near the horizon, and as he reached his own yard he stopped and looked back east, where he could see one small square of light: Marta's kitchen window, still on. He went inside. He locked the door. He sat without turning on the light for a long time. Then he got up and looked at the drawer where the letters were, and did not open it, and went to bed, and could not sleep.

Arthur's responses are appropriately terse: "It's not good." "Go home. Make your tea. I'll look into it." These feel authentic to the character profile. He had replaced the compressor three years ago and it had been running clean ever since. He knew the sound of it the way he knew the sound of his own breathing. He got up. His knee was bad this morning. He sat on the edge of the bed and worked it for a minute, bending and straightening, before he trusted it to hold him. It held him. He stood. Breakfast was a reconstituted egg, a slice of something that called itself bread, and coffee. He made the coffee from the real tin, not the substitute, which he allowed himself once a week. Today was not the day he usually allowed himself, but he allowed himself anyway. He ate standing up at the counter, looking out the window at the western ridge. The prefab was a small grey box, still there, still lit. During the night someone had run two more tracks across the regolith, one toward the Fletchers' and one toward the ridge itself. He noted this and went back to his coffee. After breakfast he went out to the water reclaimer. It had been running hot for a month—hotter than the manual said it should, hot in a way that made the housing too warm to touch for long. He had decided he would deal with it today. He unbolted the front panel and laid the screws out in the dish he kept for screws, and looked at the guts of the thing. The reclaimer was eleven years old. He had bought it secondhand, refurbished it himself, and it had run without complaint ever since. He knew every seal, every line, every thermocouple. He knew which parts he had replaced and which parts he had told himself he would replace next time. The intake manifold was one of the ones he had told himself he would replace next time. It was not the problem. The problem was the heat exchanger, which had scaled up. He could see the buildup through the inspection port—a thin chalky layer where there should have been none. He went inside and got the descaling solution and a bucket, and came back out, and spent two hours with the exchanger removed and soaking, sitting on a stool, watching the solution work. It didn't need watching. He watched it anyway. It was the kind of task he liked: specific, bounded, with a clear end. He thought about nothing while he did it. This was, he understood, one of the reasons he liked it. When the exchanger was clean he reassembled it, cycled the reclaimer twice, and watched the temperature settle. It was still slightly higher than it should be, but within tolerance. He would order a new exchanger cartridge. He would probably order it next week. He had been telling himself he would order it for four months. The morning was gone. He ate a cold lunch—no reason to heat the kitchen up—and sat at the desk with the manual for the reclaimer open in front of him, and read a chapter he had read before. He had marked three errata in this chapter over the years, in pencil, in the margin. He found a fourth one on page ninety-seven: the torque value for the housing bolts was given in newton-metres where the rest of the section was in foot-pounds. He circled it. Later he would add it to the errata list in the drawer. There were thirty-seven items on the list now. This would make thirty-eight. He thought about writing to Helen. He got out a sheet of paper from the stack he kept for that purpose. He sat with the pen in his hand for a long time. He did not write anything. After a while he put the paper back on the stack and put the pen back in the drawer and got up. He went for a walk in the afternoon. Not toward the prefab—away from it, north, across the scrubland, toward the old survey marker that had been there when he bought the claim and that no one had used for anything in his lifetime. He walked at a slow pace, because of the knee, and he stopped twice to rest, once at a rock he knew and once at nothing in particular. The land was red and flat and featureless in every direction. A dust devil wandered past, a long spine of dirt turning on itself, maybe two hundred metres away, and he watched it go. He watched it until it fell apart on the edge of a rise, and then he kept walking. He didn't think about the vein. He didn't think about Voss, or the offer, or Marta's paper, or the officer at the prefab. He tried not to think about them, and then he noticed he was trying not to, and then he noticed that noticing was itself a way of thinking about them, and then he gave up on the whole project and just walked. He sat on a rock for a while at the furthest point of the walk, at the rise where the survey marker stood, and looked back the way he had come. His habitat was a small grey shape on the plain, and the prefab was a smaller grey shape further east, and beyond that, if he squinted, he could see the track that led toward Marta's, and beyond that, the horizon. He sat on the rock for an hour, maybe longer. He didn't think about anything in particular. When he got up to go back his knee was worse than when he had sat down, and he walked back slowly, and the walk took longer than it had coming, and the sun was low when he reached his yard. He ate cold rations for supper and drank two glasses of whisky instead of one. He sat in the dark and looked out the window at Marta's light, which was on, and then at the prefab lights, which were also on. He didn't feel anything in particular. He didn't feel nothing either. He felt the way he usually felt, which was: present, tired, and aware that the version of the world he had lived in for thirty years was no longer the same version, and that this had happened without his being consulted, and that there was no way to go back. He went to bed at his usual time. He did not write any letters. He did not open the drawer. He woke up around midnight, not sure why. He lay there for a while, listening to the air system hum, and then he got up and checked the seals on the outer door, and the seals were fine, and he checked the reclaimer, which was holding at its new slightly-too-high temperature, and he checked the weather readout, which told him nothing in particular. Then he went back to bed, and after a while he slept, and the light over Marta's window went out at some point in the small hours, and after that the plain was dark.

[Analysis] Chapter 4 is a deliberate "sag" chapter—the author's plan explicitly calls for a chapter where nothing happens, where the protagonist eats, reads, walks, and thinks. The question is whether the execution earns that structural choice or merely enacts it. Arthur's relationship with the water reclaimer—knowing it better than its designers, keeping an errata list he never sends to anyone—is a quietly devastating portrait of a man who has redirected his capacity for care into objects because objects don't leave. The detail of thirty-seven errata becoming thirty-eight is exactly the kind of small, precise observation that Asimov's mode demands, and it lands cleanly. The prose is disciplined. Short declarative sentences. No ornament. The narration stays close to Arthur's perceptions without ventriloquizing his inner life. When the chapter does approach interiority—"He felt the way he usually felt, which was: present, tired, and aware that the version of the world he had lived in for thirty years was no longer the same version"—it earns the slight expansion because it's been so restrained up to that point. This is not purple prose; it's a controlled release. The walk sequence is well-handled. The dust devil is observed without being made to mean anything. Arthur's attempt not to think about his problems, and his recognition that noticing the attempt is itself a form of thinking about them, is psychologically precise and rendered without self-congratulation. The chapter trusts the reader to understand what's happening without explaining it. The ending—the light over Marta's window going out, the plain going dark—is quiet and earned. It doesn't reach for significance. It simply closes. Where the chapter is slightly less successful: the middle section, where Arthur thinks about writing to Helen and doesn't, is the most expected beat in the chapter. The character profile establishes the unsent letters as a key motif, and the chapter enacts it without adding anything new to it. It's not a failure, but it's the least surprising moment in an otherwise restrained piece. Similarly, the observation that "the version of the world he had lived in for thirty years was no longer the same version" is the closest the chapter comes to a theme statement—the one moment where the narration edges toward explaining itself rather than showing. The chapter has no dialogue, which is appropriate given the plan, and the absence is not felt as a lack. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: Arthur wakes, eats, works on the reclaimer, reads the manual, attempts a letter, walks, eats cold rations, drinks two glasses instead of one, wakes at midnight, checks the seals, goes back to bed. Every beat from the plan is present and executed with care. The retrofuturistic texture is lightly worn, as intended: reconstituted eggs, the real coffee tin, the manual with penciled errata. These details accumulate without calling attention to themselves. The chapter is not emotionally explosive—it's not meant to be. But it is emotionally present. The loneliness is real. The competence-as-coping is real. The sense of a man who has organized his life around tasks because tasks have ends is real. For a chapter explicitly designed to sag, it sags with considerable craft. Minor weaknesses: the chapter is slightly long for what it accomplishes. A few of the middle paragraphs could be trimmed without loss. The Helen beat, as noted, is the most predictable. # Chapter 6: The Question Voss came alone, on the fourth day after Chen's second visit, and she came in a rover with no markings at all. She parked beside his lander, which he had moved out into the yard the previous week and not yet moved back, and she stood looking at it for a moment before coming to the door. "May I come in," she said, when he opened it. "You're already in." "May I come in properly." He stepped aside. She sat at his kitchen table, which was small, and drank the tea he made her, which she hadn't asked for. She held the cup with both hands, the way he had made himself hold her coffee on the station, and he wondered whether she had noticed the gesture or whether she had simply been doing it all along. "You've had visitors," she said. "Several." "I'd like to be the last." Arthur sat down across from her. His knee ached, and he stretched it out under the table, and she did not look at it. "You've heard about Marta," she said. Arthur didn't answer. "You've heard," she went on, "that there's a paper she signed, that she doesn't fully understand it, and that the paper takes her mineral rights in parcels that run alongside your western boundary. You've seen the prefab. You may have guessed that the prefab and the paper come from the same place, though I'll tell you they don't, exactly. They come from two places that happen to overlap on your ridge." She drank her tea. "I know you know. I'm not telling you anything. I want you to know I know it too." "Alright," Arthur said. "I didn't arrange the paper. I want to be clear about that. Antares didn't arrange the paper. The paper was placed by a holding company that reports to nobody in particular—which is a polite way of saying it's parked under someone else's name—and it's the same kind of paper that's been placed on a dozen claims in Elysium in the last two years. Marta is not the first. She will not be the last." "Who's behind it." "I don't know. I could find out, if it mattered to me. It doesn't." "It matters to Marta." Voss looked at him. "It matters to you," she said. "That's a different thing." Arthur said nothing. She drank her tea. "Here is my offer, again," she said. "It hasn't changed, except in one respect. If you sign with me, and if you sign quickly, I'll have my legal team review Marta's paper as part of the closing. I can't promise to void it. That's outside my scope. But I can make the paper expensive to enforce—expensive enough that whoever's holding it will likely let it lapse rather than fight. That's the best available outcome for Marta. It's also the best available outcome for you, since it removes the immediate threat to your boundary." "You're bundling it," Arthur said. "Yes." "You're using her to get me." "Yes." "You're not going to dress it up as anything other than that." "I've tried dressing things up for you twice now," Voss said. "It hasn't worked. I have no reason to think a third attempt would go better." She set the cup down. "You've been treating this as a negotiation about your claim. It's not. It's a negotiation about your life. Your claim is the pretext. The amount doesn't matter, the terms don't matter, and Marta doesn't matter—not to the people on the other end of this, and not to me, if I'm being honest, which I'm making an effort to be." "Then why are you here." "Because you asked me a question last time we met, and I've been thinking about it." Arthur waited. "You asked what happens to Marta," Voss said. "I told you that wasn't my concern. I've changed my mind about that, not because I care about her, but because I've noticed that you do. And I've noticed that you're the kind of person who will refuse an offer that's good for him in order to avoid an outcome that's bad for someone else. I've met that person a few times. They're rare and they're inconvenient and they usually lose." "You're telling me I'm going to lose." "I'm telling you what the shape of the outcome looks like if you don't sign. You'll refuse. You'll refuse all of us. You'll try to fight the paper on Marta's behalf, and you'll find that the legal framework for doing so doesn't exist—the Authority created it specifically so that private citizens couldn't challenge placements. You'll lose two years of your life. Your equipment will degrade. You'll take a settlement that's smaller than any offer you've been made. Marta will lose her western parcels in the meantime. And then, sometime after all of that, someone will drill your vein. The only variable is who and when." Arthur looked at the table. He thought about Marta standing in his kitchen with the jam jar in her hands. He thought about the Fletchers, who had refused to sign and gotten a letter. He thought about Chen's drilling holes and the missing stake. He thought about his wife, who had left and whom he had written seventeen letters to, none of them sent. "You've got a daughter," he said. Voss didn't react. After a moment, she said: "Yes." "You said she's on Ceres. Logistics." "She is." "You don't see her much." "I see her twice a year." "Does she like her work." Voss looked at him for a long moment. It was the same question he had asked her on the station, and she had answered it the same way then. "I don't know," she said. "I've never asked her." "Why not." "Because I don't want to know the answer," Voss said. "If she likes it, then I'm fine. If she doesn't like it, then I'm the reason she's there. I'd rather not be the reason she doesn't like something." Arthur nodded, slowly, as though she had answered a different question than the one he'd asked. "You're very good at this," he said. "I know." "You've done it to a lot of people." "Yes." "You've been doing it for thirty years." "Longer." "And you sleep at night." "I do," Voss said. "I sleep very well. That's part of what worries me about myself, and it's part of why I'm still sitting here when I could have sent someone with a shorter answer. I want you to have the facts. That's all I'm doing." She stood up, and picked up her cup, and carried it to the sink and set it down in it, and turned to face him. "You don't have long," she said. "The other interests are getting impatient. If you're going to sign, sign this week. If you're not going to sign, decide that too, and prepare for what follows." She went to the door and opened it, then stopped. "It's a strange thing to say," she said, "but I've enjoyed this conversation more than any I've had in months. That isn't a negotiating tactic. I'm telling you because I don't want to lie to you more than I have to." She left. Arthur sat at the table for a long time after her rover had gone, looking at the empty tea cup she had left in his sink, and the light outside was fading, and on the western ridge the prefab lights came on.

Voss's final speech—"I sleep very well. That's part of what worries me about myself"—is the chapter's one moment of slight over-writing. It's a little too self-aware, a little too neatly articulated. Real people who have made their peace with what they do don't usually articulate their discomfort this precisely. It's the kind of thing a character in a play says, not a character in an Asimov story. The ending image—the empty tea cup in the sink, the fading light, the prefab lights coming on—is effective and appropriately understated. It doesn't over-explain. It was the officer's voice, the young one, saying: *Valid under the Mars Development Authority.* Then Arthur's own voice: *Which authority.* Then nothing. The recording ran on, silent, for a count of six seconds, and then stopped. "That's the whole recording," Arthur said. "You'll notice it's short." The older man's smile did not change. The older man was silent. The young officer looked at the table. "What do you want," the older man said. "I want three things," Arthur said. "Marta's paper voided, in writing, with a copy sent to her and a copy filed with the Authority. A guarantee in writing that no further paper will be placed on any of the four neighbouring claims, not just hers. And a statement, on the record, that the parcels on Marta's schedule are not contiguous with mine—which the survey proves—and that the western strip of my claim is not for sale to you or to any party acting on your behalf." "That's a lot." "It's less than I could ask." "You could ask for nothing," the older man said, "and get it. You understand that." "I do," Arthur said. "I'm asking anyway." The older man looked at him for a while. Then he looked at the young officer and gave a small nod, and the young officer left the room, and Arthur stood in the small room with the desk and the older man and did not sit down. --- He waited three hours. Around the fourth hour his wristcomm buzzed. It was the young officer, standing at the door of the prefab, holding out a folder. Arthur took the folder. He opened it. He read it twice. He read the schedule of parcels, which was attached as Annex A, and which he noticed had been slightly revised since his visit to Marta's—the parcels were now described as "non-contiguous to claim 2147/E" and "subject to future reconciliation." He read the reverse side. He read the fine print. His name was on the signature line. "The other documents would follow," the young officer said. "Upon signature." Arthur held the folder open and looked at the pages. He knew what this was. He had not known it precisely. He had known it the way he knew a machine was going to fail, from the small signs, the configuration, the way the papers had been ordered in the folder. If he signed, Marta was covered—probably, eventually—and he was not. If he didn't sign, Marta would lose her parcels and likely her claim, and he would lose his own in two years of filings, and the vein would still be extracted by someone. He read it a third time. The young officer waited. Arthur took the pen from the officer's hand and signed his name, and initialled the annexes, and dated it, and handed the folder back. Then he walked home. # Chapter 8: The Morning He woke early and lay still for a while, listening to the air system, and then he got up because there was no reason to stay in bed. His knee was bad. He worked it the way he always did, and it held him, and he stood. He made coffee from the real tin without thinking about whether it was the day for it. He drank it standing at the counter, looking west. The prefab was gone. The regolith where it had stood was disturbed in a rough rectangle, and the two tracks that had run out from it toward the Fletchers' and toward the ridge were still visible, but the box itself was not there, and there was no rover, and there was no sign that anyone had ever been there at all except the tracks and the patch of turned dirt and, he noticed, the marker stake at his western boundary, which someone had re-seated in its hole and straightened. He had not asked for that. He went outside and looked at the stake. It had been re-set cleanly, deeper than before. Whoever had done it had done it properly. He did not know what to make of this and after a while he stopped trying. He walked over to Marta's after breakfast. She was already up. She was in her small garden, tending the hydroponic tomatoes that Pedro had built, and she straightened when she saw him and waited. "Arthur." "Marta." "Have you had breakfast." "I have." "Come in anyway. I'll make tea." He went in. She made the tea, and set it down, and sat across from him, and did not speak for a while. Then she said: "The man came back last night." Arthur looked at his tea. "He said there'd been a mistake," Marta said. "In the paper. He said the document was misdrawn—that's the word he used, misdrawn—and that it would be voided, and that I'd get a copy. He said it in a friendly way. He was very patient. He said I'd done nothing wrong." "That's good." "He said it wasn't my fault." "That's good." "Arthur." He looked up at her. She was watching him with the directness she used when she wanted something true out of him, the same directness she had used in his kitchen with the jam jar in her hands. "What did you do," she said. He considered the question. He considered what to tell her and what not to. He could tell her that he'd signed a document she didn't need to know about. He could tell her that he'd made a trade, and that the trade was mostly a bad one, and that the part of it that mattered to her was the part that would probably hold. He could tell her all of this. It was her business, in a way; it was about her; it had been done partly on her behalf. But he thought of her standing in his kitchen with her hands shaking and the paper in them, and the way she had carried the jam jar home afterwards, and the way she had been embarrassed about it the next day, and he knew that whatever he said would become something she would carry. So he said: "I told them their paperwork was wrong." "That's all." "That's all." She looked at him for a long moment. He could see that she did not entirely believe him, and that she had decided not to press, and that the not-pressing was a thing she was doing for him and not for herself. He looked back at his tea. "Well," Marta said. "Then it's fixed." "It's fixed." She drank her tea. She talked about the tomatoes. She talked about a letter she had received from her oldest son, who wrote once a year and asked after her health in a way that suggested he had forgotten what her health had ever been, and she talked about a cousin on Earth who was ill, and she talked about the weather, which had been doing the same thing it had been doing for the last six weeks. Arthur listened. After an hour he got up and went home. --- He checked the reclaimer. It had held at its new temperature, slightly too high, within tolerance. He would order the exchanger. He would order it this week, probably, though he had said that before. He stood in the yard for a while with his hand on the housing, not really thinking, just touching it, the way a person touches a thing they have made work. In the afternoon he went out to the survey marker at the western edge of his claim. He walked at his usual pace and rested once, and when he reached the marker he stood beside it and looked out at the ridge and down toward where the prefab had been. Two hundred metres below him, the vein lay in the rock. He had been picturing it for three years and he could picture it now: the dark clean seam, running deep, running east-west, indifferent to any of it. Men had come from off-world to argue over it. A woman in a dark suit had sat at his table and drunk his tea and told him the truth about herself, which he had asked her to do, which she had done. A neighbour had signed a paper she didn't understand, and he had failed to go over and help her when he could have, and later he had signed a document that gave away more than he'd planned in order to cover it. None of it had touched the vein. The vein had been there for a billion years and would be there after he was gone, and whether he signed or refused, whether Antares took it or the corporations or the Federation or Mars itself, it would come out of the ground one day, and someone would accelerate some decay with it, and some other someone would be accelerated in turn, and that was the world. He stood at the marker for half an hour. The wind picked up and pushed dust across the ridge, and the dust kept going past him and past the ridge and out over the plain toward nothing in particular. After a while he stopped looking down and looked at the light instead, which was the particular late-afternoon colour Mars got when the sun was low and the dust was up, a dull orange that went on forever, that was terrible and ordinary and exactly what it had been his whole life. He walked back home. He locked the door. He did not turn on the light. He sat at his desk in the dark for a while, in the chair he had sat in the night the summons had come, in the chair he had sat in a hundred nights before that. Then he pulled the drawer open. He took out the sheet of paper he had been going to write on, the one with nothing on it, and the pen, and he set them in front of him. He opened the letters, the seventeen of them, and read them, one by one, in the dark, for the first time since he had started writing them. He read them all. Then he stacked them and put them back in the drawer, and he wrote one line on the sheet of paper—*Helen, I'm still here*—and folded it and put it in with the others, and closed the drawer. He made his dinner. He read a page of the manual. He went to bed, and his knee hurt, and he slept.

Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of science fiction writing that demonstrates genuine mastery of the Asimov-adjacent retrofuturist mode while also bringing something distinctly its own. Let me assess it carefully across the requested dimensions. CHARACTER: Arthur Neegan is one of the more convincing protagonists I've encountered in AI-generated fiction. His characterization is built almost entirely through behavior and habit rather than exposition: the stuck valve he keeps not fixing, the letters he writes but never sends, the way he takes his time getting up from under the lander because "taking your time was one of the few things no one could take from you." These details accumulate into a fully realized person — a man who has organized his emotional life around deferral and maintenance, who processes the world through machinery. Voss is also genuinely nuanced: her honesty is weaponized but also, the story suggests, partially sincere, and the detail about her daughter on Ceres is handled with real delicacy. Marta functions well as a secondary character, though she risks becoming purely instrumental to Arthur's arc. Chen is efficiently sketched and believable. DIALOGUE: The dialogue in Chapter 2 is the standout achievement. The exchange between Arthur and Voss is genuinely Asimovian in its rhythm — clipped, information-dense, with subtext running beneath every exchange. "I don't mind being outbid on facts. I do mind being outbid on framing" is an excellent line. The dialogue earns its place and reveals character while advancing plot. The later conversations maintain this quality, though they occasionally become slightly repetitive in structure (Voss explaining things, Arthur responding minimally). PACING: Chapters 3 and 4 represent a deliberate deceleration that is both the story's greatest strength and its most debatable choice. Chapter 4 in particular — "A Day" — is almost entirely composed of mundane tasks: fixing the reclaimer, walking, eating cold rations. This is a bold structural decision that pays off in establishing Arthur's interiority and the texture of his life, but it does risk losing readers who came for plot momentum. The story recovers in Chapters 5-7, though Chapter 7's resolution feels slightly rushed compared to the careful buildup. WORLD BUILDING: The Asimovian big-and-small-picture worldbuilding is handled with genuine skill. The Azra metal is introduced economically — we understand its significance without lengthy exposition. The corporate/diplomatic/settler political landscape is sketched through implication rather than infodump. The Mars setting feels lived-in: the ration cartridges, the reclaimer, the dust devils, the Covenant visible in the sky. This is retrofuturist SF done well. PLOT: The plot is coherent and follows the prompt faithfully. The "gambit" of the title — Arthur using his survey data and the recording to leverage the prefab operators — is satisfying, though the resolution in Chapter 7 is somewhat anticlimactic. Arthur signs a document that gives away his leverage, the prefab disappears, Marta's paper is voided. The mechanics are believable but the emotional stakes of the signing moment could have been developed further. The ending — "Helen, I'm still here" — is genuinely moving and well-earned. PROSE QUALITY: The prose is clean, controlled, and largely free of purple passages. The author has clearly internalized a Hemingwayesque restraint that suits the character. Occasional sentences achieve real beauty through understatement: "The planet was not beautiful from this distance. It looked like what it was: a cold, red, tired place." The metaphors are almost always earned. There are a few moments where the repetition of certain gestures (the quarter-turn of the cup, the knee, the drawer) becomes slightly mechanical rather than resonant, but this is a minor complaint. WEAKNESSES: The story's main weakness is that the central conflict — the Azra vein and its geopolitical implications — remains somewhat abstract. We're told it could "shift the balance of several things," but the larger stakes never quite materialize into felt danger. The story is more interested in Arthur's interior life than in the thriller mechanics the prompt suggests, which is a legitimate artistic choice but means the "political tug of war" element is underdeveloped. The Federation, the corporations, and the independence groups are mentioned but never embodied. Chen's role is intriguing but her affiliation and purpose remain opaque in ways that feel like setup for a continuation rather than satisfying ambiguity. The resolution in Chapter 7 — Arthur signing the NDA — is somewhat deflationary; the "gambit" of the title turns out to be a partial loss dressed as a partial win, which is realistic but may frustrate readers expecting a more decisive turn. UNEARNED TRANSFORMATIONS: The ending's emotional beat — Arthur finally writing to Helen — is the story's most significant character transformation. It is largely earned through the accumulation of detail about the letters and the drawer, though the connection between the external events and this internal shift could be made slightly more explicit. It works, but just barely. OVERALL: This is a genuinely impressive piece of writing that succeeds on most of its stated goals. It captures the Asimov aesthetic while bringing genuine literary sensibility to the character work. Its weaknesses are mostly those of ambition — it's more interested in interiority than plot mechanics, which is a defensible choice that leaves some of the prompt's thriller elements underdeveloped.
